## LETTER I.

->To the most Reverend and<-
->Distinguished Sir,<-

Time truly glides away so gradually and unexpectedly in its course that one can scarcely notice its paths. You act rightly, however, in rousing me from this lethargy and calling me forth toward the set goal of our endeavor. It would have been more fitting to prick me with spurs than to soothe me with some small gift; thus, with shame, I finally see how reckless and thoughtless a procrastinator <term>cunctator: "one who delays," often used in reference to the Roman general Fabius Cunctator, though here used self-deprecatingly</term> I have been. 

Not long ago, I received from our Most Merciful Lady Mother <note>original: "Clem: Dn. Matre nostrâ"; likely referring to a high-ranking patroness or noblewoman</note> that cleverly drawn page regarding the resurrection of the dead <note>original: "resurrectione mortuorum"</note> which you mention. I do not know, however, where it came from. I have for some time possessed the same thing in a smaller format and of the most perfect craftsmanship; so much so that unless the Author himself signs his name, another's might deservedly be substituted. "Diligence produced it" <note>original: "Diligentia faciebat"; possibly an artist's signature or a variation on the classical artist Apelles' motto</note>. The imitation is so elegantly deceptive that it presents to the eyes the blessed enduring here in eternal delights, while the damned truly suffer the most exquisite tortures of hell. 

I have not yet been able to see the works—of great skill, as they say—by your blind organ-builder <term>Organarii: a builder or player of organs</term>. However, I easily place my faith in you and in those things which we have heard from public report—that is, common rumor—and I marvel at the distribution and compensation of Nature <note>original: "Naturæ"</note>, who has abundantly restored to this man in other ways what she took from his eyes...

<vocab>Letter, resurrection of the dead, Organ-builders, Nature, procrastinator</vocab>

<summary>In this opening letter, the author apologizes for his delay in writing and discusses an exquisite artwork depicting the resurrection of the dead, as well as the remarkable talent of a blind organ-builder.</summary>
<keywords>correspondence, resurrection of the dead, art criticism, organ builder, philosophy of time, nature's compensation</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the first letter, which discussed the deceptive nature of artistic imitation and the mysteries of the natural world. It then transitions into a second letter, a formal greeting to Prince Rudolph August following his return home. The author of the first letter is revealed to be Anton Ulrich, a prominent member of the House of Brunswick.</meta>

...has taken away from the senses. Nature plays so freely among the elements, vines, fruits, trees, and beasts—why should she not also do so in man? Martin Delrio <note>original: "Martin. Delrio"; a Jesuit scholar (1551–1608) famous for his work on magic and the supernatural</note> reports, as others cite, that there is a certain kind of people known to the Spaniards whom they call *Zahuris* <term>Zahuris: individuals in Spanish folklore believed to possess the power to see things hidden underground, such as water, metals, or corpses</term>, which is to say, "Lynx-eyed." He says he saw such a boy in Madrid in years past who saw things hidden in the deepest bowels of the earth: veins of water and metals, treasures, and many other things. If this is true, I would wish that such a person had also been granted to you, who could have revealed those things which nature wished to lie hidden in your blind side <note>original: "cæco vestro latere"; likely a metaphorical reference to things unknown or perhaps a specific anatomical area being discussed in a lost portion of the text</note>. For we can only guess at those things by certain signs, but we are ignorant of the true cause of the matter. Farewell, and believe that those things which were taken from you by me as well, through this delay of time, are abundantly compensated by these words. *Wolfenbüttel* <note>original: "Guelpherbyti"; the Latin name for this city in Lower Saxony, the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note>, June 12, 1649.

<margin>
From my Lord Brother *Rudolph August*, because he returned home happily this week, you will have most many greetings for *Ferdinand Albert* and our *tutors* <term>efformatoribus: literally "those who form," referring to the governors or teachers responsible for the princes' education</term>, etc.
</margin>

->To Your Renown<-

->Most<-
->Devotedly<-

->*Anton Ulrich,*<-
->*Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg*<-

## LETTER II.

### To PRINCE RUDOLPH AUGUST.

->Most Illustrious and High Prince,<-
->Lord most Gracious by far,<-

Nothing could have been as pleasant for me to hear at this time as the news of your return home, safe and sound—a double joy [received] from your Most Serene Lord Father and your renowned brother

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on natural wonders and scientific curiosity to a formal celebratory letter addressed to Prince Anton Ulrich upon his return from a journey. It establishes the close relationship between the correspondent and the young prince, focusing on the virtues of home versus the "exotic inconveniences" of travel.</meta>

### THE YEAR 1649.

*To Anton Ulrich <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714) was the son of Duke August the Younger. He later became a prominent Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, a patron of the arts, and a famous novelist.</note>, I have received your news with rejoicing. There were indeed reasons for me to congratulate you when you departed from home, which I did not hide; but many more, and more compelling reasons for applauding your desired return have followed. I would rather you infer these for yourself, given your remarkable wisdom and accurate judgment, than for me to announce them openly. Nevertheless, I will not deny that while you were away for so long, I was never without some care and fear. In your companion Krams <note>original: "Kramio"; likely a reference to a tutor or a noble official who accompanied the prince on his "Grand Tour."</note>, a truly noble man, I had much confidence—next to the favor of* GOD *and the angelic vigils—but what does a most tender love not fear even in safe circumstances? What dangers does it not imagine for itself? Such is my love for you, joined with humble respect.*

*Therefore, I congratulate you from the heart, and I truly and sincerely rejoice for myself that you have returned to your own home, your own family, your own people, your own possessions, and to your very self—by which terms I wish to express both the embrace of your happiness and the mystery of my own feelings. For you see, hear, and possess everything at home that can be sought abroad, and which perhaps are not found elsewhere, nor anywhere else. O happy are you, while you have your Father, the solid foundation of future happiness. Your own land and fatherland will hold you; your people will love, cherish, and respect you. You yourself will adorn and increase your possessions, and you will belong to yourself with a sound mind in a vigorous and healthy body <note>original: "sanâ mente in viridi ac corpore sano"; an adaptation of the classical Roman ideal of "a sound mind in a sound body."</note>. Your wise intuition will suggest more to you than I can point out; and unless I am mistaken, the very comparison of your domestic happiness with exotic inconveniences will supply more reasons for my congratulation. Truly, I owe thanks to* GOD *the Preserver <note>original: "Sospitatori DEO"</note>, under whose shadow you completed this journey safe in mind and body, not without growth in judgment, actions, and studies. It will now be a pleasure to digest these things at home and to convert them into "juice and blood" <note>original: "in succum sanguinemque convertere"; a common early modern metaphor for fully internalizing and masterfully applying knowledge rather than just memorizing it.</note>, while your* Most Serene Lord Father <note>original: "Sereniss. D. Pater"; Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, known for his massive library and scholarly interests.</note> *according to his incredible prudence, sets forth other matters. In the meantime, unless it be unwelcome, return to my literary correspondence <term>literarium commercium: the formal exchange of letters and ideas between scholars and nobility, seen as a vital part of a prince's education.</term>, to which perhaps this* Little Book of Letters <note>original: "Libellus Epistolica"</note> *may incite you...*

<meta>catchword: stolica</meta>

<summary>A formal congratulatory letter to Prince Anton Ulrich upon his safe return home in 1649, emphasizing the superiority of domestic life and fatherly guidance over the perils of foreign travel. The author praises the prince's growth in character and intellect during his absence.</summary>

# LETTERS

...my collection of letters <note>original: "Epistolicus"; likely referring to the volume currently being read</note>, which is soon to be presented to you. When you see it, you will realize that what could have been a private treasure and a source of deep pleasure to me, I have not wished to withhold from the public glory and renown of your House. I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that you may continue to grow and excel for the sake of that House, and that you may fill the grace of your majestic body—which I behold in the portrait sent to me—with the beauty and harmony of your soul. Farewell, and be greeted along with your illustrious brothers; continue to look upon me with favor.

->To the Most Illustrious [Princes],<-
->their most humble servant,<-
Stuttgart, June 27, **Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.**
1649.

## LETTER III.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

Whether it has yet become known to you that I have now returned to my ancestral hearth from the lands of Cleves <note>original: "ex Clivensibus terris"; Cleves (Kleve) was a territory on the lower Rhine, then under the influence of the Elector of Brandenburg.</note>, I truly do not know. However, I judged it right that you should learn this from my own letters rather than those of others—all the more so since I can say this of myself to you (which others might not). For I do not wish you to be unaware that I have spent a quite happy year abroad. Most notably, I was treated with great honor and much favor by that most excellent Prince, the Elector of Brandenburg <note>Frederick William (1620–1688), known as the Great Elector.</note>, who is a mirror of virtue. Having returned to my native home, I have received the pinnacle of that happiness; for I found my parents and other kinsmen alive and still enjoying good health. Indeed, I have experienced my father’s spirit in all matters to such a degree that I almost doubt whether I should more admire his love or his care for me. I am well aware that I cannot offer sufficient praise to God and to such a parent for such great benefits, nor [adequately thank] you and the prayers of others...

<meta>catchword: ...others</meta>

<summary>Johann Valentin Andreae concludes a letter praising a young prince's character and portrait, followed by a new letter from a correspondent reporting a successful return from the court of the Elector of Brandenburg.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Valentin Andreae, Elector of Brandenburg, Cleves, Grand Tour, parental gratitude, 17th-century correspondence, Stuttgart</keywords>

# THE YEAR 1649.

...to which things I attribute <note>The OCR reads "cibus," but the context and Latin grammar strongly suggest "quibus" (to which things).</note> whatever happiness has come to me during this time; and so I confess myself to be bound to You for this. Added to this is that you wished to testify to your affection for me by sending that very recent book; just as all things that proceed from You are pleasing to me, so I say that this also was most pleasing to me. I did not want all these things to be hidden from You, whom I faithfully commend to the protection of GOD, and from whom I expect constant love. Farewell. Given at Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti"; the primary residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.</note> on the 19th day of June, in the year 1649.

->To your Reverend Dignity,<-
->**Most Respectfully,**<-
->*Rudolf August*<-
->Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg.<-

### LETTER IV.
### *To Prince RUDOLF AUGUST.*

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord most Gracious by far,<-

I had already joyfully heard from your Most Serene Father and your brother Anton Ulrich <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714) would later become a famous patron of the arts and a novelist.</note> that you had returned safe to your family, but it was a matter of greater joy to have the testimony of Your Hand. I eagerly kissed that letter, which serves as an indicator both of your health being well-maintained and of your favor toward me being everlasting; I have been flooded by this double joy from You. Furthermore, it was pleasant to read that you now understand what you owe to both your Father's love and his care, and that you bear with gratitude whatever good is present to you, and recognize how much you possess in him alone—which is the summary of your happiness. That you have furthermore taken my *Errone* <term>The "Wanderer" or "Vagabond"; Andreae often used this title to refer to his smaller published works or satirical dialogues.</term> into your trust and patronage is an addition to my joy. Thus I have received a letter clearly desired and delightful, for which I find nothing now with which to repay you,

<header>LETTERS</header>

...how warm is my prayer that these roots of Your virtue may grow into a beautiful and expansive tree of good fruit, which will one day most gloriously shade the entire Guelph <note>The House of Welf (Guelph) was the ancient and noble ruling dynasty of the Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel lands.</note> lineage. Andreas Brunner of the Society of Jesus expressed an example of this in the *Bavarian Guardian Watch* <note>original: *Excubiis Tutelaribus Bojaricis*, published in Munich by Cornelius Leysser, 1637; Brunner was a Jesuit historian.</note> with a robust style, well worth your reading, if you separate the wheat from the chaff according to your accurate judgment. If only there were someone who could depict and adorn Your Royal House with an equally skillful brush, for it will be inferior to no examples of heroic virtue. Farewell, Renowned Prince, and as you do openly, continue to favor

### LETTER V.

->Hearty greetings.<- <note>The original abbreviation "S. P." stands for *Salutem Plurimam*, a standard Latin greeting.</note>

I do not know, Reverend Sir, whether those things which you write were presented to your nostrils and which you so greatly praise, might also suit mine. For it is well known that we look more toward the cold northern pole, where those things that might soothe with a pleasant scent are not easily produced. Therefore, whatever spirit and fragrance can be in such things, you will better draw from elsewhere and from others who are more practiced and successful in tilling rougher soil and producing sweeter fruits; to these I gladly yield the palm <note>A traditional symbol of victory or superiority.</note> and all else. But now, from the garden to the shore. The *Seleniana Augustalia* <note>A title likely referring to a literary collection or festival honoring Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who used the pseudonym "Selenus."</note> (by which name, I think, you also designate our affairs) are now reaching the port

...you say. We hope you have had a Guide <note>original: *Gubernatorem*. This likely refers to a tutor or spiritual advisor overseeing their studies.</note> where perhaps they strayed, and that those things which were of no value were cast out by you; otherwise, a great tax must be paid to the more learned, who wish to stay far from literary matters because they are not cultivated by talent or refined by art. # LETTER VI.

## To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->Most Illustrious and High Prince,<-
->Most Gracious Lord.<-

While I am at Calw <note>Andreae’s residence in the Black Forest.</note>, I receive your letters, by which you testify to your affection for me and abundantly provide for those of your brothers <note>original: *D. D. Fratrum*, abbreviation for *Dominorum Fratrum*, the Lord Brothers.</note>. For this reason, I both owe and give you triple thanks—briefer indeed than you deserve, but the more sincere and devoted. Regarding the *Selenian Imperial Matters* <note>original: *Selenianis Augustalibus*. This refers to the works or the courtly achievements of the Prince's father, Augustus the Younger, who wrote under the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus."</note>, you need not fear they will be a disgrace to you, unless perhaps among savage and iron-hearted men, to whom vice is virtue and learning is infamy; it is better to despise such people than to listen to them. Indeed, I have acted rather so that it might be displayed in the sanctuary of good fame and the marketplace of German virtue, how a right and happy education and upbringing has been provided to you by the favor of God and the care of your Incomparable Father...

<header>LETTERS</header>

...and through the use of faithful and industrious tools, it has resulted that they <note>Likely referring to the young princes or their educational progress.</note> can be held up as an example to Illustrious families, by the highest merit. This [work], I believe, will present itself to you shortly; having already been sent from Ulm, it has undoubtedly reached Nuremberg, and I pray for its easy access to You and for your most merciful patronage. 

Truly, I recognize how much I owe to You, who have illuminated me with your August Selenian rays <note>original: *Selenianis radiis Vestris Augustalibus*. A play on the name of the boys' father, Duke Augustus the Younger, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus." Selenus refers to the Greek moon goddess, Selene.</note> while I lay hidden in obscurity. Since I easily understand that I cannot find anything to repay you with in my own narrow circumstances <note>Andreae often wrote of his struggles and limited resources while rebuilding the church and school system in Calw after the Thirty Years' War.</note>, I place whatever you decide about me entirely at your discretion. I am certain that you will demand no other price than the Sun itself demands for the light, heat, and vigor it bestows upon the earth; may Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, compensate this with far greater splendor. Farewell, along with your most Illustrious Lord Brothers, and continue to favor

->Your Most Illustrious Highnesses’<-
->most humble client at Calw, August 1st,<-
->In the year 1649, Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor.<-

*I subjoin a most dutiful greeting to your Guardians and Instructors.*

### LETTER VII.

->To the Very Reverend, Most Famous and Learned Man, Lord and Friend to be greatly honored,<-

I have clearly seen from your letters recently given to the most Noble Imhoff <note>The Imhoffs were a prominent patrician family in Nuremberg, often acting as intermediaries for mail and finances.</note> that you are already aware that the most Illustrious Prince, Lord Rudolph Augustus, has returned to his fatherland. Those things which you added there regarding our travels, and the various things you said in my praise, were pleasing enough—had I not known well that fame is as busy sometimes in detracting as it is often in exaggerating. But it is more certain than certainty itself that we [saw] many things in those foreign lands...

<header>THE YEAR 1649.</header>
<sig>A 5</sig>

...to have seen and heard many things that could have easily swayed a tender mind and swept it off course; such is the perversity of minds and the license of words in those regions <note>The "regions" likely refer to France or Italy, common destinations for a "Grand Tour," which were often viewed with moral suspicion by Lutheran tutors.</note>, that even one of a firmly established character might be deceived and subverted by them. But the shield of God protected our Rudolph Augustus <note>Prince Rudolph Augustus of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1627–1704).</note> against such arrows in some measure, so that they did not harm him entirely. I do not deny that he was exposed to them, and even occasionally wounded <note>Likely a metaphorical reference to being influenced by foreign customs or religious ideas.</note>, but I hope these things can be so cured that in the future he may learn to defend himself better against them: *for arrows foreseen hurt less.* <note>original: *tela enim prævisa minus nocent.* A common Latin proverb suggesting that being prepared for a temptation or danger diminishes its power.</note> May God now attend to your prayers and our efforts, so that all things may turn toward His glory and the safety of the Prince and the entire region. I commend you to His protection, and I ask you again and again to forgive my brevity. Farewell. Given at *Wolfenbüttel, July 10th, in the year 1649.*

->To Your Reverence,<-
->Your most observant and devoted<-
->servant,<-
->*Friedrich von Kramm.*<-

*given as a companion for the journey, I was greatly glad that he was very rightly provided for, so that he could not easily be harmed by foreign opinions or customs, with this vigilant guardian having been added; a fact which was further confirmed for me by the friendly testimony of the Nobleman Im Hof* <note>Likely a member of the prominent Imhoff patrician family of Nuremberg.</note> *concerning you. To this was added a third herald of your solid and truly German virtue, M. Flemming,* <note>original: "M. Flemmingius." Possibly a reference to the circle of the poet Paul Fleming or a related scholar.</note> *upon his return to us; so that one whom I previously esteemed, I now understand I must clearly look up to. I therefore congratulate the most Illustrious Prince, Lord Rudolph Augustus, on your watchfulness, through which—after the favor of GOD and the respect for his Serene Father—he returned to his own people safe and untouched by traps and arrows.* <note>The "arrows" (original: *telis*) continues the metaphor from the previous page regarding the moral dangers and temptations encountered during foreign travel.</note> *I rejoice for myself, who experience such a man persisting in love toward me, the likes of whom I have few to compare with. I truly pray to GOD from my soul that these cares and labors of yours—which I well know to be arduous and subject to envy—may not only turn out happily for the Welf lands* <note>original: "Guelphicis terris." The territories of the House of Welf (Brunswick-Lüneburg).</note> *and fulfill the expectation of the most Serene Master Augustus;* <note>Duke Augustus the Younger (1579–1666), a famous scholar and book collector.</note> *but further, that they may imbue and fortify the mind of your Illustrious Pupil with every kind of virtue. May they also bear and confer most abundantly upon you the reward and fruits of your faith and skill—not those which the Court is accustomed to give, but those which GOD, a clear conscience, and posterity promise. Farewell, Noble Governor,* <note>original: "Ephore." A title used here for a supervisor or tutor of a prince.</note> *and continue to love me, as you do of your own accord.*

<header>THE YEAR 1649.
LETTER IX.</header>

## TO THE THREE PRINCES,

### Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,
### My Most Merciful Lords by far,

I have happily learned from the letters of your Overseer <note>original: "Ephorus," a title for a high-ranking educational or religious supervisor.</note> to me and your Tutor <note>original: "Informator"</note> to my son, that the *Seleniana* <note>Works associated with their father, Duke Augustus, who wrote under the pseudonym Gustavus Selenus. Andreae suggests these books belong more to the princes than to him because of their family connection.</note>—more truly yours than mine—have already come into your hands. Your nobility, which I have observed to be joined with an unusual kindness, does not permit me to doubt that you received them with a serene countenance and an outstretched hand, even if you have not yet given a sign of it in your letters, which I used to receive more frequently in the past. 

The reason why my own letters did not accompany the books <note>original: "libellos," small books or pamphlets.</note> sent to you is that they were dispatched not from Stuttgart but from Ulm—where I saw to their binding—so that they would not travel the same path twice, but would go straight to you via Nuremberg. I would have gladly added more copies if the printer <note>original: "Typographus"</note> had allowed, from whom I received only forty—far too few for my crowd of friends, and already dispersed. 

Meanwhile, I do not hide the fact that I strongly desire your letters; and so that it may be clear how well I track the account of their delivery: you, Most Illustrious Prince Rudolph Augustus, gave your last on June 9th; Most Illustrious Prince Anton Ulric on July 12th; and Most Illustrious Prince Ferdinand Albert, more recently, on July 10th. But your renowned sister, Princess Sibylla Ursula, has—what is almost intolerable—remained silent since February 25th. 

If you should plead your more serious studies as an excuse (which I would not wish to hinder), I readily grant it, provided only that no disdain for me or weariness of writing has crept upon you—than which you could decree nothing more unkind toward me. Therefore, unless it be a burden, return to our literary correspondence—not one restricted to every single week, but free, and one which, through intervals of progress in virtue and learning...

### LETTER X.

->Heartiest Greetings. <note>original: "S. P." (Salutem Plurimam), a standard formal greeting.</note><-

I remember, Reverend and most Distinguished Sir, that I wrote to you about two months ago, but since I have received nothing from you in the meantime, I paused my writing for a little while. Now, however, by the command of our most Merciful <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Dn." (Dominus), a title of respect for a social superior or official.</note> Father, I take up the pen again; and lest that long-standing habit of ours should seem to be dissolved, I address you with these few words. I could easily guess that you had either gone traveling or were hindered by other more serious matters, and therefore I gladly hold you excused and free you from any unfavorable suspicion. If it pleases you, and if it can be done within the convenience of your affairs, please respond—at least very briefly—at the next opportunity, so that a more abundant subject for my letters may be born.

### LETTER XI.

->*To Prince ANTON ULRICH.*<-

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord most Gracious,<-

I praise the goads <note>In this context, "goads" refers to the Prince's gentle prodding or encouragement to write.</note> with which you have preceded me, even when I thought I had anticipated your needs. Indeed, I was somewhat afraid lest a weariness of our literary exchange might have crept over you, which I would not have wished to increase with my own persistent letters. Now, since I see the blame for this gap in time is turned back upon me, I will not allow my duty in writing to be found wanting. At this time, we are indeed sweating over the task of restoring the Churches and providing sufficient <term>Ministers</term> <note>original: "Miniſtris." Andreae was heavily involved in rebuilding the Lutheran church infrastructure after the devastation of the Thirty Years' War.</note> for them, and our occupations are both more numerous and more difficult; yet I cannot deny that something remains for you, whom I value so highly. I notice that even my "senile trifles" <note>original: "seniles meas nugas," a modest way of referring to his own writings in old age.</note> are tolerated by you, and therefore I freely profess that I owe you whatever may not be unpleasant. I will return, therefore, by the grace of God, to that place where you have not only liberally challenged me, but also generously led the way. My <term>small gifts</term> <note>original: "Xeniola," referring to tokens of friendship or small scholarly presents.</note>, which have been hindered on the road for almost a year now, have finally reached you, so I hear. If they delight your mind, they will bring me more pleasure than when they were with me, or when they were wandering astray on their journey. But now other things to you...

## LETTER XII.

->Greetings.<-

As you well prophesied, not long ago the *Seleniana Augustalia* <note>original: "Seleniana Augustalia." This refers to works related to Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus." The term may refer to a specific publication or a celebration of the Duke.</note> came to us through your initiative, which I have not yet been able to examine entirely. You hope for great things for our sake from this, yet our modesty hardly permits us to be led toward them. For we have sometimes written without due consideration, and since they were dispatched to you immediately, we could take away or change nothing thereafter. Meanwhile, there will be no need for another excuse; they have now seen the light, and if any darkness remains, the light of your authority, by which they have shone forth, will easily be able to dispel it among benevolent readers. Moreover, we have ascertained that you undertook these things for our benefit. For we see your spirit as clearly as those letters of yours which we behold with our eyes. Therefore, for this love with which you embrace us, we give the greatest thanks, and in turn we pledge and promise our readiness and zeal, by which we can illustrate your reputation. I have no news to write to you now,

## LETTER XIV.
### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT:

Most Illustrious and High Prince,
->My most merciful Lord,<-

I am very glad that the *Seleniana* <note>original: "Seleniana." This refers to the scholarly works or the library collection associated with Duke Augustus the Younger, who published under the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus."</note> are now in your hands and that they are not at all unwelcome; I boldly declare that much praise will come to you from them among fair judges of such matters. For who would not admire in them the quickness of wit, the refinement of style, and the tireless labor of the hand, which—by the will of your most Serene Father and the guidance of your tutors—have so fortunately set sail toward a good reputation? 

For my part, I easily see either envy or laughter prepared for me by unfair critics, who will either accuse me of ambition (because I wished to borrow light from you) or will mockingly criticize the dullness of my pen and the sterility of my subject matter—shortcomings which I freely acknowledge in myself. But it is well, because as long as I do not displease you, I care little for pleasing the many, let alone everyone. 

We have great hope for the solidifying of peace; let us pray to God as suppliants that no Fury <note>original: "Erynnis." In classical mythology, the Erinyes or Furies were deities of vengeance; Andreae uses the term here to represent any chaotic force that might disrupt the fragile peace following the Thirty Years' War.</note> may be able to undermine it. May He keep you safe and happy for the restoration of our country's prosperity. Greetings, [most] obser[vant]... <note>The text ends mid-word "observantissimus" as a catchword for the following page.</note>

### LETTER XIV.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished<-
->Lord Doctor,<- <note>addressed to Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), a prominent German theologian, social reformer, and author of the "Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz."</note>

It has been quite a while since I sent any letters to you; it is not because I have forgotten you, but rather because one or two opportunities slipped away unexpectedly, and because a certain journey intervened. Indeed, if I look at the letters which I once sent to you, and which you have now published <note>original: "publico jam donâsti." It was common for Andreae to publish his correspondence with the nobility to showcase their shared values and his own status.</note>, I could easily be deterred from writing by their insignificance. Your affection toward me and my brothers is certainly evident from this publication; however, my own imperfection and lack of skill is no less known to others. Regarding your affection, I congratulate myself; but of my own shortcomings, I am somewhat ashamed.

But however it may be, since you judged those letters worthy to be seen by others as well, I acquiesce to your judgment; and because of what you especially intended, I look up to and venerate you as the herald of our praises. Since this excites my love for you more and more, I will be no less diligent and eager in praising you and giving you thanks in return. Farewell. 

Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelph." Short for Guelphitbytum, the Latin name for Wolfenbüttel, the seat of the Duke's court.</note>, August 28, 1649.

->Your Reverence’s<-
->Most observant,<-
Rudolf August, Duke of 
Brunswick and Lüneburg. <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704) was the eldest son of Duke Augustus the Younger and later succeeded him as Duke. He was known for his piety and his significant expansion of the Herzog August Bibliothek.</note>

<header>THE YEAR 1649. LETTER XV.</header>

### To RUDOLF AUGUST. <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704) was the eldest son of Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg. He later succeeded his father as Duke.</note>

->Most Illustrious and Most Serene Prince,<-
->My Most Gracious Lord,<-

The day that was most mournful to me fifteen years ago (September 10, 1634)—when I fled from my home in Calw <note>original: "Calvâ meâ." Andreae was the superintendent in Calw when it was sacked and burned by imperial troops during the Thirty Years' War; he lost his library and many possessions.</note>, leaving behind all my substance which perished in fire shortly thereafter—you have now rendered auspicious for me with your most desired letters. What was once marked with a black pebble, you have caused to be marked with white. <note>original: "atro notatum calculo, candido ſignandum." This refers to the ancient Roman custom of marking lucky days with white stones and unlucky ones with black ones.</note> For since all my earthly hopes are placed and established in You, after your most Serene Father, I fully trust that the favor of the House of Guelph <note>The House of Guelph (Welf) was the ancient dynasty of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> toward the name of Andreae will endure. Whatever fortune awaits me hereafter, I most easily hope that under your auspices, your protection, and your support, it will be moderated and mitigated.

Even though I now deservedly refrain from demanding letters from you—as one who is preparing to take up the reins of the Guelph Steed <note>original: "Caballi Guelphici." A metaphorical reference to the White Horse of Brunswick, symbolizing the administration of the state.</note> and accustomed to submitting your shoulders to arduous business and devoting the harvest of your learning to the use of the state—nevertheless, I vehemently pray that you do not entirely exclude my own letters, should I send them to you from time to time, and that you might occasionally repay them with your most gracious ones. I promise myself this kindness from you following the example of your most praised Father, from whom I already possess 365 items as treasures—or rather, as "Gold-lamps." <note>original: "Chryſolampidibus." A Greek-derived term used by Andreae to describe the Duke's letters as shining lights or precious gifts.</note>

Furthermore, as to what you seem to fear—lest some cloud of malice should dim the light of your letters which shines in the *Selenian* works <note>original: "in Selenianis." This refers to the works published by Rudolf’s father, August the Younger, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus."</note>—I bid you be at ease; for the applause of good and learned men in the theater of good fame will most easily restrain the hissing and bites of the envious. For now, this illustrious Example has prevailed in our Universities and Courts, so that those who wish to strive for true glory have something to imi-

### LETTER XVI.

->Many greetings!<-

I now have two letters from you, Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir, and you contend with singular zeal that I should respond to them—specifically to those earlier ones which you intended to be written also to my most beloved brothers. However, matters will now be well, and my later letters will easily clear me of any charge of negligence or of an unusually arrogant disdain; I believe those letters defended my cause before you excellently and removed me entirely from such an opinion in your mind. Do not doubt the goodwill and favor with which we have embraced what you have sent to us so far. *For nothing is more pleasing to us than to rejoice in and enjoy not only the affection but also the monuments* <note>original: "monimentis." ## LETTER XVII.

### To Prince ANTHONY ULRICH.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord.<-

Just as your letter was most delightful to me, *so it grieved me that the time to respond with appropriate zeal was lacking. For while I withdrew into my* Selenianum <note>original: "Selenianum." A reference to the library or intellectual retreat of Duke August the Younger, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus."</note> *during the noise of these* Grape Harvests <note>original: "Vindemiorum." The autumn harvest was a busy and loud season in rural Germany.</note>*, it happened through an error of the* courier <term>Veredarius (a postal messenger or courier)</term> *that scarcely an hour passed between his arrival and departure. Yet, lest I should now seem to you a truant in the arena, having previously been the challenger, behold, I thought these few lines should be written, by which I might show myself grateful for your promptness and prove myself dutiful. Indeed, I understand that I should especially devote myself to this: to congratulate you from my heart on your* 17th Birthday, *which recently dawned happily on* October 4th, *and to pray for blessings heaped upon you by* GOD. *For you have laudably passed the previous year with the flowers of* Piety, *the sparks of integrity, and increases in your studies. ## LETTER XVIII.

->Hearty Greetings.<- <note>original: "S. P." abbreviating "Salutem Plurimam."</note>

**W**hat you requested from us gradually not long ago, you now have from me as well, and indeed from a more constrained hand <note>original: "manu... restrictiori." Likely implying a more concise or private communication compared to previous works.</note>. We have been a little slower, though not so as to shrink from this business entirely, but so that we might take a holiday for a while, after we submitted those things collected by our zeal and effort to the public examination to be weighed and judged. No matter by what name those things are regarded by other evaluators, we shall care little; rather, we will be intent on this: that those who so vehemently expect such sublime things from us may not at last be disappointed in their hope. This will surely be a work of much sweat, and to be completed by no other help than that of the Supreme Helper, whom we humbly implore that He might deign to be present with us and prosper all our endeavors. That peace has now been established by those reconcilers who met at Nuremberg <note>The Nuremberg Execution Diet (1649–1650) was a meeting intended to resolve the logistical and military issues remaining after the Peace of Westphalia.</note> in the name of this legation, we also have heard here.

### LETTER XIX.

->To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.<-

# Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
## Lord far most Clement.

I owe you very great thanks for returning not unwillingly to our literary exchange <note>original: "literarium commercium," referring to the formal and intellectual correspondence between scholars and nobility.</note>, the interruption of which you have excellently excused by recounting the reasons for your studies. Nor do I doubt that *your progress has both fulfilled the expectation of those observing you and has now made more certain the hope of the greatest future yields; to these I add my prayers and applause from the heart, and I promise myself nothing but the highest and most majestic things regarding you.* Concerning the peace, I have nothing to write, except that those who seriously pursue the cause of Christ rejoice less than others, because rarely are the joys of the world shared with Christ. *It appears that the beautiful pretext of religion vanishes amidst these celebrations, and the Kingdom of God is sought last, so that all other things might be cast away from us.* <note>A cynical inversion of Matthew 6:33 ("Seek first the Kingdom of God... and all these things shall be added unto you"). ## LETTER XX.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Renowned<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

I have looked into your letters given to my brother, Prince Rudolf August <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704) was the eldest son of Duke Augustus the Younger and a dedicated student of Andreae.</note>, and at the same time I noticed your desire to have my response. I do not indeed excuse my slowness, but I could not hide this from you: after I read my little letters—sent to you in place of a response and private conversation—published in public print, a certain blush <note>original: "rubor"; the Princess is expressing embarrassment or modesty at her private writings being made public without her explicit consent.</note> seemed to come over my mind. For learned men who publish something publicly do not lack many and great dangers, on account of the slippery approval of this most wicked age and the malicious desire for misinterpretation. You will therefore easily understand what I fear, and not without reason, since there is no formal edition, but only a certain "thinness" and weakness of mine that could defend me against that public sickness of the times. Forgive this modesty of mine, which indeed does not refuse to converse with you privately, but desires for many reasons to avoid public judgments. Farewell happily. Given at Wolfenbüttel <note>The primary residence of the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note>, October 2nd, in the year 1649.

->Graciously devoted<-
->to Your Reverence,<-
->Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg.<-

## LETTER XXI.

->To Princess Sibylla Ursula,<-
->Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,<-
->By far the most Clement Young Lady,<-

I have eagerly embraced and reverently kissed those most charming little letters with which you have again deigned to honor me. I admired in them both the elegance of your style and your penmanship <note>original: "picturæ"; literally "painting," here referring to the beauty of her calligraphy or the "word-picture" she creates</note>, as well as the modesty of your illustrious mind. Although such modesty greatly becomes your sex <note>In the 17th century, intellectual modesty was considered a primary virtue for noblewomen</note>, it was perhaps less required in this informal kind of writing. For although one could hardly fear that any rivalry could be provoked by the example of your learning, even if it were to face criticism, we should not expect it from even the most unfair interpreter; and if such a person dared, we would repel him by the sight of his own baseness.

For this is a unique characteristic of your August House: that with the clearest rays of Piety, Integrity, and Learning—a triad of virtues <note>original: "triga virtutum"; a "triga" is a three-horse chariot, suggesting these three virtues pull her character forward together</note> that is widely in exile elsewhere—it sharpens eagle-like eyes and dulls those of owls. It claims the former for the light and sends the latter back into the shadows. <note>Andreae uses the eagle as a symbol of those who can look directly at the "sun" of truth, while the "owls" represent the critics who are blinded by the light of virtue and prefer the darkness of malice.</note>

I wish indeed that you would learn from others rather than from me what praise and expectation of greater fame you have prepared for yourself among fair judges of affairs and literature, now that your letters have been exposed to the light. I say this so that I might not seem either to flatter you or to please myself—both of which are most foreign to my nature—so that you might be fired up to continue this noble exercise of your pen, or more easily despise the worthlessness of this most dissolute age. This age is surely unworthy of intercepting such extraordinary applause given to you among good and wise men.

Furthermore, because you have allowed yourself to be persuaded again and have blessed me with your most elegant letters, I give you the greatest thanks most humbly. I ask as earnestly as I can that you do not entirely abstain from writing hereafter, so that there may be intervals which...

I feel myself so withered by the brilliance of your genius and sinking into the depths of old age, that as often as I prepare to respond to your elegant writings, I blush entirely, and I am close to throwing away the pen; for what is more shameful, or even more dangerous, than Marsyas competing with Apollo and wishing to be flayed alive <note>original: "Marsyam cum Apolline contendere"—Marsyas was a satyr in Greek mythology who challenged the god Apollo to a musical contest; he lost and was skinned alive for his hubris</note>; or Thersites snarling at Achilles and perishing from a blow <note>original: "Thersitem ve Achilli obgannire"—Thersites was a common soldier in the Trojan War known for his insolent speech against leaders</note>. You will by no means stray from this path if you always look toward that North Star <term>Cynosuram: Literally the "dog’s tail" (the constellation Ursa Minor), used here metaphorically to mean a guiding principle or star</term>, your Most Serene Lord Father, toward whom all my prayers are directed. ->mind with secret counsels.<-

I would very much wish that your most illustrious brothers, with the respect of mind I owe them, as well as your guardians <term>Ephoros: A Greek term for overseers or tutors</term> and teachers, be greeted with all my zeal and service. Truly, I hope you strive so happily alongside their progress, with faithfulness and diligence, that fame may one day place you among the first. Farewell, grow greater than yourself every day, and look kindly upon me.

--- Page 30 ---
<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Johann Valentin Andreae. Having previously discussed his own sense of aging and the importance of the Princes' education, Andreae here transitions into a discussion of the significance of the Jubilee year—both the biblical precedent and the upcoming Protestant celebration of 1650—contrasting it with Catholic practices.</meta>

<page-num>29</page-num>
->THE YEAR 1649<-

God has bestowed distinguished favors, especially that of liberty, as a prelude to the future liberation through Christ, the memory of which Christians rightly cherish. The Pope, however, has derived his own not-insignificant and lucrative market fairs <note>original: "Nundinas"—Andreae uses this commercial term to satirize the Catholic sale of indulgences during Jubilee years</note> from this, and imposed them upon the Christian world. I truly remember, when I was already fourteen years old, in the Year of Salvation 1600, how jubilees resounded everywhere in our churches; and again in the year 1617, the memory of the Gospel reborn through the Blessed Luther was repeated—though for me it was less auspicious due to the dire fire at Vaihingen <note>A devastating fire destroyed much of the town of Vaihingen an der Enz in 1617, where Andreae was then serving as a superintendent</note>. I do not doubt in the least that the same will be consecrated by our people in the year 1650 with signs of Christian joy.

Oh, that those immunities and solemnities that once belonged to the Jubilee year might now revisit wretched Germany through the benefit of Peace <note>Referring to the Peace of Westphalia (1648) which ended the Thirty Years' War</note>: namely, release from servitude, return to encumbered properties, remission of debts, and the other things which Moses decreed from the mind of God in Leviticus 25. But these things must be left to the most just Arbiter of all things, whose role it is to decide concerning the salvation of His Church and the governance of the Earth; it is ours to obey and endure in Silence and Hope for better things.

Furthermore, for you, Most Illustrious Princes, I pray with a humble mind that this year, notable for the number fifty, may be auspicious, venerable, and favorable; so that whatever your Goskius <note>Martin Gosky (c. 1586–1659), a physician and poet at the court of Wolfenbüttel</note> (a man of greatest worth) has composed in the inscriptions of his "Arboretum" <term>Arboretum: Referring to Gosky's *Arbustum vel Arboretum Augusteum*, a massive commemorative work of poetry and engravings dedicated to Duke August</term> with an incredible variety of art and genius, may be conferred and consolidated by GOD, and may be brought forth for you into most abundant fruits under perpetual fame, and that both your Vows and those of all who wish you well may be most abundantly fulfilled. For he has so exhausted all the depths of Eloquence that I have nothing left to say after him, except for this one word: "SUCCESSFULLY," which I cry out.

->So may you grow, PRINCES, IN YEARS, IN SPIRIT, IN BODY, IN VIRTUE, IN ERUDITION,<-

# LETTER XXIX.
## To Prince ANTON ULRICH.

->I send my warmest greetings and a most happy omen<-
->of the approaching Jubilee,<- <note>original: *Iubilai*. A reference to the Holy Year or Jubilee of 1650, which was imminent at the time of writing in December 1649.</note>

### Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,
### My most Merciful Lord,

Such is the sweetness of your letters that they draw even me, though I am most occupied with the Christmas season <note>original: *Natalitiis Christi*. The celebration of the birth of Christ.</note>, and demand my turn to respond. While I perform this duty in haste, I ask for your most noble indulgence for my somewhat neglected writing. However, I strongly praise the kindness of your nature, through which you reflect the spirit of our Emmanuel <note>original: *Immanuelis*. A Hebrew name for Christ meaning "God with us."</note>; He who was sent down from heaven chose to dwell among us on the earth, and desired to find His delights in us—indeed, from Himself for us—and even went so far as to redeem and claim us for Himself with His own blood. Thus, illustrious souls do not consider it a burden to converse humanely with those of lower station, and even with their own subjects; this is a certain sign of a great-hearted and heroic spirit, and an omen of the prosperity that will overflow into the public good. Such men are called the "Love and Delight of Mankind," whereas those small-souled men who hide themselves away in pride and terrify others from without with their "rattles" <note>original: *crepitacula*. This likely refers to the empty, noisy displays of power or vanity used by arrogant rulers.</note> are hated by all and are known as the scourges of the people.

Continue, most kind Prince, with this genuine ornament of your August House; you shall be all the greater before God and men the more you are humble in your own eyes—yet without any dejection of spirit. I love the French language <note>original: *Gallicum idioma*. At this time, French was becoming the primary language of European diplomacy and high culture.</note> very much, especially if I might hear it from you, whom it is profitable to imbue with various tongues. I eagerly await the gift <note>original: *Munus*. Could refer to a literary work or a physical object.</note> produced by your own artistic hand, as I am most eager for the growth of your virtue and well-being, which may Christ bring forth, increase, and consolidate. Farewell, Renowned Prince, with your most illustrious...

### LETTER XXX.

->To the Very Reverend Lord<-
->Doctor,<-

I have duly received your reply, which is full of remarkable affection for me and distinguished by your many pious good wishes. Because you say that your old age <note>original: *senium*. Andreae was 63 at the time, which was considered advanced age in the 17th century.</note> and ill health are soothed by my "little letters," and since you demand the response owed to you, I certainly ought not to fail this desire of yours. However, I am well aware how little elegance or solace can be drawn from my letters, unless your pious kindness and benevolence are accustomed to grant them some weight despite their slightness. Since, therefore, I know you to be a most kind interpreter, I gladly send back this brief response, together with a wish for a happy New Year—one that arrives and returns according to your own prayers. # LETTERS OF THE YEAR 1650

## LETTER XXXI.

### To the Lady Sibylla Ursula.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,<-
->Most Gracious Lady.<-

I owe a great deal both to Your Highness and to that courtesy of yours, for descending to read my brief notes <note>original: *literulas*, a diminutive form implying humility regarding his own writing.</note>; and for the fact that you respond to them most kindly, adding a prayer which, because it proceeds from a pious heart, I do not think will be in vain. Indeed, how much it concerns our affairs to have God favorable and appeased—lest He withdraw that charming face of Peace He showed us this past year <note>A reference to the implementation of the Peace of Westphalia, which ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648/1649.</note> from this present one—no one fails to understand who looks into the arts and machinations of those who seek infamous and perilous profit from public harm, or rather, from the ruin of lands and the slaughter of men. On this account, the lot of the Church is very much to be pitied; for while for others, under the guise of Peace, matters have flourished considerably, she alone has felt no respite. She has been forced to live on her own vital juices as before, in the manner of tortoises or zoophytes <note>original: *Zoophytarum*. In the 17th century, these were organisms like corals or sea-anemones thought to be intermediate between plants and animals; Andreae uses them as a metaphor for a Church barely surviving on its own internal resources.</note>, currently serving as the sustenance for her own household, and soon—if war should return (which God forbid)—to be the prey of those lying in wait outside. Let us therefore join our prayers and entreat the favorable Deity that, with harmful counsels dispelled and fraudulent machinations overturned, a solid peace may be established for our altars and hearths <note>original: *aris, focisque*, a classical idiom referring to the most sacred and domestic foundations of society.</note>—a peace which may stabilize the Christian faith, restore bloom to the lands, assert the glory of the Arts and literature, and fix a perpetual seat for all virtues. To Your Highness, indeed, Most Illustrious Princess, I give immense thanks for your most delightful letters, and that this [kindness...]

## LETTER XXXIII.

->Reverend and Most Illustrious Sir,<-

Your goodwill joins us to You in such a way that it is not without merit that we now bestow our prayers upon You alone. I, among the others, should have done this promptly, as I was the first to receive Your letters this year. My studies are very meager; nevertheless, a great heap is added to them from time to time by Your recommendation, so that I do not know what I ought to return to You for such great love toward me. ### AND ANTON ULRICH.

->Most Serene Princes,<-
->Most Honored Lords,<-

The favor I received from your Highnesses, in making me aware of your desire regarding foreign languages, has moved me to come to you with this letter. I pray your Highnesses not to devote yourselves so much to French that Italian becomes neglected; both are the most beautiful daughters of the Latin tongue, yet the Tuscan tongue <note>Tuscan (Toscana) refers to the dialect of Florence and surrounding areas, which was considered the "purest" form of Italian and the standard for literature and diplomacy</note> possesses a certain majesty above all others, no less than the sun above the lesser lights. Its language is more polished, its phrasing more beautiful, its terms sweeter, and its spelling easier. If we consider the books written in it, we find rare concepts, marvelous subject matter, and an extraordinary, sublime way of writing, scattered with "flowers" <note>original: "isparso di fiori" — a common rhetorical metaphor referring to elegant ornaments of speech and poetic flourishes</note> that delight every virtuous person. I do not doubt that your Highnesses have heard Italy spoken of many times, and that just as she was once the Queen of the World in the art of making war, so she remains even now in the excellence of discourse. I, who profess to be impartial in every matter, and certainly in this one, find that to gather the fruits that come from such study, no effort should be spared; and that for Princes who desire to be eminent above other men, in virtue as well as in birth, it is fitting to learn something so beneficial. May your Highnesses pardon my boldness, which springs from the deep desire I have to see your Highnesses filled with the happiness that

### LETTER XXXVIII.

->Most Serene Lords,<-

With the flower of my age having passed, my vigor has gone with it, and with that vigor, the desire to persist and compete with Lords who are entirely unequal to me; nevertheless, the challenge that your Highnesses have sent me has awakened all my strength. Seeing that a single language was not enough to defend myself from French steel (with which I confess your Highnesses are very skilled), I have opposed the French with Italian. But as both are too soft, I thought they would need help. For that reason, Castilian <note>original: "la Castellana" — Spanish, specifically the dialect of Castile which became the standard for the kingdom</note> goes there now, which by being more masculine will serve me as sword and buckler, and end the dispute. This language, My Lords, is the most honored, the most grave, and the least frivolous bastard <note>The author refers to Spanish as a "bastard" daughter of Latin, a common way of describing Romance languages at the time</note> that exists in the world. And although the Moors—who through the Treachery of Count Julian <note>A legendary figure who supposedly betrayed the Visigothic Kingdom, allowing the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in 711 AD</note> won in eight months what they possessed in Spain for more than seven hundred years—introduced many Arabic words into it, nevertheless it seems to me worthy of your Highnesses' embrace. Do it the favor of loving it well, of practicing with it, and knowing its perfections, give it a welcome in the chamber of your wits. May God protect your Highnesses as only He can, and give you the years of life and the blessings of heaven that are desired for you by

->Of your Highnesses,<-
In Stuttgart, 27 
February 1650.
->The very humble servant,<-
->Johann Valentin Andreae.<-

### LETTER XXXIX.

#### To PRINCE FERDINAND ALBRECHT.

->**Most Illustrious and Serene Prince,**<-
->**My most Gracious Lord,**<-

Since I had written to your Illustrious brothers in the Spanish tongue, I thought I should also add a letter to you, so that you might not find my duty toward you lacking. However, I have chosen to write in Latin, so as not to weary you with exotic languages before you have firmly set foot in the Latin language, which is the Mother and Queen of all others. For although I judge nothing to be inaccessible to your intellect, nevertheless, in the process of learning languages, I have found that a mixture or confusion of tongues hinders progress more than it helps, and it greatly fatigues the memory. Furthermore, your age does not yet permit you to spread your efforts too thin. Since you are already occupied with the study of letters as well as the precepts of piety and the best of morals, those things which seem to pertain to ornament rather than the foundation of your most noble character and high birth must be postponed. Your <term>Ephorus</term> <note>original: "Ephorus" — a Greek term for an overseer or head tutor responsible for a prince's education</note> and your <term>Informator</term> <note>original: "Informator" — a private instructor or teacher who "forms" the mind of the student</note> will explain all these things to you more correctly; indeed, they will provide them through their faithful and successful work. I now ask one thing: that you greet your most illustrious Mother, that incomparable gem of Divine Virtue, on my behalf as humbly as possible, and offer her my prayers. Live happily and gloriously, and as the years pass, fulfill and exceed our hopes for you. Farewell, and look upon me with favor.

->To your Illustrious Serenity,<-

Stuttgart, 27 February ->Your most humble client,<-
The year 1650. ->Johann Valentin Andreae.<-

## LETTER XL.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Renowned<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

Your prayers for a happy beginning to this Jubilee, as well as for the final return of a firm and long-awaited Peace, I have indeed perceived from your letters—which are full of various kindnesses and a most favorable affection toward me. To these pious prayers of yours, I not without reason join my own lamentation. May God, the Thrice-Greatest and Best, grant firm strength to our common prayers and guide the minds of those in whose hands the Christian world groans, lest they wish to call it "peace" when they have created a wasteland everywhere. <note>original: "ne pacem velint illud appellare, cùm solitudinem ubiq; fecerint" — Sibylla Ursula here adapts a famous line from the Roman historian Tacitus: "They make a desert and call it peace." It is a scathing critique of the state of Germany after the Thirty Years' War.</note> We seem to have lost the true names of things; for we have "Peace" and "aid" in name, yet meanwhile we are oppressed by the miseries of war and various ruins. I wished to fulfill the debt of a brief response, since you require it, according to my meager ability; and I commit us all, and our common fatherland, from the heart to Divine protection. Farewell. At Wolfenbüttel, the 18th day of February, the year 1650.

->To your Reverence<-
->studiously devoted,<-
->Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg.<- <note>original: "D. B. & L." — Ducissa Brunsvicensis et Luneburgensis</note>

I know that there is a very great difference in character between those who have devoted their minds to the noble arts and those who distance themselves from them as much as possible. The latter only exercise their bodies, unaware that whatever elevates the soul also benefits the body. But the former [exercise] the intellect, through which they hope to lead a longer-lasting life. Nor are they mistaken, since this is the only thing that grants eternity and immortality to its cultivators.

About several days ago, the Most Serene Elector of Brandenburg <note>Frederick William (1620–1688), known as the "Great Elector."</note> departed from here again with his courtly entourage <note>original: "grege suo aulico" — literally "his courtly flock"</note>; as we received them modestly, so we sent them away with honor. He is still staying in the Bishopric of Halberstadt. May you fare well with your family and according to your heart's desire.

->To Your Renown,<-

Wolfenbüttel, March 5, <margin>Your most devoted,</margin>
1650. <margin>Ferdinandus Albertus, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg.</margin> <note>Ferdinand Albert (1636–1687) was the son of Duke August the Younger and a polymath who later founded the library at Bevern.</note>

### LETTER XLV.

->Most Reverend Lord Doctor,<-
->Most Worthy Abbot,<-

In the absence of my most dear brother, who is now staying with the Most Serene Elector of Brandenburg <note>Frederick William (1620–1688), known as the Great Elector.</note> in these neighboring parts, I nonetheless wished to respond to Your Reverence’s letter in that same language in which you were pleased to write to us. The more Your Reverence recommends the Italian language, the more I shall be eager and diligent to learn it perfectly, having already made a beginning this year. I do not doubt that diligent practice will make easy and light that which without it is very difficult; just as one can hope for a successful outcome in those matters where wise and mature counsel leads the way. Concerning languages, I am reminded of what is found in the works of Lansius <note>Thomas Lansius (1577–1657) was a celebrated professor at the University of Tübingen, known for his "Consultatio" on the dignity of nations.</note>, a most celebrated man: That one should speak to God in Spanish for its majesty; to Princes in Italian for its gravi... <note>original: "per la gra-" / "vita". The sentence refers to the famous linguistic proverb often attributed to Emperor Charles V, suggesting Italian is the language of courtly gravity or grace.</note>

<page-num>54</page-num>
<header>LETTERS</header>

The Kalends of April <note>original: "Kal. April."; April 1st.</note> were shrouded in black for us by the death of Dorothea Amalia, a most charming girl of seven years. <note>Dorothea Amalia (1643–1650) was a daughter of Duke Eberhard III of Württemberg; her death was a significant loss at the court where Andreae served.</note> Her passing was sudden, occurring alongside the illness of two of her sisters who, only a little while before, had been healthy and well. This has utterly stunned and nearly cast us down. While the sisters have struggled through their illness as best they can, we go today to perform the funeral rites for Dorothea. I serve as the administrator of these sacred laments <note>original: "threnorum sacrorum"</note> now, just as I was formerly the administrator of joys; I trust this may serve as my plea or excuse for the brevity of this letter to you.

Truly, however, your letters have delighted me wonderfully: both yours, Prince Anton Ulrich, written in the Italian tongue, and yours, Prince Ferdinand Albrecht, written in most polished Latin. These letters have taught me that you lack neither the spirit nor the natural talent for such studies, and that you do not lack suitable guides <note>original: "manuductores"</note> for foreign languages. Already, some fruits of this labor are showing. These results show me that you have transitioned to these languages not by some rushed path, but by a thoroughly mastered one. I congratulate you greatly on this wise method employed by your tutors <note>original: "Informatorum"</note>, and I predict most happy successes for you.

Furthermore, I offer the thanks I both owe and am able to give for your most kind congratulations regarding the change of my seat and station <note>referring to his promotion to Prelate of Adelberg and his move from Stuttgart</note> which is soon to occur. I shall be all the happier if, from this new location—which is only an hour and a half away from Tübingen—I might one day be permitted to look upon you in person and applaud you. I hope to see you in that *Athenaeum* <note>The University of Tübingen, often referred to by scholars as an "Athenaeum" or temple of learning.</note> renewing and doubling the same examples of admirable genius that your most serene father <note>Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1579–1666), a famous bibliophile and scholar.</note> once left behind him in the Temple of Eternal Memory. I pray to God Most High that this may come to pass. In the meantime, I shall sustain the duties of my role with my aging shoulders, by the favor of the Divine, until either a long-desired discharge <note>original: "rudis"; the wooden sword given to a gladiator upon his honorable retirement.</note> receives me, or a blessed death liberates and absolves me. May Christ lead you, in your flowering youth, more and more toward the summit of honor and fame. Farewell, and look upon me with favor.

->To your Most Illustrious Highnesses,<-
->Stuttgart, April 3rd, [1651]. Your most humble client,<-
->Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Sacred Theology.<-

*Very Reverend Sir Doctor,*

->Deserving Abbot,<-

Even though knowledge of the Spanish language has not yet fully reached me, I have nevertheless wished to express, with these few lines, the desire I have to master it in time. It is not reasonable that many languages be learned together at the same time, because they can produce nothing but confusion and mixing; however, because Your Mercy <note>original: "V. M." / "Vuestra Merced," a formal address used here for Johann Valentin Andreae.</note> has been pleased to give me the "spurs" <note>An idiom for providing encouragement or incentive.</note> even in this exercise, I kiss your hands <note>A traditional Spanish formal closing of respect: "beso las manos."</note> most warmly, recognizing that you take great care in our progress. It is true that this language is owed its own praise, and it can be placed before many others in Europe, as one may travel with it through a great part of this world, and an infinite part of that other world <note>Refers to the Spanish Americas and the global reach of the Spanish Empire.</note>; and even if all these things were lacking, there would be reason enough to call it Spanish, for it is the tongue spoken by the Lords of the World. <note>original: "Sennores del mũdo"; a reference to the Spanish Habsburgs, who then ruled a vast global empire.</note> There is no doubt that many fine authors are to be found in that language, but we shall extract the honey from them only after we have laid a good foundation in it. May God grant the increase of our studies, and keep Your Mercy, giving you much health.

<columns>2</columns>
Wolfenbüttel, the 1st
of April, in the year
1650.

->Of Your Mercy,<-

Very affectionate
friend

Anton Ulrich. <note>Prince Anton Ulrich of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1633–1714), later a famous patron of the arts and novelist.</note>

## LETTER XLIX.

### *To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished*
### *Lord Doctor,*

I have duly received your reply, which is both full of various flowers of elegance and at the same time brings news of the rest you have found. Just as your joy makes me a participant in it, so I wish that joy to be both long-lasting and most pleasant for you. *This is the true glory of a retired man: to finally behold the GODDESS of holy quiet coming into his arms—if one may be permitted to speak so.* <note>original: "Vera hæc est emeriti gloria, aspicere tandem in ulnas venientem sanctæ quietis, si ita loqui liceat, DEAM." This personifies "Quiet" or "Rest" as a divine figure.</note> A certain courtier once said that he had indeed been of many years, but had only lived seven years, indicating the seven-year period in which he had lived as a private citizen in the countryside. <note>An allusion to the Roman prefect Similis, who retired under Emperor Hadrian and claimed his years of retirement were his only true years of "living."</note> *Yet I believe that, because of your tireless love of work, you will find business even in leisure itself.* I heartily pray for the untiring vigor of your old age and the desired enjoyment of this peace in the monastery. <note>Johann Valentin Andreae had recently retired to the Abbey of Bebenhausen.</note> *Farewell happily. Given at Wolfenbüttel, April 2, in the year 1650.*

->*To Your Reverence*<-
->*Devotedly attached,*<-
->*Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg*<-

<meta>This page continues Letter L, a response from Johann Valentin Andreae to Prince Anton Ulrich of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, advising him on his linguistic studies. The previous page established the beginning of this address.</meta>

<page-num>57</page-num>
<header>THE YEAR 1650</header>

*I believe one must be entirely cautious at this time and age, as nothing is more certain to confuse the intellect than such a mixture.* <note>Andreae is advising the young Prince on the dangers of learning too many languages simultaneously without a clear plan.</note> *You are most correctly beginning with the French language; since it possesses no small difficulty in both reading and pronunciation, and departs further from its Mother, the Latin tongue, it renders the subsequent languages easier and more pleasant. In my opinion, Italian should follow closely behind, upon which Spanish should finally be superimposed. I would leave the English language to your own discretion, as it is something of a hybrid and lacks vigor.* <note>original: "Anglicam ut spuriam & mollem." In the 17th century, English was often viewed by continental scholars as an inconsistent "bastard" language compared to the structured Romance tongues.</note> *But if one were permitted to add Slavonic, he would finally be admitted into the commerce of almost the entire world.* <note>At this time, "Slavonic" referred broadly to the Slavic languages of Eastern Europe and Russia.</note> *They say that Joseph Scaliger was the one man found who mastered the languages of nearly the entire globe, and before him, Guillaume Postel, though the learned may judge him.* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609) was a renowned polyglot; Guillaume Postel (1510–1581) was a famous, if controversial, French linguist and mystic.</note> *I return to the Spanish language, which you rightly called not only the interpreter of this and the other world* <note>Referring to the Spanish Empire's reach into the "New World" of the Americas.</note> *but truly a Prince and a royal language, whose majesty hardly any other tongue can explain.* **GOD** *grant to you that, through learned progress and the increase of your years, you may reach that point where you may discern for yourself what is to your advantage and honor, and most happily obtain those things which make a Prince Pious, wise, prudent, and brave, and crown him with the fame of eternity. Farewell and favor me.*

->*To Your Illustrious Highness,*<-

## LETTER 51.

->To Princess Sibylla Ursula.<-
<note>Sibylla Ursula (1629–1671) was the daughter of August the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. She was a highly educated woman, a writer, and a translator who maintained a long correspondence with Andreae.</note>

->**Most Illustrious and High Princess,**<-
->**Most Gracious Lady.**<-

I owe you great thanks for your pious congratulations regarding the rest I have long desired and which has finally been granted to me; but in return, in this flower of your youth, I pray from my heart for a drive toward everything illustrious and praiseworthy, and a most happy encounter with the very peak of virtue and piety. You rightly distinguish between rest and idleness; for the former relaxes a weary mind, while the latter dissolves it and makes it sluggish, which would be unbecoming even for an old man on the brink of the grave. <note>original: "capsularem senem." Literally a "chest-bound" old man, referring to someone so frail they are kept like an heirloom in a box, or perhaps a reference to an old man carrying a book-box.</note> I shall not lack for something to move in this rest—and would that I might remove the obstacles before me! For who does not know what evils Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war; Andreae is referring to the devastating aftermath of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).</note> has left in her wake? To overturn these evils, there is need of a Hercules rather than a weary old man. Therefore, I pant instead toward that Center of Rest, God, from whom I shall not be moved for eternity. I write these things in haste, while I pack my bags and prepare my departure from here and my entry into my Hermitage; <note>original: "Eremum." Andreae refers to his retirement to Adelberg, which he treated as a spiritual retreat or "wilderness" away from the chaos of the court.</note> so do not wonder if these lines are unpolished or rushed. Farewell, most flourishing Princess, together with your most illustrious sisters, and look kindly upon

->Your Most Illustrious Highness’s<-
Stuttgart, 17 April 1650.
->Most humble servant,<-
->**Johann Valentin Andreae,**<-
->**Doctor of Theology.**<-

## 52.

### *The Taulerian Alphabet.*
<note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) was a famous German Dominican mystic. Andreae frequently adapted medieval mystical teachings for his 17th-century Lutheran audience.</note>

1. Seek the rule of love from Christ.
2. Take care to be freed from yourself.
3. Trust yourself entirely to God.
4. Seek where you may remain eternally.

5. Do not demand what is yours <note>original: "Tuum." Referring to one's rights, property, or desires.</note> outside of God—neither here, nor there, nor from any creature or nature.
6. Wait for and carry out the will of God.
7. Submit your own will to the Divine.

20. Forgive those who wrong you in good faith.
21. Neither judge nor condemn anyone.
22. Do not trust in your own reason or your own knowledge.
23. Set Christ before you as your teacher and your example.
24. Bear all injuries with patience and constancy.
