### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->My Lord, by far most Clement.<-

Having finished with the alternating joys and sorrows of Stuttgart <note>original: "Studtgardianis"</note>, I have withdrawn here to my wilderness <note>original: "eremum meum" — likely referring to a place of quiet retreat or his residence in Bebenhausen where he sought rest from court life</note>, where I do not sit idle, but have other work to do. For while I purge the stable of cowls <note>original: "Cucullionum stabulum" — a satirical reference to cleansing or reforming ecclesiastical or monastic institutions of corruption</note> of the filth that has accumulated for nearly sixteen years, and lay the foundations of a literary school <term>Gymnasium literarium: a classical secondary school focusing on the humanities and Latin</term>, and devote myself to civilizing the people who have been overwhelmed <note>likely referring to the social and moral collapse following the Thirty Years' War</note>, I see that little remains for me, even for honorable leisure. Yet I believe I owe nothing more urgently than a response to your most charming letters, with which you refreshed me amidst the stench of this cleaning-out. But another cause also prompts me: namely your 15th birthday <note>original: "Natalis Tuus XV."</note>, which will happily dawn for you on the 22nd of this month of May, when all things are in bloom; I congratulate you with a humble spirit and pray for every blessing.

And since, by Christ’s favor, you were recently admitted to the sacred Christian assembly <term>synaxin: from the Greek for "gathering," here referring to the Prince's first participation in the Holy Communion</term>, being newly grafted into the Body of Christendom, chosen among the citizens of the divine Kingdom, and made a participant in the Communion of Saints, I do not doubt that you understand that the faith you have confessed with your mouth must hereafter be testified to more and more by your deeds. Thus you must strive so that, amidst the growth of illustrious virtues and literary progress, Piety and innocence of character may shine forth. By these means, the contagion of evils and that harmful, deceitful flattery—a seductive plague to noble souls—may be driven far away through your vigilance, and those who rightly advise and even correct you may be granted their proper freedom and a happy outcome under your noble obedience. Since the guidance of your most Serene Lord Father, the direction of your Overseer <term>Ephori: a high-ranking church or educational supervisor</term>, and the precepts of your tutor <note>original: "informatoris"</note> provide these things to you in abundance, and the very...

## LETTER LVII.

### To Prince RUDOLF AUGUST.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**My Lord, by far most Clement.**<-

I would certainly refrain from writing letters to you, and would not at all disturb either your serious studies for the Commonwealth <note>original: "Rempublicam"</note> or your illustrious exercises, unless I feared that if I contended with you in too long a silence, I might seem either to think less highly of that former grace and kindness toward me, or to hold your letters—so highly valued by me—in neglect, or finally, to dread some disdain from you. Regarding the latter, the example of your Serene Father, which has now been passed down to you, does not allow for such a fear. My great longing for your letters will easily excuse the former. As for the middle point <note>neglecting the letters</note>, it could not be committed by me without a crime, from which I confidently believe I can be absolved, with you yourself as my judge. It remains, therefore, that I approach you more sparingly hereafter, as it is necessary for a pause to be given to the weary Atlas, so that a new Hercules may submit his shoulders to the world of the Commonwealth <note>Andreae uses the myth of Atlas and Hercules to describe the transfer of the heavy "burden" of ruling the state from the aging Duke August (Atlas) to his son Rudolf August (Hercules)</note>; to you, sometimes, if by chance there is leisure,

### LETTER LVIII.

-> Heartiest Greetings <note>original: "S. P.", an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam*, a standard formal greeting</note> <-

Perhaps you are already waiting, *Reverend and Most Famous Man*, for what I am about to say and how I will respond to your last letter, which provided me with your faithful advice regarding the various languages of other nations. I will do so now, and indeed very briefly, since I must prepare myself for the marriage solemnities which will be carried out here today. In the matter of foreign tongues, which must be learned in addition to our domestic one, I will do nothing too hastily, lest by gathering them together inconsiderately, a disturbance and confusion of the mind should follow. What you say is proper and closer to anyone <note>referring to the mother tongue</note>, I gladly acknowledge; yet regarding the majesty of the Spanish language, I add this: if it is suited to the customs of those people as the French <note>original: "Galli"</note> depict them, it will have more wind <note>In this context, meaning vanity or "hot air"</note> than virtue. *That of the English is not only bastardized and soft, but...*

### LETTER LIX.
### To Prince ANTON ULRICH.

-> Most Illustrious and High-born Prince, <-
-> Most Gracious Lord, <-

Since you write to me so frequently, and even while occupied with the solemnities of a wedding <note>likely the wedding of the Prince’s sister, Sibylle Ursula, or a related court celebration</note> you devote some time and effort to me—thereby snatching the palm <note>a metaphor for winning a prize or being the most diligent</note>, as it were, from your brothers—I acknowledge both the agility of your intellect and your singular affection for me. <meta>catchword: LETTER</meta>

Those things which have long been prepared and intended by me, I hope to one day deliver into your hands in person, so that I may be allowed to pay back some part of my debt to you; hardly anything more happy or desirable could happen to me. Now, since I understand that the skillful hand of *Martin Schongauer* <note>original: "Martini Schőnii"; a famous 15th-century German engraver whose work Andreae had previously sent to the Prince</note> was not yet known to you, I am submitting another specimen by *Lucas van Leyden* <note>original: "Lucae Leidensis"; a Dutch Renaissance engraver and painter (1494–1533) known for his technical skill</note>, so that you may perceive how much these *men* emerged from the middle of the darkness of a barbarous age <note>original: "barbari seculi"; a common Renaissance term for the Medieval period, which scholars of Andreae's time viewed as a cultural low point before the "rebirth" of art</note>. They more easily and successfully led the way for the incomparable *Albrecht Dürer*, by whom the *art of painting* <term>ars pictoria: the craft and theory of visual representation</term> seems to have been brought to its highest peak without equal, since he alone achieved as much, and of such greatness, as ten others could scarcely have accomplished through their own individual industry. 

I shall gladly convey your greetings to our young Prince *Johann Friedrich* <note>Johann Friedrich of Württemberg (1637–1659), whom Andreae tutored and advised</note> as soon as I meet with him; indeed, as he is *most fond of you and yours*, he will be greatly delighted that he holds some place in your esteem. He would much prefer to join right hands in person and to renew and make permanent that familiarity and intimate friendship which formerly existed—of most praised memory—between your *Serene Father* <note>Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note> and his grandfather *Johann Friedrich* and great-grandfather *Friedrich*. I pray as a suppliant to *GOD* that He may grant us this joy on both sides. To His protection, favor, blessing, and every kind of gift for body and soul, I commend *You, Illustrious Prince*, and *Your Most August House*, and I hand myself over to you as your servant,

->**To Your Illustrious Highness**<-

### LETTER LXII.

->Fondest Greetings.<-

->*Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir:*<-

Although I considered the place to which you recently withdrew to be quiet and full of every tranquility, I nevertheless hear that many things are found there—indeed, I hear they have followed you there—which permit little rest or breathing room, but keep you always occupied and hindered. You write that my trifles <note>original: "nugas meas"; a modest term Ferdinand uses for his own early literary or academic exercises</note> do something to combat this boredom, though I would have believed that it might instead be increased by them; and certainly, if I were able to relieve you in this way, I would send not just these small sheets, but often entire quires <note>original: "duerniones"; referring to gatherings of paper used in bookbinding, implying longer manuscripts</note>. 

As for the very happy wishes you offer for my birthday, I give you my greatest thanks. I myself also approach God, Thrice Best and Greatest <note>original: "DEVM Ter Opt. Max"; a common scholarly invocation of the Trinity, adapting the Roman 'Deo Optimo Maximo'</note>, as a suppliant, that all things may proceed well and prosperously, and that those things which you so ardently and zealously seek may match your prayer. I can hardly doubt this divine benefit, now that I have been admitted to the holy rite of confirmation <note>Confirmation was a significant milestone for a young prince, marking his spiritual adulthood and readiness for public duty</note>. With the help of God, whose gift this is, it shall grant me the ability to persevere constantly in that which I have undertaken, and to zealously carry out all those things which this new condition of life demands of me, and which all good men have always expected. 

If you—as you have shown that my health and safety are of the highest concern to you—will continue to hold the same in your care hereafter (which is the one thing I seek), you will do me a most pleasing favor, and you will render me, who am already obligated to you on many counts, even more bound and constrained. Farewell.

->To Your Reverence<-
Wolfenbüttel, the 18th day of ->Your Most Devoted<-
June, 1650. ->Ferdinand Albert, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg.<-

### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,<-
->Lord by far most Merciful,<-

I have eagerly received your most longed-for letters, which I have lacked since the 17th of last April. I was wonderfully delighted, both by the continuation of your most favorable affection toward me—which is of the highest value to me—and by the mark of your extraordinary goodwill. In the meantime, however, your silence—or more truly, your pause—and that of your **Most Illustrious brother, Lord Rudolph Augustus**, has been compensated for by your renowned brother **Lord Anthony Ulrich**. Through three letters written in both his own name and yours, he has been a great comfort to me and has made me his debtor. Nor do I doubt that you will return to your former readiness for writing, if any leisure or interval from your serious studies remains for you. Furthermore, may **GOD** favorably bless the growth of your years and studies, so that with piety as the root, and with the branches of charity, **Fortitude and Temperance** stretching themselves out, the breadth of your rule, the peace of the land, and the wealth of the people may increase, and may at last converge in the peak of every kind of happiness. I gladly and deservedly pledge my prayers to you that you may reach this point; I shall be blessed if you should even surpass my very wishes. I most humbly pray, again and again, that you commend me to your **Most Serene Mother** <note>Princess Sophie Elisabeth (1613–1676), a noted poet and composer who oversaw the education of her stepsons</note>, upon whom **GOD** has abundantly bestowed whatever there is of human and divine goods. May **GOD** preserve you for the good of the Church, the benefit of the State, and as a most brilliant ornament of **Your House**: Farewell, and look with favor upon me together with your renowned brothers.

->Your Most Illustrious Highness’s<-

Bebenhausen <note>Bebenhausen Abbey, where Andreae served as Abbot and oversaw the local school system</note>, July 10,
1650.
->**Most humble servant,**<-
->**Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology**<-

### LETTER LXIV.

->Hearty Greetings.<-

Although I do not know whether you have returned home yet, I wanted these present lines to be at your doorstep and wait for you. You always praise my letters with the most grand words, but you almost neglect your own—or rather, you call them morose and rustic. However, I think this latter part was perhaps written in this sense: because they were either penned in the countryside or plucked from a most cultivated and fertile field. For both their richness and their elegance clearly show us that they should be received and understood in this way. Regarding what has been said between us so far about the various languages of other nations, I willingly concede and grant the point; however, the lack of time and my own tongue <note>original: "lingua mea"; likely referring to his current level of proficiency or the physical exhaustion of speaking/writing</note> forbid me from putting forth more about them now. Rather, whatever eloquence and readiness is in us, let us bring it all to celebrate those things which **GOD**, Thrice Best and Greatest, has meanwhile most mercifully granted us: namely, that most longed-for peace and tranquility, which we have finally been permitted to obtain through our most earnest prayers. <note>This is a reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which had ended the devastating Thirty Years' War just two years prior to this letter.</note> I do not doubt that there are now many most distinguished men everywhere who will copiously illustrate these greatest blessings of **GOD** with some sacred eulogy; to these, meanwhile, we add this simple offering of ours, and we commend to eternal glory what He has bestowed upon us with a full hand. My most beloved brother Ferdinand Albert departed for Hamburg about eight days ago with our *Illustrious Lady Mother* <note>Princess Sophie Elisabeth (1613–1676), a noted composer and poet</note>; however, it is uncertain when he is to return. Meanwhile, may he be as well as possible, and may he finally return to us safely.

Wolfenbüttel, July 9, 1650.
Our dutiful guardians <note>original: "Curatores"; likely the princely tutors or administrators</note>
send their greetings back to you.

Your Illustriousness’s
Most Devoted
Anthony Ulrich. <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714), who would later become a famous patron of the arts, a novelist, and Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.</note>

### To Prince ANTHONY ULRICH.

## To the Most Illustrious and Most High Prince, Lord by far most Merciful.

*It is truly too much that you offer; it is an immense amount that I, in turn, owe to You. For since you now sustain this burden alone—to respond to my trifles, so frequent and so troublesome—while your **Older Brother** <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704), who eventually became the ruling Duke.</note> is girded for the arduous duties of the **State**, and your **Younger Brother** <note>Ferdinand Albert I (1636–1687), known for his scholarly and artistic interests.</note> is refreshing himself with intellectual relaxations; I find nothing anywhere that I might give back for this readiness of yours and your tireless study, except for my own vanities and rubbish. However, that generous composure of yours, long since known to me, consoles me; it is easily softened by small gifts, grants a delay of payment with ease, and is content with a frank confession of debt. On behalf of this debt, I now present* **Wendel Dietterlin of Strasbourg**, *a Painter very famous for the books and works he published in this art, singular in optics <note>original: "in opticis"; here referring to the science of perspective, for which Dietterlin was famous.</note>, and most industrious in the gathering of Biblical Histories (of which this is a specimen). He was extinguished prematurely in 1599 at the age of 49, to the great loss of the art of painting. His most excellent work survives in* **Stuttgart**, *in the pleasure Garden House <note>The "Lusthaus" in Stuttgart, a masterpiece of the German Renaissance, later demolished.</note> of the Prince my Master; it is a suite of rooms 101 feet long, 71 wide, and 51 high, to be visited not without great admiration. I believe your* **Most Serene Father** <note>Duke August the Younger, a famous bibliophile and patron of the arts.</note> *remembers it. Indeed, in* **Strasbourg**, *many houses, both public and private, are painted inside and out, guarding the fame and memory of the artist. But why mention these things to You? As if, with your sagacious and cultivated mind, You could not yourself judge skillfully and discern accurately how much anyone excels, whether in invention or in labor and diligence—You, who are destined to be a future judge and Patron of this art. Rather, let me join with you in the due praises of the propitious Divinity*

*I fulfill my debt, because a new, happy age shows itself—restored and solidified by that which was already almost despaired of, the <term>GOLDEN PEACE</term> <note>original: "AVREA PACE"; a reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648) which ended the devastating Thirty Years' War.</note>. It is felt by the Church, by the desolate Fatherland, by sluggish Literature, by the Arts that were returning to barbarism, and even by men who were becoming like beasts. This new age is to be welcomed with applause by all the most brilliant minds; it must be supported by every good man to restore things everywhere, and truly it must be kept in good repair, protected, preserved, and transmitted to posterity by those in high office. We, not forgetting the evils we have endured, but saved from the savage storm by divine favor, pray for both better fates and a sounder mind, so that, having been taught by our own loss and becoming wise, we might both recognize our own goods more clearly and arrange them more rightly. For you, Most Illustrious Prince, along with your renowned Brothers, may your time flow in every abundance of the best and most famous things. Farewell, and look upon me with favor.*

->To Your Most Illustrious Highness<-

So that I might season my otherwise tasteless letters, it seemed fit to insert these maxims extracted from a careful little book of political observations recently published regarding the recent <term>French disturbances</term> <note>original: "motibus Gallicis"; likely referring to the Fronde, a series of civil wars in France (1648–1653) involving the nobility and the monarchy.</note>:
**I.** Know well what the dispositions of your people are, and how they are to be ruled.
**II.** Do not increase tax exactions, nor provoke the people.
**III.** Employ these mitigations for them:
**1.** Demand nothing except from a Christian conscience.
**2.** Candidly explain the necessity of the tax.
**3.** Appoint only fair and honest tax collectors.

### LETTER LXVI.

->Heartiest Greetings<-

I can scarcely offer enough thanks, *Reverend Sir*, while you make me feel indebted to you for far greater things. You deal so kindly with me and bestow your gifts so generously. I do not doubt that there were more distinguished artists before our **Dürer** <note>Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), the most famous artist of the German Renaissance, known for his high-quality woodcut prints and paintings.</note> who indeed showed the way to such a degree of excellence; however, they themselves never reached it. Yet it is marvelous how he, above all others, perfected the craft so skillfully and was almost uniquely sufficient for this service <note>original: "ministerio"; referring here to the "service" of art or the "office" of the artist.</note>.

The things which you sent this last time please me greatly; and since they seem remarkably made and precious because of their antiquity, I keep them with more intent care, and I show them to others who are accustomed to visit me in my Museum <note>original: "Musæo"; in the 17th century, this referred to a private study or a "Cabinet of Curiosities" where a scholar kept books, art, and scientific instruments.</note> as rare and distinguished items. He rejoices that you still enjoy prosperous health, and he sends his best wishes to you along with our leaders.

->To Your Reverence<-

*Wolfenbüttel, July 23, 1650.*
*Most Devoted,*
*Anthony Ulrich.*

### LETTER LXIX.

### To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA,

## Most Illustrious and High Princess, most Gracious Lady,

The more slowly I received your little letter, the more eagerly I welcomed it and the more reverently I held it. Truly, that you are not unmindful of me, nor disdain my letters, and that you are delighted by literary exchange—all this is to me a most certain sign: the first of an excellent character, the second of maidenly innocence, and the last of illustrious nobility. A harbor, found at last after a long voyage tossed by various storms, is quite suitable both for the tranquility of my mind and the health of my body; it seems all the more secure and lasting now that Peace <note>The Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War.</note> has finally been strengthened and ratified. And yet, there are things we must fear even from Peace itself, since human affairs are always such that...

->[ *The Wheel of the World.* ]<-

War, poverty, and grief; Peace, plenty, and luxury,
->Revolve forever as the wheel turns 'round.<-
War <note>original: "Mars"; the Roman god of war, here personified.</note> is sweet to those who have not tried it, yet terrifying to those who have,
->As it lays waste to famous towns and great fields alike.<-
The wretched burden of poverty then weighs down the nations,
->And grief burns even unto the very end of life.<-
Peace is sought by the afflicted; once found, it produces
->Prosperous times; and these lead to excessive luxury.<-
Most foul wars follow upon such excessive luxury,
->And thus nothing is seen to be stable in our World.<-
With You as our leader, O most peaceful GOD, may we be established in that harbor,
->Where there is no place for crime or for punishment.<-

*This is the sum of my prayers, directed namely toward that eternal Asylum; meanwhile, for you, most flourishing Princess, and for your Most Serene House, I pray that all things may flow in abundance from the horn of plenty of Peace—everything that can be conceived by human prayers or obtained from GOD, whom I heartily pray may always be gracious and favoring toward you.*

->Your Most Illustrious Highness's<-

...what I have gained from that City, with its multitude of merchants and its especially noble beauty, and brought home with me? For nothing seems more pleasant to me than to see the customs of many men and their cities, and to traverse lands warming under another sun, provided that we bring back from there not foreign gestures, pretenses, and ridiculous hand-kissings <note>The author is likely criticizing the superficial courtly affectations often picked up by travelers on the "Grand Tour."</note>, but only those things that are beneficial and which prove that we have walked the right path. Of these things, I could recount one or two (for I was allowed to view certain things privately), were I not aware that they have long been much better known to you. A rumor from the neighborhood has reached us that those states in the Netherlands <note>original: "Belgio"; in the 17th century, this term often referred to the Low Countries or the United Provinces as a whole.</note>, once most closely joined in concord, no longer agree among themselves; indeed, that the others have already committed many hostile acts against the primary city of Holland <note>Referring to Amsterdam and the political tensions following the Peace of Westphalia.</note>, because it would not decide by common opinion. Let us, meanwhile, enjoy the leisure which GOD has most mercifully granted, and let us pray from the heart that the same may happen for others. Farewell.

### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**Most Gracious**<-
->**Lord.**<-

I heartily congratulate you on your successful excursion, and I foretell it as a precursor to a someday fruitful journey—one which may not so much affect the eyes with pleasant sights, as it may instruct with the lessons of wisdom and prudence; nor infect the traveler with foreign vices, but rather perfect him with virtues visible everywhere. For regarding a journey, whether well or poorly undertaken, one can pronounce nearly the same as Aesop wittily decided about the tongue: that it is at once the best and the worst thing <note>Andreae references a famous fable where Aesop serves his master tongues, arguing they are the best thing because they are the source of philosophy and the worst because they are the source of strife.</note>, which German youth especially demonstrate openly to their own benefit or harm. 

But it was sad for me to hear what you hinted at regarding the discord among the Belgians <note>original: "Belgarum"; at this time, the Latin terms for "Belgium" or the "Belgians" referred generally to the people of the Low Countries (the Netherlands), who were experiencing internal political friction following the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.</note>, a disease which is accustomed to arise from excessive successes and fortunes, and has always been lethal to all the greatest Empires and Republics. And what else has so greatly afflicted and almost overturned our Germany? To heal which, all of us who are held by love for the Fatherland should most zealously apply ourselves; and we should especially take care lest the Peace, so eagerly sought, having turned into abundance, generates luxury; that luxury brings forth ambition, ambition excites rivalry, and rivalry breaks out into animosities, which, by stirring up dissensions, might revive war and bring back the chain <note>original: "cathenam"</note> of all evils.

# THE YEAR 1650

...however, <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought from the previous page regarding the "Grand Tour"—the traditional journey through Europe taken by young noblemen to finish their education.</note> you rightly advise what should be most considered in travels [peregrinationibus]. One should look not only at the country estates, cities, and provinces, but rather at the customs and institutions of the inhabitants, their societies and treaties, and the form of Virtue and Governance <term>Politiæ; refers to the structural administration and civil order of a state</term>. An accurate knowledge of these things will be most beneficial for us for many reasons, but especially in times of Peace and War. Those who neglect this, I would say, are wandering rather than traveling; indeed, they stray far from the true purpose of travel.

*It is certain that those Belgian States* <note>original: "Status illos Belgicos." This refers to the United Provinces of the Netherlands, which had recently achieved full independence following the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.</note> *are now resting again from the dissent that recently arose; some say, however, that the other party has not yet entirely laid aside its confidence, but continues strenuously in strengthening garrisons and fortifications, and other things that serve to repel enemy attacks—for what end or with what success, let them see to themselves. Other distinguished men have also foretold that excessive prosperity, quiet, leisure, and luxury are the surest signs—indeed, the causes—of future ruin. To these, punishments usually come, which, though late, are rarely light. We have many examples of this among both the ancients and the moderns, yet there are few who recall these and other varieties of the human condition to mind. We wish these people to be more cautious, and we commend ourselves to divine protection with most ardent prayers.*

### LETTER LXXIX.

->To PRINCE FERDINAND ALBERT.<-

->Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,<-
->Lord most Gracious,<-

*I would wish you not to doubt that your letters are always a great delight to me, and I strive with all my effort to prove this to you. For I see in them the traces of your progress along the paths of virtue, which you are pursuing correctly, and I praise this greatly. Regarding your eventual Travel* <note>The "Grand Tour," an essential educational journey through Europe for young nobles.</note> *your most Serene Father, that most prudent Prince, will provide; it is not for us to dictate to him. Yet I place the perfection of such travel in this: that you may be abroad while at home, so that you may be at home while abroad. If you do not grasp this riddle yourself through your natural cleverness, your instructors will solve it.* <note>Andreae is suggesting that a truly educated mind is never a "stranger" in foreign lands, nor should it lose its core identity while away; one should carry "home"—their character and values—everywhere.</note> *If it should happen that we are joined together either at home or abroad, I would consider that the happiest day of my declining life. But while Death is at my gates* <note>Andreae was 64 at this time and in failing health; he would pass away four years later.</note> *I pray to God, who wishes you to be safe and flourishing, that Death remains far from your path and that the threads of your life be drawn out long. Farewell and look favorably upon*

->Your Illustrious Highness’s<-
Bebenhausen, <note>A former Cistercian monastery in Germany where Andreae served as Protestant prelate.</note> October 2, 1650. ->Most humble servant,<-

## LETTER LXXXI.

### To PRINCE ANTON ULRICH.

**Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,**
->Lord, by far most Clement,<-

Last week, indeed, an unexpected illness <note>Andreae suffered from various ailments in his later years, which often hindered his prolific writing.</note> had cast me down so that I was not equal to the task of writing letters. Now that I have recovered myself somewhat, I see that I must discharge my duty and respond to your most kind letters; yet I find no way to satisfy them according to their worth. For such is your constant and incredible benevolence toward me, and you so repeatedly make me indebted with testimonies of it, that however much I strive to release myself from your debt <note>original: *Tuo ære* (by your money/debt). Andreae uses a common Latin legal and financial metaphor to describe social obligation.</note>, I remain more and more stuck in it; and yet I do not find you to be a difficult creditor or a harsh debt-collector. From which the burden of my debt is now almost pleasant to me, since it seems more glorious to your Generosity to give than to receive, and to have a debtor who confesses his debt rather than to strike his name from the accounts. But setting aside these things, which might seem more like flatteries than actual payment, I turn to your letters, than which nothing was more pleasing to me. May God <note>original: *DEVS*</note> keep those whom He has joined inseparable for many ages, and multiply them a thousandfold. Truly, may He so bless your most honorable studies and desires that whatever you contribute to them, whether at home or abroad, they may make you a most distinguished Prince and beneficial to the State <note>original: *Reip.* (Republic/Commonwealth)</note>; and let all those who hold the glory of your Most Serene House in their hearts happily join their efforts. In this regard, and especially in fervent intercessions with the Supreme Deity <note>original: *supremum Numen*</note>, I would not want anyone to precede me, so that what is lacking in my resources may be supplied by my excellent goodwill. 

Between the 18th and 19th of this month, at night around one o'clock, the earth moved quite perceptibly <note>This refers to a localized earthquake in the German territories in 1650.</note>, though without damage among us; which same...

### Hearty Greetings. <note>S. P. stands for "Salutem Plurimam," a standard Latin greeting meaning "very much health" or "hearty greetings."</note>

## LETTER 84.

->Greetings and Best Wishes<-

### LETTER 87.

#### TO PRINCESS SIBYLLA URSULA.

## Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,
->Most Merciful Lady.<-

How much I value the delights of Your Highness’s letters, you may gather from this: that I dared to request them—though modestly—not long ago. Now that I have obtained them, just as I truly rejoice, so I humbly profess that I owe very much to you. And since you congratulate me with a sincere mind and innocent prayer (which have the greatest power with GOD) on reaching a harbor of tranquility after a long-lasting storm <note>Andreae refers to his retirement to the monastery of Bebenhausen after the upheavals of the Thirty Years' War.</note>, I give thanks with my whole heart. In exchange for the East and South winds <note>original: "Euro Notoque." In classical literature, these are the turbulent, stormy winds.</note>, which have troubled me long enough, I wish for you perpetual West winds or Favonians <note>original: "Zephyros sive Favonios." These are the gentle, warming winds of springtime, symbolizing peace and favor.</note>. 

Furthermore, that you look kindly upon my little tokens <term>Xeniola<note>A Latin term for small guest-gifts or tokens of friendship.</note></term>, which are indeed cheap and unworthy of your greatness, is itself something I may greatly boast of. For it is the character of a noble soul not to look at the smallness of the gift, but at the most ample goodwill of the giver. This goodwill is indeed so great in me that I have no equal wish or desire than to reveal itself by any token. I shall dare to prove this to you hereafter with all the more confidence, because you voluntarily promise that I shall deposit [my service] within your mindful soul. I pray to GOD that all things may turn out happily for you, for the use of the Church and the Fatherland, for whose welfare you were born and educated...

### LETTER 88.

->Greetings.<-

->**Reverend and Most Famous Sir,**<-

Since I know that you derive a certain pleasure from my letters, I will handle this zeal for writing between us more confidently in the future, and I will much more promptly fulfill those things which you expect from me with curiosity. It is altogether fitting for me to comply with the will of my guides. For this is our age <note>The Princess was about 21 years old at this time.</note>, which can easily be bent this way and that, stray from the right path, and be carried headlong into danger, unless there are those who lead us by the hand, and through whose care we can emerge safe. 

I believe those things which you wished to present under a covering and a wrapper <note>original: "sub tegumento & involucro." This refers to Andreae's use of allegory or symbolic language to teach moral lessons.</note> pertain entirely to this course of our life. For while I labor to unwrap them, I see that he especially can and ought to be "at home while abroad" who retreats as far as possible from those things which are done wrongly within private walls—and which least suit his character, age, and condition—and who conducts himself toward these things as if arriving from elsewhere: one who looks upon it with his eyes, but in his soul execrates and detests it. And such a person is honored even as any other traveler who has traversed foreign lands and acquires the customs and virtues of those peoples to his own praise and benefit. This is how I think they should be interpreted; but...

## LETTER 89.
### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,<-
->My most gracious Lord,<-

Why should I not love your letters, and be most deeply affected by them, since they breathe nothing but the aura of your illustrious goodwill toward me, and smell sweetly of the roses of your elegant wit <note>original: "ingenii," referring to the Prince's natural talent or character</note>. Therefore, the more often you write to me, the more brilliant a favor you will bestow, from which I might infer your progress—which is indeed quite evident—and have more abundant reason to congratulate you and rejoice for myself. My <term>Peripatetic riddle (a puzzle referring to the school of Aristotle, who taught while walking; here it signifies a riddle about traveling while learning)</term>, although you have explained it cleverly enough, still holds (by your leave) something hidden according to my own meaning. Specifically, that when you are about to travel abroad, you should be "at home"; that is, in whatever place on earth you may be, you should carry with you your domestic precepts and examples of virtue—especially piety and modesty, tenderness of conscience, the company of your attendants, and caution against foreign corruptions—as if you were carrying your own inseparable House. Conversely, when you have returned home, whatever elegancies and treasures scattered throughout the world you have collected here and there with a keen eye and the wise guidance of your advisors, you may bring all that back home and adorn it with such precious merchandise, that you can be "abroad while at home," rich in the choice spoils of various lands. Therefore abroad...

### To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA.

->To the Most Illustrious and Highborn Princess,<-
->A Young Lady Most Merciful by far.<-

In this boundary between the passing and the emerging year, I have considered it a matter of duty, debt, and even my religious devotion to send you a letter in which I might offer **GOOD WORDS** in the Christian manner. I have long been persuaded by clear evidence that such a gesture would not be unwelcome to you. Truly, your kindness toward me during the course of this year has been so great and illustrious that you deigned to bless me five times with your conversation through most elegant letters. I have nothing to give in return for these except to pray that your disposition toward me continues, and that this happiness remains perpetual for me as long as my life lasts. To obtain this, I believe I must seek from **GOD** through constant and burning prayers that all things remain safe, happy, and desired for you. 

But since you can hardly be safe unless your Serene Father is safe, your Mother safe, your Household safe, your lands safe, and your **ALTARS AND HEARTHS** <note>original: "aris & focis," a classical idiom referring to one's most sacred religious and domestic foundations</note> safe, may God, the Best and Greatest, command all these things and each one individually to be **SAFE AND AUSPICIOUS** for you according to your wish at this year’s beginning, middle, and end, so that you may count them among the happiest hallmarks of your life. 

May this year also grant an evident and immense increase to your **PIETY, PROBITY, AND ERUDITION**, a triad of gems with which you already shine in the Temple of Memory. May it erect a **GOLDEN STATUE** as a reward for this Virtue—so rare in the female sex <note>Andreae often praised the intellectual achievements of the sisters of the House of Brunswick, noting how they defied contemporary stereotypes about women's education</note>—which posterity might be able and willing to remember. And so, farewell, Most Illustrious Princess, and may you have many favorable years to your **GLORY**, which my whole soul favors and applauds.

->Your Most Illustrious Highness's<-
->Most humble worshiper and client,<-

Bebenhausen <note>A former Cistercian monastery where Andreae served as abbot</note>, December 15, 1650. Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.

### LETTER 93.

### S. P. <note>An abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam*, a standard Latin greeting meaning "Heartiest greetings" or "Much health."</note>

->*Reverend and Most Illustrious Sir,*<-

I clearly perceive that you always take great pleasure from my letters, given that you respond to them so promptly and kindly, and await and desire them with such longing. You call them "roses" indeed—or rather, everything that can move the senses sweetly and pleasantly. Do not wonder, then, if they reach you more rarely. For you know that in this **autumn season** <note>original: "tempestate autumnâ." This likely refers to the author’s advancing age or the bleak period following the Thirty Years' War.</note> such things are not easily produced; and whatever hint of a more pleasant breeze approaches is driven back again by the sharp force of the cold. Nor should you interpret this as if I were now so withdrawn that I would wish to refuse, out of some growing lethargy, what I owe you with a loving hand. Rather, you may expect of me that I shall never fail to respond in love to those who continue to cherish me with the rays of their own kindness. 

I see only now that you intended to indicate far more, and far different things, with those **enigmatic words** <note>original: "verbis illis ænigmaticis," referring to a previous letter containing allegories or perhaps Rosicrucian-style symbolism common in Andreae’s circle.</note> than I could grasp through mere guesswork. They certainly contain healthy precepts, which it would have been well for many to obey today. But who understands these things well enough, even when they are most fitting? All things are turned toward a blindness of the mind; we are so disturbed—or, I might truly say, **bewitched** <note>original: "fascinati," implying a state of being under a spell or irrational delusion.</note>—that we do not submit to the authority of those who advise us well, unless we have first experienced everything else to our great detriment. May **GOD** therefore grant that your vow be confirmed and firm, and bestow His grace, so that those matters we have discussed between us thus far may become more familiar to me also; and that, with **favorable omens** <note>original: "secundis avibus," literally "with favorable birds," a classical Roman idiom for good luck or divine approval.</note>, I might one day [reach] that...

# LETTER 93.
## HEARTIEST GREETINGS. <note>original: "S. P." for *Salutem Plurimam*, a standard Latin greeting meaning "very much health" or "heartiest greetings."</note>
### *Reverend and most Distinguished Sir,*

I perceive from this that you always take great pleasure from my letters, because you respond to them so promptly and kindly, and you await and desire them even more vehemently. You speak plainly of roses—or rather, of everything that can move the senses sweetly and pleasantly. Therefore, do not wonder if they reach you more rarely. For you know that in this autumn season they are not easily produced, and whatever more pleasant air approaches is driven back again by the sharper force of the cold. Nor should you interpret this as if I were now so constricted that I would wish to refuse, having become a little more sluggish, what I owe you by hand and from my mind. Rather, anything may be expected from me sooner than failing to respond in love to those who continue to cherish me with the rays of their benevolence. 

I see only now that you wished to indicate far other and more things by those enigmatic words than I could achieve by conjecture. They certainly contain salutary precepts which, if most people today had wished to obey them... but who understands well enough those things which are most fitting? Thus all things are turned toward the blindness of the mind; we are so disturbed—indeed, I might say, so fascinated <note>original: "fascinati," meaning bewitched or under a spell of delusion.</note>—*that we do not admit the authority of those warning us well, unless we have first experienced all other things with the greatest loss.* 

May God therefore wish your prayer to be ratified and firm, and may He grant His grace, so that I may also make that matter, which we have dealt with between us until now, more familiar to myself; and one day, with favorable omens <note>original: "secundis avibus," literally "favorable birds," a Roman idiom referring to the practice of taking auspices to determine the will of the gods.</note>—as they say—...

->feli-<- <note>Catchword for "feliciter," meaning "happily" or "successfully."</note>

# LETTER 95.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Doctor, a most beloved friend,<-

Your response, full of pious affection and kindness, draws forth my own reply in return; not because I have matters of great importance for you to know at this time, but rather to offer a brief word and a prayer in answer to your wish, and to join my returning affection through this letter. The time of the New Year approaches, and at last the face of public peace shines in Germany <note>original: "Germania". A reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which had recently ended the devastating Thirty Years' War.</note>; may God grant us this merciful peace as a lasting and ever more beloved thing. As for you, surrounded as you are by venerable gray hair and sweet rest, may you count and recount those years as many times as we once counted, with groaning, the years returning with **Bellona** <note>The Roman goddess of war; here used as a personification of the war years.</note>. May God, the Thrice-Best and Greatest, confirm this brief and heartfelt prayer! Farewell and be happy. Given at Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "VVel-ferbyti".</note>, the 24th day of December, in the year 1650.

->*To your Reverence*<-
->*devoted with gracious affection,*<-
->*Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg.*<-

<header>LETTERS</header>

...saved from destruction, and the goods restored to wholeness are used not for establishing what was most fitting, the **Kingdom of Christ**, but rather for overturning it and establishing the **filth of Babylon** <note>original: "Babilonis colluviem." A common Protestant polemical term referring to the perceived corruption of the Roman Church or general moral decay.</note> through force, fraud, robbery, and waste; through quarrels and foul dances; through lust and pride; and through various other most different vices. With **Hypocrisy** busy on one side and **Tyranny** on the other, both openly and in secret, we contribute to this state and boldly provoke the somehow appeased wrath of **God**. The various portents of earthquakes, floods, violent winds, and similar great evils—the precursors of judgment—prove that He is angry with us and reproaches our extreme ingratitude. They convince us that we have learned nothing from the memory of earlier things, but instead progress toward the worse, so that to live longer among these things is to be tortured, as if one wished to wait for the final devastation and ruin. 

But let these sad things depart, and for **Your House**, most illustrious **Princess**—a house of good reputation, cultivated piety, strengthened justice, practiced discipline, nurtured literature, and the safe guardianship of the lands under the "prime mover" **AUGUSTUS** <note>A reference to her father, Duke Augustus the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg, comparing his leadership to the 'primum mobile' or the outermost moving sphere of the heavens.</note>—let all things portend good omens. Let there be prophecies of **LONG-LASTING HAPPINESS** and **GROWTH**, to which, from your own natural brilliance <note>original: "Genio"</note>—which the present age admires and posterity will marvel at—may the greatest support and increase be added. May all things turn out according to desire for the glory of **GOD**, to whom all things are owed, and for the public good, for which I believe you were born and given. 

For your most elegant letters, than which nothing is sweeter to me, I give huge thanks; and I ask with all the humble respect I can that you might hereafter also sometimes indulge me with this serene countenance expressed on paper. When my little votive gifts <note>original: "Xeniola." Small, symbolic gifts often exchanged at the New Year.</note> arrive—very meager indeed and unworthy of such an illustrious sight—if you receive them with that serene brow as is your custom, nothing will be more fortunate for them. Farewell, most noble Princess, ornament of the age, and look with favor upon

->Your Most Illustrious Highness’s<-

->Bebenhausen, 14 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *most dedicated servant,*<-
->Jan. 1651. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.<-

### To Prince ANTON ULRICH,

## Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,

### My far most Clement
### Lord,

<margin>+</margin>
I had fully promised myself that you would perform the noble duty entrusted to you at the solemn Academic Ceremony of your **AUGUSTAN JULIA** <note>The University of Helmstedt, also known as the Academia Julia, founded by the House of Brunswick.</note> with outstanding skill and great applause. I have now received the joyful news that this has been happily accomplished, through the testimony of your Serene Father, your **Governor** <note>original: "Ephorus," a term for a supervisor or tutor responsible for a prince's education.</note>, and indeed from the Julia itself. This news floods me with such heaps of joy that I am scarcely able to contain them all at once. For when I contemplate the very image of your Father expressed in you, and now your partnership in his distinguished praise; this specimen of hereditary virtue and dexterity in you; the pledge given for the future expectations of the Julia-Augusta; the noble emulation of your brother **Ferdinand Albert**; and the prayers of all who cultivate **PIETY** and **LETTERS** <note>original: "PIETATEM & LITERAS." This was the central educational ideal of the time, combining religious devotion with classical learning.</note>, I cannot but call the Father most happy in this genuine son; the Son—endowed with his Father’s genius—**MOST WEALTHY**; the Julia-Augusta **MOST ILLUSTRIOUS** by the continuation of the light of Brunswick; and the student body by the rising of a new favoring star. It is fitting to congratulate and applaud each of these from the heart, but most of all, to pray that these joys—which belong properly to your **MOST AUGUST** Father—may be **LONG-LASTING, INCREASED, SOLID**, and beneficial to the **KINGDOM OF CHRIST** in these lands, and that they may spread and fill the fame of the **GUELPH** <note>The Welf/Guelph dynasty, the noble house of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> name. For you, most flourishing Prince, as the beginnings of your public appearance were joyful and praiseworthy, may your progress increase more and more with the years, so that while no one will easily dare to compare themselves to you, you yet

### LETTER C.

->Many greetings.<- <note>original: "S. P.," abbreviation for Salutem Plurimam, a standard formal greeting meaning "heartiest greetings."</note>

I have been silent until now and rested a little, *Reverend Sir*, and I have been vehemently anxious as to how I might excuse that long silence. But since I see you are now content with a little, and take pleasure even in my rarer letters, I fear nothing further, but embrace your kindness with both hands, and consider with myself how I might satisfy you abundantly in the future. I rejoice greatly that my studies, of whatever kind they may be, are pleasing to you; however, the bond of friendship that exists between us does not permit me to either desire or expect a formal expression of thanks. It seems rather to fall to me to respond to your wish for a most auspicious year—a wish which I am convinced proceeded not so much from custom as from love, given the many tokens of your goodwill. Concerning me, may God ordain what He wills in that regard, and may He provide what He knows is beneficial for me and for the public good. Meanwhile, may He grant you the same happiness, so that I may see you flourishing for a long time, and myself truly blessed by your friendship. What you have prayed for elsewhere, at some... <note>The text breaks off mid-word "aliquando" (at some time/eventually), which is completed on the following page.</note>

I testify for certain that your most loving letters would be answered more frequently by my Prince <note>This likely refers to Prince Anton Ulrich or another young prince of the House of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel whom Friedrich von Kram served.</note> if the act of writing letters were as pleasant to him as the reading of them is; you would never be without them. But, as is your experience, you easily know the *nature of young Princes* <note>original: "juniorum Principum ingenium"</note>, who either never or rarely take delight in the exercise of writing—that is, as they see it, a sedentary life—but rather love that which is joined with the movement of the body. Since, therefore, *my Most Serene Prince* was also born this way, and being well aware of it himself, he greatly fears lest you might either interpret his silence poorly or be moved to repay him in kind <note>original: "par pari reddendum," meaning to give back like for like, or "tit for tat."</note>. However, so that you do neither, he frequently wishes and most graciously requests that I address you with this letter for that reason.

Just as I trust you will easily grant him this, I also promise that even though the letters have been interrupted, nothing of his love toward you will diminish. If you persuade yourself of this, I have achieved the goal I intended with this letter; as for other things remaining to be written about our affairs, I will add them in the future if it pleases. Indeed, you will see a letter from *the Prince himself* within eight days. Now I end the letter with a prayer, and with the same I will inaugurate the year which we have now entered. May GOD grant that all things in this and many following years may succeed happily for you according to His will and your own desire, and that the vigor of body and mind may correspond on both sides, so that you may be able to be of much use to yourself, your family, and the Church for a long time. Farewell and be favorable.

->To Your Most Devoted,<-

Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelfferbythi"</note>, January 7, 1651. Friedrich von Kram.

That some memory of me remains with you, Most Noble and Distinguished Man, and indeed that an affection full of goodwill persists toward me, is something for which I should greatly congratulate myself; I owe the greatest thanks to you, my exceptional patron. Nor am I so ignorant of the **Court** <note>original: "Aulæ"</note> as not to know that different ages of Princes require different pursuits and different occupations of the mind, and that a far different account and estimation must be held of the younger than of the more mature.

This, however, I desired: lest I should entirely slip from the most generous mind of the Prince (in which I trust I was once somewhat planted), that I might cherish the fire of his mercy at intervals with most humble addresses, and make the hereditary and perpetual affection of his Most Serene Lord Father <note>Referring to Duke August the Younger, a long-time correspondent and patron of Andreae.</note> my own in the Son. If this is safe, I judge that everything of mine is safe. Since you promise this affection to be firm and solid to me—which I attribute greatly to your loyalty and virtue—there is no reason for me to seek further. Nor shall I do anything other than compose myself with most humble devotion according to the Prince's will. Indeed, I shall venerate you for this remarkable favor—that you keep your Master mindful of me—and I shall value your incredible virtue. Since this is joined in me with the indelible memory of my former **Wensius** <note>Likely a reference to a deceased mutual friend or colleague from the court circle.</note>, you will have done kindly...

### LETTER 103.

-> To the Very Reverend and Distinguished Master <-
-> Doctor, a Friend to be cherished, <-

I have received not only your letter, full of love and pious devotion, but at the same time your small votive gifts; and while I was contemplating a brief reply, another response of yours followed. I thank you for the images sent; they are sacred, nor is artistry lacking, and therefore they instill a memory of heavenly things in the viewer. I also note your laments at length regarding the diseases of our age; although I do not fully grasp these myself, I easily understand that **Divine vengeance** <note>original: "vindictam Divinam"</note> will at last be most heavy upon those hardened people and scoffers. The worst kind of ingratitude is to use the granted **Peace** <note>original: "Pace." A reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War.</note> in the worst way. Happy is the man who, far from the contagion of vanity and left to his pious mind, intercedes daily with groans! I pray from my soul that, along with the golden Peace, the times of golden **integrity** <note>original: "integritatis"</note>...

### LETTER 104.

## To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA,
## Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,
## Most Clement Maiden,

That which you wished to serve as a conclusion in your letter with a pious vow, let it be my beginning: Would that with golden Peace, the times of **GOLDEN INTEGRITY & PIETY** might return. For we owed this to **GOD**, that with Peace restored <note>Referring to the end of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which had devastated Germany.</note>, we should seriously wash away whatever pollutions we had been contaminated and stained with by the wickedness of Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war; a poetic way of referring to the horrors and moral decay of wartime.</note>, and that we might earn back a reconciled **GOD** through a more corrected life and more holy worship. All history speaks of this one foundation for firm and lasting Peace and happiness, without which whatever settlements and transactions were built upon it easily collapse and vanish. For as the Divine Power does not allow itself to be mocked, so it is accustomed to avenge itself through other mockery; for "there is no peace for the wicked," says the Lord, Isaiah 48 <note>original: "non enim est pax impiis, dicit Dominus, Es. 48." Reference to Isaiah 48:22.</note>. How timely it would be in this age to restore the other part of the Evangelical Reformation, which is **DISCIPLINE**, and for all ranks to devote all their studies, duties, and efforts to that care. For since the Christian Religion consists of both purity of **DOCTRINE** and integrity of **LIFE**, it will be neither pure nor whole, nor conforming to Christ and the Apostles, if it boasts of one while the other is corrupted, or fights hostilely to assert one, while meanwhile possessing neither in practice— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

*...wicked.* <note>Continuing from the quote on the previous page: "There is no peace for the wicked."</note> *For just as we owe a great deal to the sincerity of doctrine, so we are no less bound to **GOD** for an honorable life; for He shrinks from outrages and crimes just as much as from idolatry or heresy. For if the desire of the Queen of Sheba <note>original: "Sabeæ Reginæ"</note>, who visited Solomon because of the fame of his wisdom from more than two hundred and forty miles away, was praised and given as an example by Him who is infinitely greater than Solomon; who could find fault with me for [visiting] another Solomon of our age, your Most Serene Lord Father <note>Duke Augustus the Younger (1579–1666), famed for his immense library and wisdom</note>, who for more than ten years now, with an unheard-of example of mercy and generosity, has favored me of his own accord, [attaining] here an age long-lived and vigorous, of virtue and glory, with an always steady course of life and reputation,*

### LETTER CX.
->Heartiest Greetings <note>original: "S P.", abbreviation for Salutem Plurimam</note><-

**I** have little to write to you now. However, since I saw that your later letters also concerned me, I thought a reply should certainly be added here. Indeed, you promise many things about me—great things that would illuminate my name not a little. Whether I can truly live up to them, or when it may be possible to reach the point you desire for me, is a matter of uncertain conjecture. Nevertheless, I may place something in the uncertain outcome of time, because I have not yet lost heart, nor do I think that what has been achieved by others will be impossible for me. I have heard that you are already preparing a journey to us; may GOD grant that you arrive among us safe and sound. You will have a convenient time for traveling, and perhaps you will find a comfortable lodging with us, provided other things do not intervene to hinder you or draw you away from your undertaking altogether. We are ready to deserve well of you in the manner that is fitting, and to deal with you kindly and graciously, as the laws of hospitality <note>original: "recipientium jura," literally the rights of those receiving guests</note> require. ### LETTER 113.

->Greetings.<-

*I clearly perceive, Reverend Sir, how much you value me in your singular mind by the immense joy you write that you feel because of my recovered health. Would that my hands were truly free and at leisure! I could then joyfully pronounce that I have been entirely liberated from the unexpected illness by which I was tested not so long ago. ### To Prince ANTON ULRICH.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**My Lord, most Gracious by far**<-

->Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,<-

This has kindled in me a desire—all the greater and more uncontrollable—to see You and to testify in person to the respect I owe; yet I see, most unwillingly, that the opportunity to visit You is denied me, whether by the seasons of the year, the cares of the Fatherland, or my very health and physical strength. Meanwhile, I rejoice greatly that my excuses—true and valid as they are—are accepted by You, and that your readiness to receive me into the bosom of your grace upon my eventual arrival persists of its own accord, without any prompting from me. But truly, the sad relapse of my Fatherland—which seemed to be recovering from a lethal disease by the benefit of Peace <note>Referring to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the devastating Thirty Years' War.</note>—now weighed down by a mass of debts, so distresses and exhausts me that I consider all life hereafter, spent in the sight of such calamity, as a punishment. 

*Curse that maleficent Mars* <note>The Roman god of war, here personifying the spirit of conflict.</note>, *who, even though put to flight by the rising of kindly Peace, being a wondrous Teacher, left behind for his teachable disciples those arts of harming which declare an incurable internal war against Religion, Liberty, Wealth, and all Discipline; a war to which all Posterity, willing or unwilling, knowing or unknowing, must necessarily submit its neck. That this evil hanging over the Church and the German Republic* <note>original: "Reip. Germanae." Andreae uses the term "Republic" in the classical sense of the "commonwealth" or the state.</note> *may be further delayed by the Piety, Wisdom, and Fortitude of your Most Serene Lord Father—the most noble star of our salvation—is to be earnestly prayed for: that he may set* <note>In the sense of a star setting below the horizon, a metaphor for death.</note> *only much later, for in his vitality and longevity our Happiness consists.*

With this prayer I conclude, and I join my own petitions for the success of your flowering and growth, Illustrious Princess; may Christ grant them His favor. Farewell, and look kindly upon

->Your Most Illustrious Highness’s<-

Bebenhausen, 23 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; most humble client,
July, 1651. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Joh. Val. Andreae, Doctor of Theology.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished<-

I confess myself indebted to you for many reasons, but especially because you take such singular care of my health and are so solicitous of it, offering every favorable prayer for me. ## EPISTLE 125.

### To PRINCE ANTHONY ULRIC.

**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**
**My most Gracious Lord.**

As gladly and deservedly as I congratulate You on your recovered health, I pray that a merciful God might make it firm and constant forever. Since you acknowledge His benefit with gratitude, you will labor all the more so that health of mind may always be joined with that of the body, active in the service and praise of the Creator; so that, by whose gift you possess whatever you have, you may rightly offer to Him the sacred duties of Piety and Temperance with a ready and mindful devotion. 

Indeed, how excellent it is to hear that you are preparing a Library, following the example and emulation of your Great Father <note>A reference to Duke August the Younger, whose massive collection became the Herzog August Bibliothek.</note>. Even if it is not yet of equal magnificence (of which no abundance will ever be lacking to you in the future), it is nevertheless not unequal in the selection of books and the investigation of chosen works. May *Christ* favor this, and would that I were able to contribute anything from my own bookshelves and poverty. 

But it has long been since the Italians, French, Spanish, English, and others of foreign nations—as well as mathematicians, architects, and other similar craftsmen—obtained their dismissal from me <note>Andreae is metaphorically describing the disposal or gifting of his collection of foreign and technical books.</note>, because they saw no heir in my house to whom they might one day be of use. If anyone...

*You know what grief I have truly conceived in my soul from that; I could not easily express it in any words. But who would dare, or wish, to resist God, the Fatherland, Nature, and health? ### EPISTLE 128.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Excellent Lord<-
->Doctor, my Worshipful Friend.<-

Your letters and writings persuade me more and more that Kindness itself, and all the charms of Old Latium <note>original: Veteri Latio — a reference to the wit and refined language of classical Rome</note>, dwell with you in your Bebenhausen <note>The monastery of Bebenhausen, where the recipient, Johann Valentin Andreae, lived and worked</note>; indeed, they seem to me to have been entirely dictated by the Graces themselves. You press for a reply from time to time, and I do not refuse; rather, I am held by a spontaneous desire to respond. Yet I do not have at hand anything that I might say fittingly or elegantly enough to match your words. However, I find by experience that you accept whatever response I give as sufficient, and what my style lacks, you generously supply from the promptings of your own goodwill. The hope I had of seeing and speaking with you in person seems to have slipped further away in your recent letters, due to some public misfortune weighing upon the Fatherland <note>Likely referring to the ongoing political tensions between the city of Brunswick and the Ducal house, or the slow recovery from the Thirty Years' War</note>. We shall hope for better things, however, and that all prosperity (though with a slow step) will finally be brought back along with a prosperous Peace; and so, little by little, the causes that have hindered your journey until now will vanish. Fare you well and happily. Given at Wolfenbüttel, August 26, in the year 1651.

->To your Reverence and devotion<-
->most devoted,<-
->Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg.<-

->Heartiest Greetings.<-

Because you have undertaken a vow for my health, *Reverend Sir*, as it is indeed of the greatest importance, so it makes me most deeply obliged to wish and desire all things for you in return. However, my condition is such that I remain subject to the doctor's orders <note>original: *medentis imperio*</note>, and I am still compelled to drink down the liquids <note>Likely medicinal tonics or "potions" prescribed by a court physician.</note> intended for this task. As these are not only effective within the body, they also move the mind vehemently, leading me to weigh more curiously how full of evils this life is, and how uncertain and weak all things are—just as in a *clock* <note>original: *Horologio*</note>, some iron part is always either loosened or moved out of its place. Regarding my books, although they may not deserve a grand or precious name, there is nonetheless a festive abundance of them, and they contain various kinds of subjects and doctrines. From these I receive infinite pleasure, and they sometimes hold me so fast that (let boasting be absent from my words) I spend most of my leisure and time in paging through and reading them. They certainly receive their increase from elsewhere, but I would not wish to be so ungracious as to expect anything from you, who have been so kind toward me before now; being yourself most dedicated to these matters, you collect and hunt down all the most highly approved works. Let your favorable goodwill be enough for me, along with your tireless zeal for serving, which I acknowledge with a most grateful soul; thus, I shall not cease to honor and observe you most diligently. Farewell.

->*To Your Reverence*<-
->*Most Devotedly,*<-
->*Anton Ulrich.*<-

Wolfenbüttel, 26
August 1651.

## LETTER 131.

### To Prince ANTON ULRICH.

->*Most Illustrious and Most Serene Prince,*<-
->*My Most Gracious Lord.*<-

That your health is still uncertain and remains under medical inspection and care—I do not know whether I should grieve more, or if I should instead approve of **GOD'S** <note>original: *DEI*</note> plan for you and interpret it as a sign of His singular love. For we are often accustomed to looking at our blessings through wrappings <note>meaning: we see our benefits as if they are hidden or disguised</note> with a restless eye, while we more willingly admit evils because they are smeared with sweetness on the outside. Hence, with a stronger body, we more boldly either admit or commit those things which, with a weaker one, we either dismiss or omit. Regarding myself, I must indeed confess this: since I have been of very frail health <note>original: *pertenuis valetudinis*</note> from my earliest years, it has been a great benefit to me at many intervals; for it restrained me from things which a more unrestrained mind and a present opportunity might have persuaded me toward. I have found it to be true that things go well with those who act rightly of their own accord; better with those for whom it is necessary to act as they ought; and best of all for those who are not permitted to commit evils—because the vices of the human race need to be restrained not so much by warnings as by bridles and muzzles <note>original: *frænis & capistris*</note>. Certainly poverty, low spirits, vexation, diseases, and the like do not allow many things to happen which are more easily accomplished elsewhere when the reins are loosened. Yet I would not want this said specifically of you—whom I know to be led by right reason, as well as by the precepts and examples of your household, to be carried toward everything distinguished and noble—but I wish it related so that you may patiently and with a more level mind bear what **GOD** <note>original: *DEUS*</note> disposes for you according to His inscrutable wisdom. And as you feel the lot of human physical imperfection within yourself, may you strive all the more for the integrity of the nobler part of your soul, and embrace the more sublime delights of the mind in place of the baser recreations of the body, and from this, all sick...

<meta>catchword: -ness</meta>

<summary>Johann Valentin Andreae writes to Prince Anton Ulrich, offering the consoling thought that physical illness can serve as a divine "bridle" that restrains the soul from vice and directs it toward higher spiritual and intellectual pursuits.</summary>
<keywords>Anton Ulrich, health, sickness, divine providence, virtue, self-restraint, Johann Valentin Andreae</keywords>

## LETTER 132.

-> Hearty Greetings. <-

As much as there was in you, Reverend Sir, a desire to depart from there, so much was there joy here among us at the prospect of receiving you. ### LETTER 136.

->Greatest Greetings.<-

Just as nothing else happens by chance, I easily believe that those things which occur by reason of health <note>original: *valetudinis*; referring here to illness or physical state</note> are not in vain, unless nature, and He who governs it, wish to turn toward new laws or change something from lesser things. # LETTER 137.
## *To Prince ANTHONY ULRICH.*

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My most Gracious Lord,

When I was just now girding myself to respond to your letters, the ambassadors from Augsburg intervened: Thomas Hopfer, a preacher, and Michael Miller—distinguished men sent out from their fatherland to test our generosity as well in the rebuilding of their sacred house <note>referring to a church in Augsburg requiring reconstruction after the devastation of the Thirty Years' War</note>, for which purpose they had traveled for an entire year through various kingdoms and provinces. When they had been satisfied by my Prince and Master <note>Duke Eberhard III of Württemberg</note>, as much as the present condition of affairs allowed, they hastened to Tübingen and turned aside to visit me. Immediately, they caught sight of **Your Portraits**, which are successfully painted from life <note>original: *ad vivum expressas*</note> and placed in the primary and most prized position among the ornaments in my study <term>Musæo: in the 17th century, a scholar's private library or room for study and collections</term>. They looked upon them, wondering what to praise first or last...

### LETTER CXXXVIII.

->Greetings.<-

->*Reverend and Most Illustrious Sir,*<-

Since it has seemed best to postpone your visit to us to another and more suitable time, it is also our duty to accept this and most willingly grant what is done for the benefit of your health. Meanwhile, we shall always hold the same goodwill toward you as if you were here with us and saw us in person. I am glad to hear that your renowned Tübingen <note>The city and University of Tübingen, where the recipient, Johann Valentin Andreae, was then living</note> has again grown so significantly that it can host any number of more illustrious guests. However, I do not recall seeing the aforementioned *Duke of Holstein* <note>original: "Holsatiæ Ducem"</note>, nor do I quite grasp who that *Son of the King of Denmark* <note>original: "Regis Daniæ Filius"</note> might be, of whom you write that rumor has brought news to you. Indeed, we have long desired such a celebrated home for the Muses <note>a poetic way of referring to a university or center of learning</note>, in which we might stay with profit and devote ourselves to the best disciplines and arts; even now, neither the years nor the inclination would be lacking, if only our *Most Clement Lord Father* <note>Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1579–1666)</note> shared our wishes. Our tutor <note>original: "informator"</note> says that he has not seen all those more distinguished authors whom you have listed, but only the first, Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy." The work mentioned is *De re metallica*, a landmark text on mining and geology</note>, who discusses subterranean mining most excellently; and since he is chiefly occupied with sacred studies, he also asks you for the names of those who are most helpful in unearthing those immense and eternal riches <note>the Prince uses a metaphor: just as Agricola teaches how to mine for ore, he asks for authors who teach how to "mine" for spiritual or theological truth</note> and who show a simpler path of entry. You will perhaps have a large supply of these, but it will be enough to have noted a few of the more select ones. Farewell.

->Your Reverence's.<-

Wolfenbüttel, October 7, 1651.
->Most devotedly,<-
->Ferdinand Albert, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg.<-

THE YEAR 1651. LETTER CXXXIX.

## To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Most Clement Lord,<-

Although your desires are noble and your wishes praiseworthy regarding the growth of your *virtues and studies* <note>original: "Virtutum & studiorum"</note> to be gained abroad, you act more rightly by submitting them to the *wisdom and prudence* of your Most Serene Lord Father. His wisdom, joined with his greatest *goodness and love* for you, cannot fail to decide most perfectly for you and to arrange your affairs most happily. Whichever *seat of the Muses* <note>A poetic term for a university or center of learning</note> finally receives you, I am certain that it will not improve your character and mind as much as you, in turn, will adorn it—following the example of your most praised Father.

Unless it is a burden, please pass on my greetings to your tutor <note>original: "Informatori"</note> and tell him that for investigating the riches of the earth, I believe the reading of the *Veronese Calceolarian Museum* <note>The *Musaeum Calceolarium* was a famous "cabinet of curiosities" or early natural history collection in Verona. This book, published in 1622, was a detailed catalog of minerals, fossils, and biological specimens.</note> brilliantly described by the physician *Andrea Chiocco*, will be of the greatest benefit to him. But if he prefers to unearth the riches of *Heaven* <note>original: "Caeli"</note>, then just as the *Philosopher* <note>likely referring to Aristotle or a similar classical authority</note> once said of *Truth*: first, second, third, and continually the *Bible* must be consulted and unfolded. Anyone is permitted to approach it, yet it is the lot of no mortal to fully exhaust it; truly, it sends no one away who is devoted to its sacred words without making them rich and wealthy.

He will perhaps reply that these things are already known to him, and I can easily believe it; but you also have the best guides at home who can introduce you to these inner shrines and sanctuaries by both voice and example, so that my work is less needed. Farewell, most flourishing Prince, amid the flow of heavenly gifts, *and continue as you are doing.*

<margin>
Bebenhausen,
Oct. 29, 1651.
</margin>

->To Your Most Illustrious Highness,<-
->The most humble client,<-
->Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.<-
