### LETTER CXL.

-> Much Health. <-
<note>original: "S. P.", an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam*, a formal Latin greeting wishing the recipient the greatest health.</note>

*Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir.*

The praise which the *Gentlemen of Augsburg* <note>Augsburg was a major center of banking and culture; the "Gentlemen" likely refers to city officials or patrons who had recognized the Wolfenbüttel court.</note> whom you mentioned left for us, they seem to have also won for themselves. For it is no less a Virtue to acknowledge benefits with a grateful heart—if indeed our actions should be called such—than it is to confer those same benefits upon the well-deserving. I truly wish that enough had been done for them so that they might have something to boast of, and that they might free our mind from anxious care and render us ready and unencumbered for other matters. Whatever praise can be gathered and spoken from this, let it be attributed to GOD, for whose sake this sacred business was undertaken, and by whose breathing grace it will have such great success that even those of a different mindset and party <note>likely referring to theological or political opponents during the post-Thirty Years' War era</note> will finally be forced to confess that we have not yet renounced all good fruit. Instead, they will see that there are many among the companions of our profession for whom religion and other works of holiness are a care; and just as they labor to build outward houses for GOD <note>a reference to the construction or restoration of physical churches</note>, so too in the heart—which we piously gather—they shall leave some seat for Him.

*Our Brother* <note>Referring to Rudolph Augustus, Anthony Ulrich's elder brother</note> unexpectedly returned yesterday with his companions from the *Barby funeral* <note>Barby is a town in Saxony-Anhalt; the funeral likely concerned a member of the local nobility or a relative</note>, at which I know no one else was present other than the *Count of Stolberg* and a certain other man from *Schwarzburg*. Regarding what you predict concerning his future and assistant labor, may God grant that it happens so, and that it turns out most happily, especially as an aid for the old age of *our Distinguished Father* <note>Duke August the Younger (1579–1666), a famous scholar and book collector</note>, and as a benefit and increase for us all. This I myself now pray, and I desire from the bottom of my heart that you also, with your family, may fare well.

-> Your Reverence's <-

*Wolfenbüttel, 18*
*November 1651.*

-> Most Devoted, <-
-> *Anthony Ulrich.* <-

THE YEAR 1651. LETTER 141.

-> Much Health. <-
<note>original: "S. P.", an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam*, a formal Latin greeting wishing the recipient the greatest health.</note>

### Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir.

Those things which one can scarcely hope or expect, I gladly refrain from responding to at length. Such are those matters which you desire for us concerning the continuation of our studies in some foreign but famous seat of the Muses <note>The "Muses" here refers to a university or a center of higher learning.</note>. Since these opportunities seem to be denied to us, we shall nevertheless attempt to progress as far as we can through private work; nor do we doubt that we shall have you, among others, as a companion and most faithful guide. This is something which both your prayers and the feelings of your mind—which agree perfectly with ours—promise as an almost certain fact. Our <term>Tutor: "Informator" in the original, referring to the private educator responsible for the prince’s intellectual and moral formation</term> acknowledges this very thing to you with a grateful heart. Your counsel was most welcome to him, since those things he desired are drawn more safely from the source itself; to these opportunities is added the greatest healthfulness and an abundance of perennial and living waters, which are offered and given freely for the salvation of the soul to us who thirst.

I remember that our friend Mr. Gosky <note>Probably Martin Gosky (1586–1656), a physician and poet at the Wolfenbüttel court.</note> has the *Calceolari Museum* <note>The *Musaeum Calceolarium* (1622) was a famous illustrated catalog of the natural history cabinet of Francesco Calceolari in Verona, Italy. It was a standard reference for early modern "cabinets of curiosity."</note>, in which many things occur that were collected with great zeal and are most worthy of note. Among these is that account of the indomitable diamond—if it is right to believe in a gemstone—that it almost never resists the stroke of a hammer, and can most easily be crushed and ground down in a mortar with an iron pestle. Now for three days and more, we have had such great and constant rains here that the water floods our lands everywhere and blocks the roads. Nothing is yet certain about the winter, except what the annual revolutions of the seasons require. May **GOD** keep us safe and

I am so confirmed and certain of Your most clement mind toward me that I would consider it an insult to even question it. But now, while two-faced Janus <note>original: "Ianus bifrons"; the Roman god of gates and transitions, whose two faces look both to the past year and the coming one.</note> approaches us—at which time it is a Christian custom to offer pious prayers for those you especially wish well or to whom you owe the most—I would be impious and most ungrateful if I did not bring my good words to that place where God has deposited the sum of my earthly good, namely the House of Brunswick <note>original: "Brunoniam Domum"</note>, and to You, its first Prince. Regarding the correspondence of moles <note>original: "naevorum"; birthmarks or skin spots</note> scattered through the body, I myself have experienced it to be so in many examples, not without admiration; I leave the reason for that matter, along with many others, in the depths, because it is far easier to promise an explanation in words than to actually achieve it, even if Septalius himself brings forward arguments that are not improbable. But I leave it free to you what you decide about him. 

As for your condolence for my ill health, which indeed was very difficult for me for over a month and more, I give you immense thanks; and I humbly pray that GOD may hear your pious wishes for me, and that He may continue firm and solid health for you, and crown your years with treasures of mind and body sent down from heaven. Farewell, most illustrious heroine, diamond of the House of Brunswick <note>original: "Brunoniæ Domus"</note>, and continue to favor me.

### THE YEAR 1652. LETTER 148.

->Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir,<-

I was moved in no small measure by your ill health, which you write is fluctuating and being increased by other more serious trials. I truly wish that our modest <note>original: "imbecilliores," literally "weaker" or "feeble"; a term of humility regarding his own writing</note> letters had been of such great efficacy that they could have assisted you in your pain in at least some way, and that more joyful remedies might not be lacking from us in the future, so that you might easily reach your former bodily health. I pray for that health to be firm and whole for you from my heart, along with the most happy course of this year; indeed, I have almost no doubt about a happy outcome, for in the meantime, your condition seems to have settled enough that it will shortly return to a better habit of body and a most longed-for strength. 

Regarding our letters of whatever sort sent this year, there is no reason for you to give great thanks; even your remarkable kindness, with which you have pursued us until now, and your singular devotion demand far greater things so that your wishes may be satisfied. To preserve that goodwill, it will rather be our duty to testify our gratitude to you in whatever way we can. May the most merciful GOD grant that, just as this is done now with words, it may also be done eventually by the deed itself, and indeed face to face; I commit us to His will and His most firm protection.

## LETTER CXLIX.
### To Prince ANTON ULRICH.
### Most Illustrious and High-born Prince, my far most Merciful Lord,

**E**ven if the persistence of my illness is troublesome enough to me, the refreshment I receive from your letters is most pleasant. It was also most effective in reviving my weary spirit and raising my dejected body to hear from your Master Goseky <note>Martin Goseky (1606–1674) was a scholar and tutor to the princes at the court of Wolfenbüttel</note>, a most approved witness of all things, that your Serene Father is even now of

> Such excellent strength of body and mind
> That he breathes no harsh look, nor do his ears ring,
> Nor his eyes stumble; nor his hands tremble;
> Nor does his nose run with the "Pleiades" <note>original: "Virgiliis," a poetic reference to the Pleiades stars, which were associated with the rainy season and here used as a metaphor for a runny nose or catarrh</note>, nor does a dry wrinkle
> Seize his brow, nor does pain pierce his head:
> Nor does a storm of diseases twist him, whether from the heat,
> Or the rains of the brain, or the thunder of the stomach.

These all lean upon him as their pillar; he is like a crown of that Restored Peace <note>A reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War; Augustus was seen as a stabilizing figure in the post-war recovery</note> (that peace being fixed and firm, and he being its garland). I, along with everyone who desires the common Good, pray earnestly that he may remain unwithering for a long time to come.

## LETTER CL.

->To the Very Reverend and<-
->Most Distinguished Sir,<-

I see that I remain so firmly fixed in Your mind that, although you are struggling with many difficulties of illnesses and other adversities, no forgetfulness of me takes hold of You in the meantime, as is often wont to happen at other times in such a disturbance of the body and senses. Therefore, I cannot do otherwise than acknowledge this singular love of Yours with a most grateful heart, and respond to it as much as the brevity of time now allows. The new cycle of this year will be able to provide the occasion for this, which indeed has long since had its beginning, yet is not yet led to its end; within whose span, fortune can weigh down our lot in various ways, so that it may not seem absurd to forestall with God, almost every single day and with as much speed and constancy of prayer as we can, whatever calamities may happen. Indeed, I congratulate myself greatly that in this spring of your life and in such a gathering of Illustrious pleasures, my funeral dirges <note>original: "capularis neniae," literally "songs of the coffin-edge," referring to the writings of an old man like Andreae which he expects the young prince might find morbid or dull.</note> do not yet seem so loathsome to You that You should not think they ought to be called forth further, or as I interpret it, commanded from me. Since I attribute this deservedly both to the indulgence of Your Most Serene Lord Father <note>Duke Augustus the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note> and to Your own ease and readiness, I think I must take serious care lest, by producing too many of them or by troublesome interruptions, I should cause weariness. I wish the present and future age to know how much your letters mean to me, and to set them forth as an example; I would wish that it remain unknown to both how much my own letters, compared to them, wither, become cheap, and grow obsolete, lest Your glory produce my infamy. Yet the closer I see the end of my life approaching, the more ardently I shall think I must labor so that, with what strength of mind and body remains in me, I may prove to You and Yours—if not erudition, then certainly zeal; if little labor, then at least much loyalty; if nothing of delight, then much of obedience and devotion. And so I may reverently [hold] you who are absent and (O, may God grant it) one day present...

### & Weimar,
### Most Serene and High Prince,
### Most Merciful Lord,

As soon as it was reported to me that Your Serene Highness had been established and declared Head of the most Illustrious and renowned Fruitbearing Society <note>The *Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft* was the first and most important German literary society, founded in 1617 to promote the German language and literature.</note>, by the greatest merit of virtue and dignity and by the public consensus of the order, I rejoiced incredibly; and I congratulated Your Highness on this wise judgment of the Society, as well as the Society itself, to which much splendor will be added from Your light, with a prayerful heart. -> To Prince ANTON ULRICH. <-

## Most Illustrious and High Princes,
## Lords by far most Clement.

I could announce nothing so joyful or desirable to myself as that my little gifts <note>original: "Xeniola mea." From the Greek *xenia*, these refer to small tokens of friendship or guest-gifts, specifically the engravings and globe-maps mentioned on the previous page.</note> were not unwelcome to you. Whenever I understand that these items are of use to your affairs and your studies, I count it as my greatest gain and a part of my happiness. You are quite right to apply such things not so much for the delight of the eyes as for the instruction of the mind, which will one day render you as Knowing and Wise Princes—indeed, as auspicious rulers of men. 

As for your accusation regarding the infrequency of my letters, I attribute this to your excessive favor toward me; for I do not know of any occasion for replying to yours that I have ever missed. Truthfully, I am weary of being able to announce nothing about myself except for querulous and morose news, as I would much prefer to report things that are joyful and pleasing to you. I pray for the auspicious arrival of the Most Serene Lord Elector of Cologne <note>Maximilian Henry of Bavaria (1621–1688), the Prince-Archbishop and Elector of Cologne.</note> to you; the reading of your letters regarding this matter will bring me the greatest pleasure. Farewell again and again, most flourishing Princes, most happy branches <note>original: "palmites." A botanical metaphor comparing the young princes to the fruitful new growth of a noble vine.</note> of illustrious virtues, and look upon me with favor.

-> Of Your Illustrious Highnesses, <-

Bebenhausen, March 3rd,
In the Year 1653.

The most humble client,
Johann Valentin Andreae,
Doctor of Theology.

# LETTER 156.
### To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA.

-> Most Illustrious and High Princess, <-
-> *Heroine by far most gracious to me.* <-

**T**ruly, you could have prayed for nothing more desirable or more necessary for me from God the Best and Greatest than better health, and more constant health at that, since adverse health is never kind, and at intervals breaks out more harshly and mercilessly. I count the hours before noon as profit, which I devote to my duties and labors. But immediately after any food—taken however moderately or for medicinal purposes—my tormentor, my stomach, seizes me and treats me inhumanly, so that I drag through the rest of the day with difficulty, and spend the night sleepless amidst sobs <note>original: "singultus," which can mean gasping, sobbing, or hiccups, here indicating severe gastric distress.</note>, and weary, I wait for the dawn. Such a life could more rightly be called a perpetual dying, were it not that the supreme and most just Judge of our life and death commands us to live so; to obey Him is the best and most whole... <note>The text cuts off mid-word at "saluberr-", intended to be "saluberrimum" or "most beneficial."</note>

->Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,<-
->Most Merciful Young Lady.<-

Whether it was my own curiosity, or an honest and excusable desire to know if you had devoted any effort to the French language <note>original: "Gallicæ etiam linguæ"</note> amidst your distinguished studies, the inquiry certainly turned out happily for me. For I have obtained your elegant letters written in that language, and I have become more certain of your praiseworthy progress in every kind of knowledge. That language has indeed gained a preeminent place in every German Court due to its charm <note>original: "leporem"</note>, and I am still wonderfully delighted by reading it, even though my own practical use of it has grown cold. But what delighted me above all was seeing that whatever exists in every faculty, science, art, discipline, and knowledge of things has been successfully translated into French from the source languages <note>original: "Matricibus linguis," referring to Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note>, so that a Frenchman of more noble birth and inquisitive mind can find his own native tongue entirely sufficient for his needs. Our own Germans have dared to do the same, now that the barbarism of the previous century has been removed and the culture of letters reborn—especially the Swiss—though with a harsher sound and further removed from the original sources. I wish that our "Fruit-bearers" <note>The *Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft* (Fruit-bearing Society) was the first German literary society, dedicated to the refinement and standardization of the German language.</note> would soften this harshness, occupying themselves not so much with anxiously and superstitiously polishing letters and words, but rather, along with Opitz, von Werder, Hübner, and others <note>Martin Opitz, Dietrich von dem Werder, and Tobias Hübner were prominent poets and members of the Fruit-bearing Society who translated foreign classics into German.</note>, with transporting the delicacies and delights of foreign languages into our mother tongue. But let others tell you of these matters. It is my duty, if I have pried too untimely into your studies, to ask for your pardon, to extol your courtesy, and to offer the greatest thanks I can for your pious prayers, by which you desire my health to be eased and supported. I share your desire that we might see one another, even though for me, while I draw the Lord’s yoke, and

### LETTER CLIX.

->Heartiest Greetings.<-

->Most Reverend and Most Distinguished Man,<-

I am not so fastidious that I would wish to look down upon those things which I myself plan at last to reach, or at least ought to: namely, your venerable age and the more mature fruits of your intellect, which may now be hoped for and gathered in abundance. ### LETTER CLXV.
#### *To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA.*

->Most Illustrious and High Princess,<-
->Most Gracious Lady.<-

For your pious and most kind compassion for my infirmity, I return great and most humble thanks, and I pray suppliantly to God that you may never have need of such sympathy in your life. Furthermore, I am not now experiencing the discomforts of old age and the common lot of man for the first time in this, the sixty-sixth year of my age; rather, I have led almost my whole life as an old man. That is to say, I have had as constant companions various symptoms of physical defects, which vary with every change in the breeze and which usually accompany a body of the most delicate constitution. Thus, old age brings almost nothing unusual to me, except that—like travelers who are burdened and weary—the longer the journey they make, the more they grow faint and the more ardently they pant for the destination. 

Truly, as many companions as I had in my childhood, adolescence, and youth—men of healthy, excellent, and robust temperament—have all long since met their final day. I have been left behind, weak and bound to a strict <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "ad amussim victus astricto" — literally "bound to the ruler's line of living," referring to a highly disciplined diet and lifestyle required to maintain his fragile health.</note> of living; no one would have ever promised that I would reach manhood (the age at which I immediately turned gray), let alone a more advanced age. There is therefore no reason why I should complain about old age, which most people curse...

be able to be known: But I think it cannot be denied that the *French Language*, if one takes away the *Latin* and *Greek* <note>original: *Latina & Græca*</note>, suffers from a supreme poverty of words, and is entirely unsuitable for translations; but from this fact a supreme suitability is added to it: that any Latin and Greek words, once French articles are applied and the pronunciation adjusted, become French; and so any translation of the arts or disciplines, and the knowledge of these, is not impossible for the French, provided they know Greek and Latin. 

However, the property and genius of our *German language* <note>original: *Germanicæ... linguæ*</note>, which you mentioned, as a mother tongue <note>original: *matricis* — a "matrix" or source language, emphasizing German as a primary language rather than one derived from Latin.</note>, seems to stand apart; it is indeed most copious, and successfully equipped with the skill of compounding words, but it is not usually honored with any other study for learning, besides that which is commonly known: for common usage is ignorant of the technical terms of the arts. Therefore, I think the purpose of certain members of the Fruit-bearing Society <note>The *Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft* (Fruit-bearing Society) was the first and largest German language academy, founded in 1617 to standardize and promote the German language as a literary and scientific tongue.</note> is worthy of praise, as they strive to demonstrate the foundations of the German <note>original: *Teutiscæ*</note> language more deeply and to instill a love of learning in the youth. I shall gladly await your judgment. Farewell. Given at *Wolfenbüttel, April 27, in the Year 1652.*

->To Your Reverence<-
->devotedly attached<-
->Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick & Lüneburg<-

<meta>This page concludes Letter 167, written by the theologian Johann Valentin Andreae to Princess Sibylla Ursula of Brunswick-Lüneburg. Andreae is responding to the Princess's previous points regarding the limitations of the German language in technical and scientific contexts.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>
<header>THE YEAR 1652</header>

...[by which] you have educated [me]. In this one thing, however, we seem to disagree: that while you readily grant the abundance of words and the richness of our mother tongue <note>original: *Maternæ nostræ linguæ*</note>, you nonetheless deny its suitability for expressing technical terms of the arts, because it stays further away from mixing in such things from Greek and Latin.

But I, on the contrary, confidently assert that our language possesses this suitability and all other necessary qualities. I remember seeing the more obscure parts of Euclid and all the technical terms of mathematics <note>original: *Matheseos*</note> successfully expressed in our German vernacular, and correctly understood by unlettered craftsmen. It seems to me that nothing is missing for this excellent goal except for our own effort and regular use, which soften even the most difficult attempts. 

Of this, even the single example of the "learned dust" <note>original: *Eruditi pulveris* — a classical idiom referring to the sand-table used by ancient mathematicians like Archimedes for drawing geometric figures; here it refers to scholarly mathematical work.</note> of Maurice of Nassau, which is available in the Dutch language, could be enough to rouse our spirit. Hence I repeat my prayer, that those from the Fruit-bearing Society <note>The *Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft*, of which Andreae was a member, sought to prove German could be a language of high culture and science.</note> who are strong in intellect and skill in the arts might contribute not only poetic elegances and flowers to the cultivation of our vernacular, but also the knowledge of the arts and sciences through a fitting translation of technical terms <note>original: *Terminorum*</note>. In this way, they would bring the wisdom of Greece and Rome <note>original: *Græciamq; & Latium*</note> into their own Fatherland, thereby deserving the highest and most noble praise. 

But I say these things more to elicit another of your most pleasant letters than to appoint myself either as a judge or an instructor. Everywhere there is enough literature and knowledge; would that there were as much faith and conscience, which may Christ further root and confirm as heavenly gifts within you. Farewell, renowned Princess, and look with favor [upon me].

<margin>
Bebenhausen,
May 19, 1652.

->Much Greeting<-

Truly, *Reverend Sir*, the letters you continue to send so abundantly are of great benefit to us. From them, we can clearly see that the strength of your mind is quite different from that of your body—which, as you have several times written to us yourself, has now become greatly weakened. I truly grieve for your situation, and I pray from my heart that you may soon regain your former vigor and health. It seems only right that the body should match the mind, so that such a noble guest <note>original: *hospiti* — a common philosophical metaphor where the soul or mind is a "guest" residing in the "domicile" of the body.</note> might have a dwelling place that is sturdy and well-equipped in every way—if not for the sake of assistance, then at least for the sake of dignity.

Since I have mentioned a "guest," you should know that about two weeks ago, His Serene Highness the Elector of Cologne, *Lord Maximilian Henry, Prince* <note>Maximilian Henry of Bavaria (1621–1688), who served as the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne.</note>, arrived here from the neighborhood. He is a Prince distinguished by his courtesy, the kindness of his expression, and—as it certainly appeared—his great devotion. I might say the same for almost his entire company, which included Counts and Barons of the highest rank, many nobles, and others. Indeed, the quartermaster <note>original: *designatore diversoriorum* — the official responsible for arranging housing and stables for a traveling court.</note> counted one hundred and sixty-four horses and nearly as many people. We showed them as much honor and respect as the short duration of their stay permitted. 

For they departed again the very next day, having also visited our noble kinsmen <note>original: *Agnatos* — male-line relatives, referring here to the Ducal family of Württemberg whom Andreae served.</note> living nearby. It is still uncertain how long they will remain in the neighboring Bishopric. May God grant that these visits contribute much to the goodwill [of all]...

## LETTER 169.
### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Most Clement Lord,<-

*Whether you perceive any remains of vitality in this weak body of mine, I do not see; I attribute these flatteries to your courtesy. Indeed, I am dealing with a disease which the Greeks call maransis* <note>original: μάρανσιν — a medical term for a wasting away or decay of the body, often associated with old age.</note> *and the Latins call decay* <note>original: *marcorem* — a withering or fading of strength.</note>*, which dulls, casts down, and exhausts all the intellect. Nor, in truth, did a vessel of bronze ever fall to my lot as a home for my soul, but rather one of clay or earthenware* <note>Andreae uses the metaphor of the body as a "vessel" (vas) for the soul; a "bronze" vessel would be strong, while his is "testaceum" (made of fired clay) or "luteum" (made of mud/unfired clay).</note>*. Thus it was all the more necessary for me to keep it from those shocks, lest it be shattered by a blow—though Death itself has long since crushed most of it, while I am even now floating in the marsh* <note>The "marsh" (palude) here serves as a metaphor for the stagnant, difficult state of his final years or his physical infirmity.</note>*. I count the meeting of the Most Serene and Most Auspicious Elector of Cologne with your Lord Father among the good omens of a pacified Germany. But if there is in the Elector that goodness of nature and perfection of character which you, along with others, proclaim, and which is innate to the House of Bavaria, then there is for us a surer hope of a more solid and lasting con-*

### LETTER 171.

#### TO PRINCE FERDINAND ALBRECHT.

### LETTER CLXXIII.

->To Prince ANTHONY ULRICH.<-
->Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord.<-

Out of all those things, both joyful and desired, which you have brought to my attention, the prize for me is the safety and enduring vigor of your Most Serene Lord Father. Such blessings are joined not only to your own particular happiness, but to the welfare of the entire Roman Empire <note>original: *salute totius imperii Romani* — referring to the Holy Roman Empire, of which the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel was a part.</note>. These are things which all good men demand from heaven with their prayers; and that the divine powers might long grant them is what I gladly and deservedly profess to be my primary duty. It would be a small thing for me to labor and be consumed, for I have nothing that the Christian Commonwealth <term>Christian Commonwealth (Respublica Christiana): an idealized vision of a unified European society governed by Christian ethics and intellectual cooperation</term> might expect from me, or in which it might lose anything. 

Indeed, I truly congratulate you that by pious supplication you have unlocked heaven and obtained a generous rain to revive the parched earth. For thus we are taught by the Psalmist in the 67th hymn, verse 10 <note>original: *Psalmista edocti hymno LXVII. v. X.* — In modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 68:9: "You, O God, sent a plentiful rain, whereby you did confirm your inheritance, when it was weary."</note>, that the fertility of the earth is to be sought not from the arrangement or aspects of the stars <note>Andreae here prioritizes divine providence over the astrological "aspects" or positions of planets, which were a common focus of the era.</note>, but from the same Ruler. The storehouse for sustaining life is not to be attributed to anything but prayers for its present use, and it must be replenished time and again in the future. 

How wise indeed are those who keep the granaries of God ready and open for feeding the starving Lazarus <note>referring to the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus in Luke 16</note> and caring for the one covered in sores, rather than for enriching merchants of purple and fine linen <note>original: *Purpureis Bißiq;* (byssique) — a reference to the "purple and fine linen" worn by the rich man in the Gospel.</note>, or for fattening the servants of gluttony and greed! Let them not store up for themselves a "treasure of wrath for the day of wrath" and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God (Luke 16, Romans 2) along with the Rich Man <note>original: *Epulone* — "Epulo" or "Dives" is the traditional name given to the unnamed rich man in the parable of Luke 16.</note>, whose infamous memory is recorded there, while the Church now honors the memory of the other. But I do not wish to mix this sweeter Philosophy with the pleasantries due to a letter; rather, I thank you for the ease with which you excused my indolence, and for the sincerity with which you correctly understood that what was written to your Brother pertains to you as well...

## LETTER CLXXIV.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Excellent Lord Doctor, my most beloved friend,*<-

I have duly received your most recent letter, and I have most gladly read and reread everything you assert at length regarding the promotion of the study of the German language. I found it quite delightful because I feel exactly the same way on this matter. Hitherto, our mother tongue has been learned in no other way than commonly from common use, and therefore the name "Vernacular" <note>original: *Vernaculæ* — derived from *verna*, a house-born slave; here implying a language learned naturally at home rather than through formal study.</note> is not undeservedly given to it. However, if a regular method of cultivation and the refinement of the arts were applied to it, it could lay aside this label of commonness, just as once in Rome a distinction became known between the common tongue and the Roman language <note>The writer refers to the historical distinction between *Sermo Vulgaris* (the speech of the people) and Classical Latin (the language of literature and law).</note>. A certain and stable system of instruction—both for using the language correctly and for preserving and expanding our speech—seems to be required among the Germans. It is indeed true that outstanding works by learned men, who have joined the **Fruitbearing Society**, currently exist <term>Fruitbearing Society (Societas Fructifera): Founded in 1617, this was the most significant German literary society, dedicated to the standardization and "purification" of the German language from foreign (especially French and Latin) influences.</term>. From these works, the beauty, eloquence, abundance, and fitness of this language becomes daily more known; a perfect...

## LETTER CLXXV.

### *To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA.*

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,**<-
->**Lady most gracious by far,**<-

That you deign to honor me with the continuation of your most elegant letters, I accept as a great and most certain sign of favor; and because you refresh me greatly with them in my weakness <note>Andreae often complained of his failing health and "languor" in his later years</note>, I willingly profess that I owe you infinitely. Just as my own letters lack the bloom and fragrance of yours, I must seek from elsewhere ways to season my tasteless writings, so that I might present them to you with less distaste. But while this prison of the body holds me here, and this desert itself produces nothing noble or clever of its own accord, I yield, and I depend entirely upon your generosity, which is joined with incredible courtesy.

I come, however, to your letter, where you rightly and skillfully advise that a more abundant Lexicon is needed to advance our vernacular tongue and adapt it for the arts and sciences. Long ago, the incomparable Christopher Helwig <note>original: *Ch. Helvicus* (1581–1617), a German chronologist and theologian</note>—a man matchless in piety, erudition, industry, and perpetual labor (which is the four-horse chariot of perfection)—undertook this Herculean venture in imitation of the Italian *Accademia della Crusca* <note>The oldest linguistic academy in the world, founded in Florence to purify the Italian language</note>. He was brought to Augsburg by the Ratichian method <note>original: *Ratichiano commento* — referring to the educational reforms of Wolfgang Ratke, which emphasized learning the mother tongue before Latin</note> and supported by great expense; but those works which were begun, and for a large part finished, perished <note>original: *occubuere* (from catchword)</note> with the author himself, to the greatest loss of the German cause...

*...for me, and a relief for my weary body, for which reason I both give the greatest thanks and pray for this perpetual favor of yours toward me. We in these parts are being harshly tried by an unkind sky, by the greater force of a storm, frequently struck by lightning, cast down by hail, washed away by clouds, and scorched by the north wind, with the greatest destruction of pastures, crops, orchards, and vineyards, and with some loss of men and animals—certainly a sad omen, or perhaps a prelude to impending evils, for the averting of which I worship a merciful God.* <note>Andreae is likely referring to the severe summer storms that often devastated agricultural communities in the 17th century, which were frequently interpreted as divine warnings.</note> *Meanwhile, I wonder at our prognosticators* <note>astrologers and makers of almanacs</note> *that they smelled out nothing of this instability nor indicated it to us—to me, an indubitable proof of their vanity* <note>original: "inanitatis"; meaning emptiness or lack of substance</note> *whenever I see them predict a hot summer, a cold winter, and indeed the remaining parts of the year in a mixed fashion, quite probably, yet never consistently. It is easy to guess how much they should be believed regarding the power of the stars over the minds of men, the fates of the Church, and the affairs of states, when they pronounce so slipperily about the disposition of the weather.*

*But I would not wish to provoke this threatening race of men; it is enough for me to be tranquil and secure in mind from their ambiguous oracles. Indeed, I would never persuade your Illustrious heart to submit itself to such nonsense* <note>original: "næniis"; literally "dirges" or "trifles," implying old wives' tales</note> *of the constellations, which fill the mind with vain curiosity and terrify it, but empty and enervate it from noble and prudent counsels and actions, and finally expose it to mockery and wild regret.*

*But to where the calamity of my native soil has carried me! Rather, let me do this: pray for all things joyful and fertile for you; a safe and flourishing House; a Court established as an example; harmonious neighbors; happy lands; and promoted studies and arts. To you, Illustrious Prince, I pray for years increased with goods and gifts, and glory crowning you from every side; which he vows with humble prayer,*

->Your Illustrious Highness’s<-

->most humble client,<-
->Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor.<-
Bebenhausen, July 14,
the year 1652.

->Many greetings.<-

While you say it is a matter of great pride <note>original: "palmarium"; literally a masterpiece or something worthy of a victory palm</note> for you to see our **Merciful Lord Father** <note>This refers to Duke Augustus the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1579–1666), Andreae's patron</note> long safe and surviving for our lives and the lives of others, you truly seem to snatch the palm of victory from everyone else. Hence, so that this prosperity of life in our **Merciful Lord Father** may always continue and increase, and never be pressed down by any weight of evils, we—together with you—invoke **GOD** with most ardent prayers. And just as we obtained most timely rains for the recent drought of the land, so also in these harvests we hope for the most desired success and blessing.

What you write about yourself so sparingly and modestly seems to us to be of the greatest importance. For it is no light thing for the primary part of any house to be destroyed or consumed, for in that way a greater evil—namely the shaking and demolition of the rest—will follow. You are this primary part, *Reverend Sir*, in the house of our GOD; while you remain safe, many can still be led to salvation, but if you fall, there is a danger that others too will perish. Therefore, as much as you take away from your own credit due to your accustomed modesty, so much do we bestow in due praise, so that it may seem to you that more is increased in you than consumed, and more is added than taken away.

Eight days ago, among other illustrious persons, there came to us **His Highness Prince Manfred from your house**, not only for the sake of greeting or visiting us, but for a far greater cause: namely love, and that a most burning love, by which—so that more freely...

### LETTER CLXXIX.
### To Prince ANTON ULRICH.

#### Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
#### Lord of far-reaching Clemency,

As much as firm health and consequently alacrity of mind departs from me, so much does it remain with your Most Serene Lord Father <note>Duke Augustus the Younger, then 73 years old.</note>—though he is older than me by seven years and four months—which I both infinitely rejoice in and willingly accept as a most abundant compensation for my own misfortune. For I know that the salvation of Germany and the glory of our age turn upon this; I freely acknowledge that the loss of myself is the lightest of all, however much you might flatter me. In addition, there arrived the most welcome news concerning the closer marriage alliance of the Most Illustrious Prince Manfred of Württemberg <note>Manfred (1626–1662) was of the Württemberg-Weiltingen line.</note> with you through the Royal House of Oldenburg, for which I congratulate you from my heart and rejoice for us. ### LETTER CLXXXI.
->Sends many greetings.<-

Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir,
Regarding what you write about the extreme severity of the weather <note>original: "cœli intemperie," literally "the intemperance of the sky."</note> in your climate, we have experienced the same with equal or even far greater loss and damage. I can hardly describe the droughts, winds, lightning, thunder, and other turbulent storms we have faced here as well. Consequently, we should expect not a bountiful harvest this year, but rather more widespread and frequent diseases. Many are still vulnerable to these, and many have been completely overcome by them, so that they cannot enjoy or find pleasure in any way in what little happiness remains to us in these times. Not long ago, two corpses <note>original: "cadavera"</note> of travelers were found in these nearby fields. Already decaying from exposure and breathing out worms from their rotting entrails, we first thought—with shock, as it was right in the vicinity of our castle—that they had been struck down by the cruelty of bandits <note>original: "latrocinantium," referring to the highwaymen and lawless soldiers common after the Thirty Years' War.</note>,

...but from many and most certain circumstances it later became known that it had been struck by lightning <note>original: "fulmine"</note>, as has happened elsewhere too. From these things it is also clear to you what the calamity is of both our land <note>original: "fundi," literally "soil" or "estate"</note> and the stars <note>original: "syderum"</note>. As for why the observers <note>astrologers and meteorologists</note> of these things did not warn us beforehand, or so rarely agree at other times, there is no reason for you to wonder. For it is known that the motion of the heavens <note>original: "coeli motum"</note> is extremely rapid, and accordingly the scheme <term>schema: a celestial map or horoscope showing the positions of the planets</term> of the same changes in many ways in the space of a single moment. It can easily happen, therefore, that their own minds are swept away and generally find themselves in various states. I add that there are many other causes of these effects, lying hidden not only in the sky but also on earth—the varying constitution of different horizons—so that it seems almost impossible that they could all equally produce something certain. Much less, however, can this happen in natural inclinations, as you rightly write; and accordingly you see more than they claim to have foreseen themselves. An occasion will be given to respond concerning more of these things. Meanwhile, fare you well, and continue to educate me with these things.

->*To the Reverend Sir,*<-

### L E T T E R CLXXXIII.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Man,<-
->Honorable Doctor, and dearly beloved<-
->Friend,<-

Yesterday, as is my frequent habit to refresh my mind when it is weary from my duties, I turned to your *Augustalia* by Selenus <note>The *Augustalia Seleniana* was a collection of writings and tributes associated with Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who used the scholarly pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus." Andreae was a close friend and correspondent of the Duke.</note>, and having been abundantly restored, partly by the pleasant variety of the material and partly by the elegance and weight of the style, I finally fell into contemplation of the Reverend and Venerable Andrean Icon <note>original: "Iconis Andreanæ," likely referring to a portrait of Johann Valentin Andreae himself or a prominent member of his family included in the Duke’s book.</note>. I then noticed that this very day on which those Selenian *Augustalia* were delighting me was the 17th of August. I realized that on this same day, through the paternal favor of the Highest Power and Preserver of life, you have completed your sixty-sixth year of age. I considered it my duty, by this letter as a testimony of my perpetual love for you, to congratulate you from the heart on this occasion. I rejoice for myself that throughout the course of these past most sorrowful years <note>A reference to the hardships of the Thirty Years' War and its aftermath, which devastated the German lands.</note>, a merciful GOD has kept you safe and unharmed, advanced you, and crowned you with longevity and a vigorous old age. I adore His omnipotence, praying that He may further cherish, support, and protect you in this advanced age; that He may refresh the strength of your body along with your sound senses and gifts of the mind; and that He may grant you the years of Moses <note>A biblical reference to Moses living to 120 years (Deuteronomy 34:7).</note>. May He so bless your other affairs with divine and earthly goods, and with manifold blessings in every coming and going, so that you may long remain for His Church—

# LETTER CLXXXIV.

->To the Very Reverend Lord Abbot,<-
->Most honored friend,<-

One and then another week has passed, where every day some hindrance was not lacking to prevent me from being able to return my turn of responding; I hope, however, to compensate for the delay of my response in some way with the news of an announcement that will not be unwelcome: For just this past week, without doubt by singular divine Providence, my most beloved sister Clara Augusta <note>Clara Augusta of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1632–1700)</note> was betrothed to the Most High Prince Frederick of your House of Württemberg <note>Prince Frederick of Württemberg-Neuenstadt (1615–1682). This marriage represented a significant political and familial alliance between the two ducal houses.</note>; may the Thrice-Greatest and Best God <note>original: "Ter Optimus Maximus," a common Christian adaptation of the Roman title for Jupiter, used here to refer to the Holy Trinity.</note> grant that this most sacred covenant may turn to the benefit and splendor of both houses! Of which I certainly do not doubt, since fortune and prosperity are accustomed to go as companions whenever such a matter is begun, concluded, and piously recommended to the heavens themselves, well and with God, with the consent of parents, and the common wish of all. I did not wish to hide this love and the sacred rite <note>original: "Sacrum," referring to the religious solemnity of the marriage contract.</note> of the future marriage from you on this occasion.

->Farewell<-

## LETTER CLXXXVII.

### *To PRINCE ANTHONY ULRICH.*

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->My Most Merciful Lord,<-

From your twin joys, I easily predict a doubled happiness for us, and I pray as a suppliant that God may ratify our vows and grant that they be auspicious. From this, beyond the usual joys, some hope is born in me that—before the burial which my chronic illness, worsening with my age, threatens—it may yet happen that I look upon and venerate the branches and saplings of the **Augustan Oak** <note>original: "AUGUSTÆ quercus." A play on the name of Duke Augustus the Younger, Anthony Ulrich's father and Andreae’s patron. The "branches and saplings" refer to the Duke's children.</note> in person. This is after I was denied the chance to see the tree itself and the most celebrated arboretum of Germany, which was among my greatest desires. To this hope I apply the words of Simeon: *Now you let your servant depart in peace* <note>original: "Nunc dimittis animam," referring to the Nunc Dimittis (Luke 2:29), suggesting the author is ready to die once he sees these princes.</note>. Furthermore, just as we promise ourselves the best things from the illustrious virtue of your Most High Sister; so in turn we pledge equal things regarding our renowned **Frederick**, whose goodness of nature, generosity of spirit, and loveliness of character—along with his fervor for Religion and his steady course of Justice—exactly reflect the true image of his Serene Lord Father, **John Frederick**, surnamed the **Titus of Württemberg** <note>John Frederick (1582–1628) was Duke of Württemberg; he was compared to the Roman Emperor Titus for his benevolence.</note>, to be devoted to the public welfare. 

But joys were also recently born in our own Court, with the happy birth of a Prince, the thirteenth offspring of this fruitful and most Illustrious lineage; let us make pious vows to GOD so that each and every one of these may contribute to the growth of Religion and our territories. Truly let the expected day come, O let it come, on which the Dukes **Frederick** and **Manfred** might bring **Clara Augusta** and **Juliana**—those new stars—and lead them into their marriage chambers, accompanied by that retinue of yours which we long to see with our own eyes. In the meantime, it shall be my duty to zealously seek all happiness for you and for us before GOD with burning prayers. Farewell again, most Noble—

### Most Reverend & Excellent
### Sir,

The joy I receive from absent friends is truly great when, through gracious letters, they offer me testimony of the memory they keep of me; but it is far greater when those friends are not common or ordinary, but excellent in learning, in goodness, and in merit. Consider now, *Your Reverend Lordship*, how—waking me as if from a certain sleep—you have sweetly restored my weary spirits with your most pleasant letter of the 17th of last month. By this letter, I see clearly not only that you deem me worthy of your most singular favors, but that you were also pleased, with such complete diligence, to recommend my person to such a great and most August Prince. Such a one is *His Serene Highness of Lüneburg*, the *Phoenix of Potentates* <note>A "Phoenix" was a common Baroque metaphor for a person of unique and incomparable excellence.</note> of this century, for whose incomparable clemency toward me I return infinite thanks. I pray to our Lord God that He grant to *His Serene Highness* that fullness and fulfillment of His most exquisite gifts and graces which he deserves for his most high virtues—which are easy to envy, difficult to imitate, and impossible to explain.

Within a few days, I shall deliver, according to my promise, to *Mr. Hirs* the portrait of our more than most beloved *Mr. Philipp Hainhofer* <note>Philipp Hainhofer (1578–1647) was a famous art collector and merchant-diplomat from Augsburg.</note>, my uncle, may he be in glory. His daughters send this to *Your Reverend Lordship* with their due reverence. Because it was made at the very hour <note>This likely refers to a "deathbed portrait," a common practice intended to capture a person's final, true likeness.</note> that he surrendered his soul to his Creator, believe me, *Your Reverend Lordship*, it is more lifelike and natural than the other two painted many years ago. In the remain—

### LETTER 192.

->Most Reverend and<-
->Distinguished Sir,<-

Since we must so greatly fear those over-confident soothsayers <note>original: "ariolis," a term often used pejoratively for superstitious astrologers or diviners.</note> of whom we have made mention between us until now, I also gladly dismiss them and leave them to the protection of others, against whom the authority of all who perceive the truth cries out. However, regarding those aggressive interpreters of the stars <note>original: "interpretes astrorum," referring to astrologers who claimed to predict the future with certainty.</note>, even if they are held most harshly and are cast out from the respectable company of men by the ancient decree of the Jurists <note>The Duke refers to the "Codex Justinianus," which contained Roman laws strictly banning the practice of astrology and divination as harmful to the state.</note>, what will happen if they designate a more dangerous exile for us, as we read happened to **Vitellius**? <note>Aulus Vitellius (15–69 AD) was Roman Emperor for eight months; his reign was marked by conflict with astrologers (Chaldeans), whom he attempted to banish from Italy.</note> For when he, among the first affairs of his Empire, was also expelling the Astrologers from the city and ordering them by a published edict to depart from all Italy within a set time, they conversely described for him on their tablets the day of the night within which he would depart from life—which they say was indeed done with great persistence. Among us, indeed, not everyone has had such a harvest <note>A metaphor for one's lot in life or the outcome of one's endeavors.</note> as they themselves desired; nevertheless, there was as much as seems sufficient for everyone. We live content with this and pray to GOD that He may wish to bless it and most mercifully preserve it for our use. I ask that you explain at more length in the future what the final punishment of that criminal man was; for I already have many examples of this kind from the tragic histories of others at hand. Meanwhile, farewell.

->Your Reverence<-

Wolfenbüttel, 28th of September, 1652.
Your most devoted,

### To Prince FERDINAND ALBERT.

->**Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,**<-
->**My Most Gracious Lord,**<-

I strongly praise your judgment regarding the divining astrologers, both the more insolent ones and the more modest ones. I consider the former to be tricksters <note>original: "praestigiatoribus," implying those who use illusions or "sleight of hand" to deceive the public.</note> while they cast out their Delphic Oracles <note>A reference to the cryptic and often misleading prophecies of the ancient Greek Oracle at Delphi.</note> to satisfy the curiosity of the common people, often throwing sound political advice into confusion. However, I recognize the latter—the investigators of celestial motions and actions—as Philosophers and Physicists when they apply probable conjecture to practical matters <note>original: "rebus Oeconomicis," referring to the management of a household, agriculture, or the state.</note>. Among these, **Abdias Trew** <note>Abdias Trew (1597–1669) was a Professor of Mathematics and Physics at the University of Altdorf, known for his work in astronomy and "physical" astrology.</note> is a particular favorite of mine. I prefer his <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>Tables providing the positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</note> to those of many others, for I am not myself entirely ignorant of the astrological art. If his works contain a sprinkling of "curiosities," I believe they are included for the sake of the marketplace—so that his wares might be properly sold and the printer not suffer a loss due to the competition from street-peddlers—rather than being his own serious or heartfelt conviction. I hear now for the first time that this most distinguished man of sound judgment is not held in high regard according to his dignity and merits, and I grieve at it; yet I am not unaware that the best citizens often find their own fatherland to be a stepmother <note>A Latin idiom ("patriam suam novercam habere") meaning one is poorly treated by their own country while being more valued abroad.</note>, and are less esteemed at home than they are elsewhere, often to the great detriment of the public welfare. 

Meanwhile, my mind is fixed on that perpetual opinion regarding the dominion of the stars over us, which I remember expressing once in the birth-chart of the *Christian Cosmoxenus* <note>original: "Christiani Cosmoxeni genitura." The "Cosmoxenus" (World-Guest) was a pseudonym and character used by Johann Valentin Andreae in his writings to represent a Christian pilgrim or stranger in the world.</note>: namely, that the stars have no rights over a person who devotes and yields himself to God, the Arbiter of the stars. Instead, the stars are a subject and a support, since even the Sun itself might stand still or be driven backward at the command of Faith—which is the bond between God and men. To such a person, everything above is favorable and nothing is harmful. **Moses** records the most certain prognostications of this in Deuteronomy 28, 29, and 30, and **Paul** summarizes it in Romans 8, verse 28 <note>"And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God..."</note>, by which we may most safely

<sig>K 2</sig>

I agree, and I wonder greatly that there are those who can persuade themselves or others that true Theology can be joined with this most vain art of soothsaying <note>original: "vaticinandi arte," referring here to judicial astrology or the predicting of the future.</note>. *That notorious thief, a very old man, having broken out of prison and thrown himself headlong, dislocated his aged limbs. Because of this, he was hindered and burdened by shackles <note>original: "numellis," a type of neck-shackle or pillory used for transport.</note>; having barely reached the first milestone, he was caught and dragged back from his flight. With new evidence of his robberies coming to light, he now expects a sharper interrogation through torture, and will finally undergo the punishment his crimes deserve along with his two sons. By a Divine gift, a bountiful vintage has followed our rich grain harvest—the likes of which has not been seen for many years—though in some places the wine is of a less noble quality. We owe the greatest thanks for this heavenly benefit, and I pray it does not lead us into midseeds <note>A common sentiment that abundance might lead to overindulgence or sin.</note>. But now, most flourishing Prince—for whom, along with your illustrious brothers, I pray from my heart for the favor of Heaven and Earth—I send infinite greetings. Fare you well in safety, and continue to look upon me with favor.*

...we took part in the hunts that had been organized. A particularly tranquil serenity of the sky invited us there, which was so great even in the forest glades themselves—which are otherwise most rugged—that one could hardly notice any turbulent weather at all. All things were accomplished well; many wild beasts were struck down, and among them a massive and bristling wild boar, which even mangled several hunting dogs before it was pierced by the spear of one of the hunters. However, yours escaped safe and bore himself strenuously against the rest—the dog you sent not long ago as a gift to *our Illustrious Father* <note>original: "Cl. Dn. Parenti noſtro." Referring to Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, a famed scholar and book collector.</note>—so that he is now held in the highest estimation above all the others.

I am glad that my judgment regarding Astrologers, however weak, was of some weight to you; for thus there will be less to fear from those critics who subject both heaven and earth, and all things, to their own whim. Since these matters are of a deeper level of inquiry, I leave them to be judged by the conjectures and talents of others. This one thing I add: a very great eclipse of the sun <note>original: "defectionem solis." This refers to the total solar eclipse of August 12, 1654, which was the subject of much astrological dread in Europe at the time.</note> was predicted here by them to occur around the fifty-fourth year of this century, and from it, unusual and hitherto unheard-of changes in affairs. I both know and believe that such an event can certainly happen; but whether they all agree on these matters and can define anything with certainty, I doubt. If, however, something should perchance hang over our necks <note>A metaphor for an impending threat or "Sword of Damocles."</note> which the mind cannot grasp, may GOD so moderate it that we may be able to endure it, and most mercifully enlighten our eyes—currently blinded by earthly filth—so that we may turn away from or avoid it. To His protection, along with a most happy New Year’s wish, I devotedly commend us, and I

->To Your Reverence<-

Wolfenbüttel, November 30, 1652.

profess myself forever your most devoted,
*Ferdinand Albert, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg*

## LETTER CXCV.

### ->To PRINCE FERDINAND ALBERT.<-

**Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,**
**Lord most Merciful by far.**

*Among the sorrows that surround me, confined as I am in this prison of the body* <note>Andreae was 66 years old and in failing health at this time; he frequently referred to his body as a "prison" or "shackles."</note>*, nevertheless, the happy news of your recreations uplifts me in no small way. This is especially true regarding the favor shown to your Most Serene Lord Father* <note>Duke Augustus the Younger (1579–1666), a famous scholar-prince.</note>*, for whom—like an Atlas weary in his shoulders amid Herculean labors and his advancing years—this relaxation of the mind is entirely deserved, healthful, and fitting. For you and your brothers, it seems an opportune and suited way to rouse the nobility of your character. That the memory of me has not faded meanwhile is a reason for me to give you my greatest thanks humbly, and I pray as earnestly as I can that you do not further neglect me, prostrated as I am on the ground and breathing out all my life-sap* <note>original: "succum exhalantem." A metaphor for the loss of vital energy in old age.</note>*. I congratulate the dog sent by me that she is held in some esteem among you, as she could not have been placed more splendidly; I rejoice for myself that something not unpleasing has come from me. Regarding the threats of the Astrologers for the coming year, there is no leisure now to respond in kind. They already have something suspended in the heavens* <note>Referring to the solar eclipse discussed on the previous page.</note> *over which they may cross swords among themselves and fill the ears and minds of the curious. May Christ our Sun, the Lord of all years and of all sublunary things* <note>term: "sublunary" (original: "sublunarium"). In the old geocentric model of the universe, this referred to the changing, corruptible world below the moon, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note>*, our Light and Heat, rule, illuminate, and warm our hearts, lest we ever dwell in darkness or experience a fearsome eclipse of the Church itself. Farewell in Him, together with your Most Serene House, and be mindful of me.*

->Your Most Illustrious Highness’s<-
Bebenhausen, Dec. 15, ->most humble servant,<-
1652. ->Johann Valentin Andreae,<-
->Doctor of Theology.<-

### LETTER CXCVI.

### To LADY SIBYLLA URSULA. <note>Sibylla Ursula (1629–1671) was the daughter of Duke Augustus of Brunswick-Lüneburg. She was a highly accomplished scholar, writer, and translator, part of the "Society of the Noble Sirs" and the "Ister Nymphs."</note>

### Eternal greeting in Christ.

->And the HAPPINESS of the approaching Year.<-

**Most Illustrious and High-born Princess,**
**Lady most Merciful by far,**

The devotion I owe you, and the admiration of those virtues by which you stand out among the most illustrious Maidens <note>original: "Nymphas." A classical poetic term Andreae frequently used to refer to the learned noblewomen of the German courts.</note> of Germany, exhaust for me all material for congratulating you and speaking GOOD WORDS. With this languid spirit and decaying body, already withering away, I can find nothing to bring except a prayer for the CONTINUITY of such great happiness of yours, which now reaches the peak of GLORY and GOOD REPUTE. Indeed, it might seem more a thing to be envied than further advanced, were it not that your PIETY and MODESTY merited imitation more than jealousy. Bravo, then, on this your high station, which all good men venerate with me and follow with praises; and may the rarest gifts of Heaven which you possess result eventually:

> Happily for the Church,
> Happily for the Most Serene House,
> Happily for the lands to be blessed,
> Happily for the advancement of Letters,
> Happily for the propagation of Virtue.

May GOD grant it, and add happiness to happiness; may He establish it and crown it with ETERNITY.

### LETTER CXCVII.

->To Prince ANTON ULRICH <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714) would later become a famous patron of the arts, a novelist, and Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.</note> and<-

Wretched as I am, I pray from my soul and vow for all happiness for You; though sick in mind and body alike, I wish you firm health and vigor; sad and groaning, I wish you a thousand joys; withering and broken, I wish you great growth and abundant fruit; solitary and deserted, I wish you public applause and many greetings; though I am near the finish line <note>original: "metae proximus." Andreae frequently refers to his impending death during this period.</note>, I wish that you may run a long race of life and Virtue <note>original: "stadium." A reference to the ancient Greek running track, used here as a metaphor for the course of a noble life.</note> at the start of this year and through the passage of many more. May GOD hear me, and whatever I lack or lose, may He graciously deign to add to you and cause to increase. The longer this vitality remains with us by Divine gift, the more ample, illustrious, and wealthy it will turn out for you and for your most illustrious House. In my own time, I saw a similar example of this, which perhaps will not be unpleasant to recount to you. The most illustrious Count, who possessed very extensive lands comparable to a Principality <term>Principatus: the territory or jurisdiction of a prince</term>, still ruled wisely, justly, and with great profit even in his decrepit old age. Meanwhile, his only son, Count *Eberhard*, was established in a comfortable seat and an elegant table with his most praiseworthy Wife. They were the parents of a numerous offspring, whom their Grandfather raised in his own illustrious court with such clear education and instruction that, in managing affairs and arranging marriages, they often carried away the palm <note>original: "palmam... praetulerit." A classic symbol of victory or preeminence.</note> in every kind of virtue. During this time, the father *Eberhard* spent his time on Piety, the study of literature, and the arts, growing gray in these pursuits with that absolute Tranquility of mind which *Seneca* <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Stoic philosopher whose work *De Tranquillitate Animi* (On Tranquility of Mind) was a favorite of Andreae.</note> expressed in his golden little book on the subject.

Moreover, since there was no shortage of sycophants <note>original: "Gnatones." Referring to Gnatho, a parasitic flatterer in the Roman comedies of Terence.</note> and whisperers who exaggerated the excessive liveliness of *Gottfried* and criticized *Eberhard's* long absence from business, I myself heard how his uncle, Count *Philip*, replied to them piously and wisely: 

"Be gone, all you who neither understand nor worthily value the father's merits and favors toward me! In him alone, who is most dear to me, I have a wise Advisor for all my affairs to be overseen; a prudent Administrator for those to be conducted; a powerful Protector for those to be preserved; a foresighted Treasurer <term>Quaestor: an official in charge of public revenue or a financial manager</term> for those to be increased; and indeed a faithful and successful Guardian of my children, with whom all my well-being and fortune stands or falls." 

Nor was the truth absent from this prediction when the outcome followed. For when the former [the grandfather] met his fate, and the latter [Eberhard] was caught in the disturbances of Germany <note>Likely referring to the political instability during and after the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).</note>—scarcely admitted to the government by turns, now installed, now ejected—he finally ended his life as if in exile. He was never unhappier than when he had to rule, yet in all other things he was worthy to be crowned with the glory <note>original: "adoria." An archaic term for praise or military renown.</note> of all Christian virtues. 

But perhaps these things are too long-winded, according to the talkativeness of old age; I finish and conclude: ***WHILE THE LORD FATHER IS SAFE*** <note>original: "SALVO D. PATRE." This refers to the Princes' own father, Duke August the Younger. Andreae is emphasizing that the sons' security depends on their father’s well-being.</note>, all things will be safe, happy, desired, secure, and magnificent for You; which I pray may be long-lasting and perpetual for you, for...

# LETTERS OF THE YEAR 1653.
## LETTER CXCVIII.

-> *To the very Reverend and most Renowned Lord Doctor, my uniquely honored Friend,* <-

I give you the greatest possible thanks for your recent wish, sent as a happy omen for the New Year. As for what you add in that same letter concerning my "glory and fame," I certainly recognize in those words your singular kindness and affection toward me; yet I am well enough aware that such praises cannot apply to my own modesty and insignificance. However, I shall redouble my prayers to God, the Thrice Best and Greatest <note>original: "DEVM Ter Optimum Maximum." A common formal Latin invocation of God (often abbreviated as D.O.M.) combining Christian and classical phrasing.</note>, for your lasting happiness and especially for your health—which I was sorry to hear is currently weak. May He grant that you begin this present year healthy, happy, and whole, and that you finish the same year even healthier and filled with all prosperity. Farewell. Given at Wolfenbüttel, January 18, in the year 1653.

### To Princess SIBYLLA URSULA.

# Most Illustrious and Most High Princess,
# By far the most Clement Lady.

Neither you nor I shall be reproached for these excessive praises by anyone who either estimates your virtues at their true worth, or who knows that my own free tongue has more often hindered me than a servile one has helped. Those praises which you, in your modesty, so bashfully decline, shall one day be publicly sung according to your merits in the Temple of Good Fame, with a voice clearer than mine and by a more fortunate pen. For your prayers for a desired omen for this year, and for my own stronger health—which I need above all else—I both give my humblest thanks and, as they are pious and warm, I pray as a suppliant to GOD that He may ratify them and return that warmth to you. 

And yet, what becomes of me—a man with one foot in the grave <note>original: "capulari sene," literally an old man ready for the coffin or bier.</note> and a candidate for death—matters very little, provided only that our Fatherland remains safe. To this land, the sons of the Aether, Air, Water, and Earth <note>A reference to the four elements, likely personifying natural disasters or astrological portents.</note> seem to threaten and portend dire things (which may GOD avert), while even now a sufficient amount of evils hangs over us from the triple plague of Atheism, Tyranny, and Barbarism, which is even now about to flood us. Our posterity, born into, imbued with, and nourished by the beginnings of this plague, feels no sensation or pain from it; we, however, like Janus and Noah <note>Janus was the two-faced Roman god looking to the past and future; Noah witnessed the world before and after the Flood. Andreae feels he stands between a lost age of piety and a coming age of ruin.</note>, bear a countenance wet with tears and a melting heart amidst our lamentations. 

Yet the Lord of Heaven and Earth lives, who is able to make guest-houses of Egypt, the deserts, Chaldea, and overseas dwellings (places He has destined as prisons for those who oppose Him), and who stands ready to be present before us. Upon Him we cast our cares and our fear of recurring calamity following the loss of peace. No small hope remains to me of averting <note>original: "averruncandi," a specialized Latin religious term for turning away or weeding out evil omens.</note> or delaying evil through the vitality of your Most Serene Lord Father <note>Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note>, a kind of blessing which GOD [bestows] upon his holy Heroes...

### LETTER CC.
->Heartiest Greetings.<-
->*Very Reverend and Most*<-
->*Renowned Sir,*<-

I have learned well enough how exhausted your strength is and how troublesome a life you lead now, even in your rest—not only from almost all your letters, but also from the envoy of your Most Serene Prince, *Master Dr. Müller*, a man of great experience in many affairs and of the utmost sincerity. Consequently, I myself feel the bitterest sorrow because of this ill health <term>valetudo</term> <note>In 17th-century Latin, "valetudo" refers to one's state of health, often implying a state of sickness or infirmity.</note> of yours, and I frequently implore the aid of the Supreme Helper on your behalf. For it is most certain that just as the formation and growth of the body depend on Him, so too do its preservation and restoration. I cannot marvel enough at His ineffable and almost inscrutable providence <note>original: "providentiam," the theological concept of God's foreseeing care and guidance of the world.</note> toward you; for while He wishes you to be subject to these infirmities, He awakens in you a far greater and firmer desire for eternal perfection. While He keeps you confined to your bed so that, as they say, you cannot be raised up <note>original: "erigi," a play on words meaning both to physically stand and to be spiritually encouraged.</note>, He raises up within you everything that looks chiefly toward obedience to Him.

->To Prince **ANTON ULRICH**, and<-
->Prince **FERDINAND ALBERT**.<-

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Princes,<-
->Lords by far most Merciful,<-

While I re-read your recent letters—which I was previously prevented from answering due to a shortage of time—and while I refresh myself with their sweetness and elegance, I find many things that I believe should by no means be passed over by me in silence without giving you the praise you deserve. Of these, the clear "prize-winning point" <note>original: "palmarium"</note> is what you, Most Illustrious Prince Ferdinand Albert, reported regarding the truly unusual modesty shown at the **sacred washing** <note>original: "sacra ablutione"; a reference to the sacrament of baptism</note> of the Illustrious Infant **Dorothea Sophia**. This ceremony was completed both in good time and with only three witnesses, and those from the household. I value this so highly that, although I do not deny that something more [splendid] might be granted to your brilliance and dignity, I nevertheless greatly wish that this example—than which none more beautiful could be given or is rarer in a Court—might spread to those of lower rank and the "sons of the earth" <note>original: "terrae filios"; a classical idiom for people of humble or obscure origin</note>.

They should learn that when we offer our **impure mass** <note>original: "impure massam"; a theological term referring to human nature corrupted by original sin</note> to be washed by the most holy blood of Christ and to be grafted into the covenant of divine grace, it is least appropriate of all to weave together displays <note>original: "pompas"</note> or behaviors hateful to GOD, or to make ostentatious shows. In such displays, more of the tears and blood of the subjects <note>meaning the common people who pay for such festivities</note> is often spent than the sacred stream and the Spirit <note>original: "sacri fluminis & Flaminis"; a wordplay on the water of baptism and the Breath or Spirit of God</note>. Our thanks often end in foul drunkenness and revelries <note>original: "vitulationes"; literally "leaping like calves," used here for rowdy celebration</note> which, when compared with the baptism of Christ himself at the Jordan—where the Holy Trinity was present in person—should rightly strike us with a blush of justified reproach. We, who have been affected by no less a benefit, ought to be more concerned with paying **offerings for salvation** <note>original: "Soteria"; from the Greek *sōtēria*, referring to sacrifices or gifts given in thanks for deliverance</note> than with instituting **wild rituals** <note>original: "Orgia"; used here in the sense of excessive, pagan-like festivities</note>. Whoever was the author and advisor of that [modesty], whenever he [gives] of his own for the use of the Church and the poor, never, and not without envy inter-

I would also rightly count it to your credit that, after the relaxation of the mind granted by your Most Serene Lord Father for the purpose of hunting, you have so willingly returned to the focus of your holiday studies and your noble duties. But your instructors and guides <note>original: "Informatores & Condùces"</note> will point these things out more correctly than I; let it suffice for me to have indicated in a few words how much I approve of and admire the character and studies of your Court, and how I prefer them to others—which may redound to the glory of this century, should Christ grant it. at the funeral pyre of Calw.* <note>In 1634, during the Thirty Years' War, the town of Calw was burned by Imperial troops; Andreae lost his library, manuscripts, and possessions.</note> From that time on, I have 
kept myself within my shell, content with the literary 
exchange of a few, except for what had to be expended 
by a bound spirit, out of duty, for *the August Selenians, 
than whom nothing more fortunate covers the earth.* <note>The "Selenians" refers to the family of Duke Augustus the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus."</note> 
*To this has been added the infirmity of the body, the 
inseparable companion of old age—slow and troublesome—*
whence comes a weariness of mind and a dejection of 
strength, so that if I wished to be sufficient for performing 
the duties of friendship, I could not; and if I could, I am 
sometimes so weary that I would not even wish to, 
satisfying neither myself nor others on either side. 
Nevertheless, Your Illustrious Generosity and courtesy, 
Lord Baron, have stirred me, however truly *withered* 
I may be; you are so adorned with skill and experience 
in letters and affairs, and so refined by your great 
devotion to our mother tongue, <note>Stubenberg was a significant figure in the "Fruitbearing Society," dedicated to the refinement of the German language.</note> that I gladly and 
reverently rise to meet your freely offered favor. I 
consider it a great benefit and believe it should be 
embraced with my own services ready in turn; I ask 
again and again that you do not grow weary of 
continuing it. If it should happen that you are joined 
more closely to our lands—which our most noble 
**Harsdörffer** <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658), a famous Nuremberg poet and founder of the Pegnesischer Blumenorden.</note> greatly desires along with **von Buwinghausen**—
this proximity will be to me the most certain support 
and remedy for refreshing my spirit and relieving 
my body. I earnestly pray that God may grant this 
to me, and may He keep you safe and unharmed for 
a long time, and always increase and adorn you. 
Farewell, and look kindly upon me, your Most 
Illustrious Generosity.

Bebenhausen, 26 Feb. -> *most devotedly,* <-
1653. -> Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology. <-
