### LETTER CCX.

-><note>original: "S. P." (Salutem Plurimam)</note> Fondest Greetings<-

The reason I have been unable to respond to your last letter, **Most Distinguished Sir**, is not only a lack of time, but also the unexpected setbacks of ill health, to which it was necessary I again be subject, as God so ordained. For several weeks now, I have been bedridden with a most troublesome fever, <note>original: "febris"</note> which rendered me quite sluggish and useless for any other business. However, by the grace of a most kind God, I have been freed from it, so that I may go out and once again keep watch over my studies. Yet it can hardly be said how widely this evil creeps among others, almost like a contagion <note>original: "contagium"</note> from which no one is immune. I could list many people even in our Court who are still most gravely afflicted by it, among whom are also the *Betrothed Sister*, *Brother Ferdinand Albert*, <note>Ferdinand Albert I (1636–1687), son of Duke Augustus the Younger.</note> and the younger *Antonia Sibylla of Barby*; <note>Antonia Sibylla (1641–1684) was the daughter of the Count of Barby and lived at the Wolfenbüttel court.</note> as for the rest, and especially the townspeople who do not enjoy the same standard of living and sustenance, you can easily judge for yourself. We have as companions in this misfortune all our neighbors, and it touches those even many miles away from us; yet I hope and pray to God that you remain untouched by it. We see now, and experience to our cost, what those immoderate storms <note>original: "tempestates"</note> and those unusual celestial portents <note>original: "cœli prodigia"</note> intended; the observers of such things, as they examined the causes for prediction, warned not inappropriately about these imminent evils. Therefore, having been warned, let us return to a better way of life, and better things will follow us—especially if we bear these present circumstances with an even mind, for which [I] most humbly [implore] <note>The catchword "implo" indicates the word "imploro" (I implore) continues on the next page.</note> God...

# LETTER CCXI.
->To Prince ANTHONY ULRICH.<-

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My far Most Merciful Lord.

As your letters were longed for by me, so the news—and indeed the testimony—of your restored health was most pleasing to me, for which I was diligently keeping watch in prayers before God. However, it pains me greatly what you added regarding the contagion <note>original: "contagio"</note> of diseases creeping <note>original: "serpente"</note> through your Court; I fear lest it disturb or delay your wedding joys. <note>Anthony Ulrich married Elizabeth Julian of Schleswig-Holstein-Sønderburg in 1756, but marriage negotiations and festivities often spanned years in this era.</note> In turn, it is like the sum of all joys to me that light has been restored to your Most Serene Lord Father, as if by a right of return <term>postliminio</term> <note>A legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person who has returned from captivity; here used metaphorically for the Duke's recovery of his sight.</note>, and granted on his 85th <note>Augustus the Younger was born in 1579, making him 74 in 1653. The transcription "LXXXV" (85th) may be a scribe's error for "LXXV" (75th), referring to the start of his 75th year.</note> birthday as a truly heavenly and miraculous gift. I pray to God with all my heart that this light may happily endure for him until the end of a long life and never set. 

Among us, there is no infected air, nor any dangerous diseases, except that pleurisy <note>original: "pleuritis"</note> has suddenly finished off a few people. Yet, there is such a cheapness of grain as has not been heard of in living memory; it almost induces poverty because of the lack of coin, quite contrary to what the double-tongued <note>original: "ambidextra"</note> Delphic Oracles of the fortune-tellers threatened. As for me, I suffer miserably from a relapse <note>original: "recidiva"</note> of the disease that holds me captive, following a brief pause. I am uncertain where to turn, since I am not permitted to move from this place or to mingle among people. Therefore, one must obey God, to whom alone it belongs to decide what is best for us and what may turn to His glory.

### LETTER CCXII.

->Reverend Lord, Honored<-
->Godfather,<-

I received your little letter with astonishment—it was written, unexpectedly, on a narrow scrap of paper—when it was finally delivered today after a week’s delay. From it, I learned of the calamity you hinted at, which is rather our common misfortune as well as yours; who would not grieve at it? I certainly do, more than others, as one who is an exile, a stranger, and in flight, I am even now being stripped of my refuge, or at least I fear I am. But truly, my own private fortune has afflicted me little, and clearly will not crush me, believe me: but to look upon your misfortunes and perceive them with my own ears—that indeed was most hard and nearly intolerable to me. 

And the wretched crowd increased this sorrow; while they strive to avoid the cruel hands of the soldiers, they have flowed to this city in immense numbers, displaying their grief through complaints, their very expressions, and groans. Furthermore, the lack of all things, the poor quality of food, and hunger <note>original: "inedia"</note> have brought on diseases, which were followed by a contagious plague <note>original: "lues contagiosa"</note> that daily snatches many from our midst. Then, from the devastations and plunderings, there arose a scarcity of grain <term>annona</term> <note>The "annona" refers to the year's harvest and the regulated supply of grain essential for survival.</note> and of all necessary things; it reveals a great dearness <note>original: "caritatem"; here referring to high prices or inflation caused by scarcity.</note> of goods and threatens even greater hardship. Thus, we feel nothing but Divine punishments. But God has protected me thus far with my family, so that

...from the heart. I have also read your *Tomb of Calw* <note>original: "Bustum Tuum Calvense"; a work by Andreae lamenting the destruction of the town of Calw in 1634</note>, and two other writings, among which I was especially pleased by the *Defense Against Slanders* <note>original: "Defensio contra calumnias"</note>, which have been spread about here much to your disadvantage. I see from these that there remains something for me to rejoice in: that your family is safe, that you have Divine help, and regarding the strength of your spirit. I hope that this strength may increase daily, for the comfort of your listeners and for my own as well.

Who and of what sort your people are, I do not indeed know, and therefore I do not dare to suggest anything regarding their fortune. For here, certainly, and in the surrounding areas, I experience that the old ways persist, and some even become worse through calamities and punishments; so much so that, unless their dispositions are changed, I despair for the safety of this Province. For both a clearly unlawful greed for possessions burns, and mutual charity grows cold, and concern for both the public good and religion is lukewarm—things which they otherwise desire to remain safe through idle prayers. 

Yet they undertake nothing that contributes to the matter with the care, zeal, and devotion that is fitting. They meditate on fleeing rather than enduring the cross <note>A common metaphor for Christian suffering or divine testing</note> which hangs over their backs. If they could be relieved of its burden, even in the slightest degree, they would think nothing of changing their Religion. For even while still sticking in the deepest mud, they would not be afraid to drag their children to the [Catholic] temples and exhort them, to praise their ceremonies in marvelous ways, to extol their alms, to assert that they have the same concern for eternal salvation, and to show themselves prone to their precepts. They are so ignorant of every distinction that the ignorance of the common people <note>original: "ruditas plebis"</note> is a miracle to their teachers, who cast the blame for this on the pastors and hold them up to the people as a mockery. 

I do not indeed have the same judgment regarding men of our order <note>Referring to the Protestant clergy</note>, although I do not exempt everyone. [Let] the past teach you that the care of the common people must be vigorous for you hereafter...

...will teach: <note>The Latin fragment "cebunt" likely completes "docebunt," meaning "they will teach."</note> First, that you should ensure repentance and the amendment of such great sins, without which not even God repents of His punishments. Otherwise, you implore the help of others in vain; it will be of no benefit to a people who return to their sins and have not seriously reformed their former ways. For you will strive in vain to restore the altars and the hearths <note>original: "aras focosque"; a classical idiom referring to the most sacred foundations of a community: its religion and its homes</note>. Although these might suffice for worldly happiness and sharpen the love of restoration through their sweetness, they will then cause more damage without the aforementioned warnings, since no one will offer to be torn away from them even at the risk of Religion.

Regarding the sufficiency of others—which some envious people seem to me to criticize too much—I think nothing is to be hoped for. This is because your characters are so well known to me that each prefers his own private gain at the expense of another’s loss, and because the danger to others is not correctly estimated among you. This danger has certainly spread through every corner, leaving others unable to repair either their own difficulties or yours; for even what was not consumed by the fire, greedy hands did not overlook. 

I have not said this, however, so that you should think the hope of help is completely cut off from you. I do not doubt that some upright and capable men will remain to help. I believe you should first seek these out by right so that they may bring you aid. As for me, both the mercy of God and the kindness of the King of Hungary <note>Ferdinand III (1608–1657), who was King of Hungary and Bohemia at this time and later became Holy Roman Emperor</note> have willed me safe from all violence thus far. Yet I still find the local inhabitants lacking in good faith; their feigned poverty <term>indigentia</term> <note>a state of extreme need or lack of resources</note> has resulted in my no longer having control over what remained before. Nor do those I wished to help have any consideration for me now; indeed, they take it badly when what they owe is requested, as if they had suffered an injury. I want you, Venerable Sir <note>original: "V. R.", likely "Vestra Reverentia" (Your Reverence) or "Venerande Reverende" (Venerable/Reverend)</note>, to know these things, so that while you hear I am safe from physical harm, you do not expect a duty from me which you yourself are not even performing.

# EPISTLE

<note>The following text is a fragment of a letter where the right margin was trimmed, cutting off the ends of some words. The translation reconstructs the likely intended meaning.</note>

Finally, I must discourage you from the journey which you intend to undertake to see me: for what would you do here? Amidst the noise of soldiers, women, camp followers, and servants <note>original: "lixarum, calonumq;"; terms for the non-combatant laborers and servants who followed 17th-century armies</note>, from the disgust of which I scarcely step foot out of my house. It will be better for you to remain where you have grown accustomed to calamities long-seen, than to look upon the miseries of neighbors and to hear their complaints, which would only cause you more grief. This is especially true of my own house, where you will find everything has shrunk and we suffer from extreme poverty. My family remains the same size (except for one youth who is devoted to the studies of my younger sons) and is large, yet must be fed, even though what remains to us is thin and meager; for within these four years I have been deprived of all the income from my property left behind in Austria. Farewell; and forgive me for intruding with these external troubles.

->Esslingen / March 14, 1635.<-

***

### EPISTLE CCXIV.

->Reverend Lord, Honored Godfather.<-

Your response to my last letter was received on the seventh day of this month, which was most mournful for me. By His fatal decree, God took both my sons, *Marcus* and *Christopher*, from the living at the same time. They had been seized two days earlier by a contagious disease <note>The "contagious disease" likely refers to the plague, which ravaged Germany in 1635 during the war.</note>, and on the following day I buried them with honorable funeral rites. Thus, the "multiplication of offspring" for which you prayed for me in your letters (the meaning of which I did not then understand) has instead turned into a decrease. Meanwhile, some who are too rigid wish to forbid mourning for deceased sons and advise us only to bear it patiently—as if mourning and patience were opposites. Certainly, this was by the will of God, which is favorable to me, and even more so to my sons, who are now rescued from the followers and henchmen of Satan who are everywhere...

...sought after, but now I know they have been snatched from the snares of those very men. But to restrain oneself from the grief of the soul seems too hard, although I may patiently bear whatever God has inflicted; it stands by His will, not only this, but everything that happens to us. Truly, I do not believe that patience is interrupted by such grief, nor that the endurance of one who commits all to God is removed—a duty I consider a sin to omit, nor do I refuse it. 

Yet, that I should not mourn sons so obedient, and advanced so far beyond their years that I had conceived the highest hope for them—that they would be an honor to themselves and their kinsmen—that, indeed, I cannot endure. Furthermore, the manner of their death moves me deeply: as it was untimely and naturally horrible, so it is to be detested for the violence of that plague <term>luis; likely referring to the bubonic plague which ravaged Germany in 1635</term>, since its cruelty is such that, by creeping through the blood of all near relatives, it threatens nothing further but total bereavement <term>orbitas; the legal and emotional state of being deprived of children or parents</term> unless God prevents it. 

*Finally, I believe it is the mark of a Christian to mourn, not with the voice and plaintive cries, but in mind and soul; it is a debt owed for our sins, by which God, being incensed, brings such things upon us; He is to be appeased only by patience and repentance <term>poenitentia</term>, not by the forgetting of grief.* 

Nor do I call it "mourning" to beat the air with lamentations or to tear out one's hair, which are more the images of impatience than of sorrow. I do not consider tears to be foreign to grief; rather, I believe they are especially to be permitted in those who are naturally closer to us. To you, however, Reverend Lord, as a true judge of conduct, I leave the matter to be judged, and I seek your opinion on this case if you are at leisure. For my part, I certainly mourn until time diminishes the pain—not for things that can be recovered, but for things lost, or more truly, sent on ahead. Meanwhile, I remain deserted in this miserable valley of darkness, stuck in this mud, now nearly decrepit and exposed to I know not what hardships; yet, that they have been snatched away from these troubles, I [rejoice] <note>The catchword "lætor" on the bottom of the page indicates the next page begins with "rejoice."</note> somewhat even in the midst of my grief...

## LETTER 215.

->Greetings and Peace<- <note>Original: "S. P.," abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam*, a standard Latin greeting wishing much health or safety.</note>

*Very Reverend and Most Illustrious Sir,*

The letter with which you congratulated me on my son's return, dated December 16 of last year, I received today here in Stuttgart <term>Studgardia; the Latin name for the city of Stuttgart</term>: but I have not yet seen my son. However, I have received his letters, which he wrote to me at the end of the month of November, in which he excuses this delay as being by his Prince's command, because the Prince has thus far required his service in the funeral rites of certain Princes. 

But when he arrives, I will send him to you, if it pleases you, so that you may learn from him in person whatever you wish. However, I do not want him to urge your departure by his encouragement; for I can imagine no cause for your leaving other than despair for the safety of this Province <note>Likely the Duchy of Württemberg, which was devastated by the Battle of Nördlingen in 1634 and subsequent occupations</note>: although we all see with sorrow that it is suffering, I nevertheless think it inadvisable for it to be abandoned by its natives, who will not find a homeland elsewhere. For who would not rather succor his country? To which we all owe everything. 

Our Mr. Wensius, truly a most excellent man, as I myself have experienced in my son's case, and to whose affection I know you also grant much, will not a little, I believe, advance this matter. If he succeeds, I shall also consider myself summoned there, if the affairs of this Province do not cease to be in such a bad state, but those who [hope] to fare well...

...should he receive it? If the good men depart, the wicked occupy their places, and there would be no one to faithfully devote their own effort to the *restoration of the Duchy*, which is now nearly wretched. 
Then for you, *my Lord*, your age must also be weighed, as well as your health, which can scarcely be maintained on an unaccustomed diet, let alone restored when it is weak. But I pray to God as my Counselor. My other affairs almost share in the fortune of the Duchy and the faith of men: that fortune is already wavering through all ranks and estates, and soon, unless I am mistaken, it will utterly collapse if there is no one to sustain or raise it up. Indeed, your city has the best reputation of all; elsewhere, even the Magistrates imprudently offer their help to the most unjust and fraudulent customs: if they continue to do this, even justice will necessarily go into exile. But we complain in vain if we do not recover our senses. It appears the last days are imminent <note>A common sentiment during the 1630s in Germany, as the devastation of the Thirty Years' War led many to believe the apocalypse was near</note>. 
Finally, the greeting with which you closed your letters, I heartily pray back for you, Reverend Sir <note>Original: "R. D.," an abbreviation for *Reverende Domine*</note>. Farewell, January 18, 1637.

->Yours most devotedly,<-
->Ludwig Hohenfelder.<-

...that you direct all your efforts and labors toward the utility and edification of His church, and that you are not at all burdened by facing any dangers for its sake. All of which thoroughly persuade me that in this your principality, you seek nothing so much as the honor of Him whose Vicar you are—namely, the honor of GOD; moreover, they give the best hope that you will refuse no labor in the future, provided you can serve the Church. When I considered these and similar things in my mind, I could not restrain myself from writing to you things that seemed to contribute significantly to the utility and progress of the Church.

*And indeed, concerning the Doctrine and the administration of the Sacraments (which ought to hold the primary place in the Church) which all the Doctors and Pastors in your Duchy* <note>Original: "Ducatu"</note> *profess, there is no reason for me to doubt. For it is without doubt the doctrine of Christ Himself, which He not only promulgated in the territory of Judea, but also [ordered] His disciples to scatter and spread* <note>Original: "spargere ac propagare"</note> *among all nations.*

As for what pertains to **Discipline** <term>Disciplinam: In the Reformation context, this referred to the church’s power to monitor the morality of its members and exclude the unrepentant from communion.</term> and good morals (which is the second part of **Ecclesiastical** <term>Ecclesiastical: relating to the organization and government of the Christian Church.</term> governance), there is no godly person who does not find something lacking. What, I ask, **Illustrious Prince**, is holier than the Body of Christ handed over to death for us? What is more precious than His blood poured out for the remission of sins, which are offered and presented to us in that most holy Supper? What, I say, does **Your Highness** <note>Original Latin: "Celsitudo Tua." A formal title of respect for a high-ranking noble.</note> think I should do in this matter? Are they to be admitted? And yet I know they are dogs and swine, to whom I cannot administer these things unless I wish to transgress the precept and **command of Christ**. I indeed see this; for when **Paul** had heard about that Corinthian fornicator, who had his father’s wife—concerning whom he wrote in **1 Corinthians 5**—he did not wish to excommunicate him by his own authority alone (an act which he himself calls "delivering to Satan" <note>original: *Satanæ tradere*. In the early church, this was a formal exclusion from the community, intended to lead the sinner to repentance.</note>), but said: *when you are gathered together, and my spirit... let him be delivered to Satan.* Since, I say, Paul was unwilling to do that alone, how, I ask, should I dare to do it? 

As I have weighed these matters on both sides for several years now, I have had scarcely any other desire more at heart, and have earnestly asked of the Father of our Lord **Jesus Christ**, than that He might restore and recall to us a lawful **Excommunication**, as if by *postliminium* <term>Postliminiò: A legal term from Roman law referring to the restoration of rights or status to a person who had been a prisoner of war upon their return home. Here, it refers to the "return" of an ancient church practice.</term>. For I have already foreseen that these evils cannot be helped by any other way except this one, and I have discussed and conferred on this matter in a friendly way with certain godly and faithful ministers of **Christ**. Chief among these is Master **Jakob Andreae** <note>Jakob Andreae (1528–1590) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and a primary architect of the Formula of Concord.</note>, the most vigilant pastor of the Church of **Göppingen** and my brother and kinsman in the Lord, regarding how we ought to approach this matter.

**Hesiod** <note>A Greek poet (c. 700 BC). This refers to a famous passage in his poem *Works and Days* (lines 293–297).</note> identifies three kinds of men, and quite rightly so. The first are the **Wisest**, who understand and follow the best things by their own light. The second are those who obey someone giving good advice. But those who know neither how to counsel themselves nor how to obey another, these belong to the last group, whom we call "useless weights upon the earth" <note>original: *telluris inutilia pondera*.</note>.

I certainly, **Best of Princes**, although I by no means believe myself to be among the first—those who see and understand all things for themselves—likewise I have no wish to be among the last. I would boldly declare myself to be among those whom he places in the second rank: those who, even if I am not wise on my own, nor foresee what must be done in every situation, nevertheless do not at all despise those who give good advice.

I wished to write these things to you first, earnestly (as to a Prince who desires from his heart the welfare of the Christian religion and the Church), asking you by the honor of our Lord **Jesus Christ**, our only Redeemer and Savior, and by the salvation of the Church, that you...

*...kindly grant me that I might be permitted to persist in restoring that* **Ecclesiastical Censure** <note>original: *Censura Ecclesiastica*. This refers to the church's authority to investigate and punish the moral failings or heterodox beliefs of its members.</note> *with your peace and favor, so that I may be able to boast piously that I am attempting nothing against the* **Prince’s** *will.*

To them I testify (if I may respond with your peace) that I attempt nothing which you have not approved by your own judgment* <note>original: *calculo tuo*. Literally "by your pebble," referring to the ancient practice of using stones for voting or calculations; here it means the Duke's formal approval or "vote."</note>. *I do not doubt that in the future the* **Lord** *will bless and give increase to my labors, according to that saying of* **Paul: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord, 1 Corinthians 15.**

*Furthermore,* **Excommunication** *must be held in such high regard by all godly people that I would judge that those who neglect it can in no way boast of the reformation of the Church. For did not the* **Lord** *through* **Moses** *seriously command that we should not only add nothing to His* **Word**, *but also take nothing—not even a jot—away from it? We are accustomed to accuse the* **Papists** <note>A term used by Reformers for Roman Catholics, suggesting they follow the Pope rather than the Bible.</note> *fiercely, and indeed not without merit, because they have attached many figments of human ingenuity to the* **Divine Word**, *which none of them can deny. But what if they, in turn, were to object against us that we are stuck in the same mud* <note>original: *in eodem luto hærere*. A common Latin idiom meaning to be stuck in the same difficulty or to be guilty of the same error.</note>, *because we cut out certain things from* **GOD'S Word** *that ought least of all to be removed? What, I ask, will we be able to respond?*

*Certainly, to deny it would be a mark of excessive wickedness. Who is ignorant that this (I mean* **Excommunication**) *flowed from the mouth of* **Christ**, *when He says in* **Matthew 18: Tell it to the church?** *Furthermore, these are the words of* **Christ** *as He sends His* **Disciples** *to spread the doctrine of the* **Gospel** *into the whole* **World: Teach all things which I have commanded you, Matthew 28.** *It must truly be noted diligently that He says "all." Those who do not strain every nerve toward restoring that* **Discipline** *do not satisfy this mandate.*

I do not know what kind of difficulty some imagine <note>original: *somnient*; literally "dream of."</note> in restoring that discipline? It is as if we were undertaking a private matter, and not the business of Christ himself; and as if the governing of the Christian Church depended on our own strength, and not on that of Christ himself, who promises in that very place <note>A reference to the Great Commission in the Gospel of Matthew.</note> that he will be with us until the end of the world. Finally, it is as if it would not have been just as easy for the Apostles themselves to object? But they did not imagine some unknown difficulty; instead, they were immediately ready and eager to perform the duty entrusted to them. In this matter we must follow them, if only we wish to be numbered among the godly and faithful servants of Christ. For it is the part of Christ himself, as our **Leader**, to command and prescribe, while it is ours to take up his orders—as he says—and to do so without any hesitation <note>original: *tergiversatione*; a legal or rhetorical term for stalling or evading a duty.</note>. The Apostles were able to establish this discipline in their Churches, and the **Holy Fathers** and their successors maintained it for about three hundred years—and indeed in that century when not only were there no Christian **Princes**, but nearly all of them, as if they were declared and sworn enemies of Christ, attacked his kingdom from every side. Shall the same thing be impossible for us under a **Christian Prince**? Are we not also servants of the same Christ as they were? Do we not also announce the same Gospel? Has it not also been promised to us that he will remain with us until the end of time? **Matthew 28.** Has he not promised that he will give the increase to our planting and watering? **1 Corinthians 3.** He himself will undoubtedly be present with us, provided we do not fail in our own duties.

Some further complain that they fear a certain **Tyranny**, lest we begin to exercise it little by little over the sheep of Christ, just as the **Roman Antichrist** <note>A standard Reformation-era polemic referring to the Pope and the Roman Catholic hierarchy.</note> exercised it for many centuries. But there is nothing for them to fear. For I ask you, **most wise Prince**, what similarity does that form of **Discipline** <term>Ecclesiastical Discipline: the system of moral oversight and the power to exclude unrepentant sinners from the Lord's Supper.</term>, such as we have described, have with the **Tyranny of the Papists**?

<summary>The author argues that restoring church discipline is a divine mandate that should not be feared as too difficult or as a return to papal tyranny. In the Papacy <note>original: *Papatu*; referring to the Roman Catholic ecclesiastical system.</note>, a single lazy monk—not to mention the Pope, that supreme Tyrant—terrified even the highest Monarchs of the world with the lightning bolt of his excommunication. I, however, will not claim this power for myself alone, nor will I exercise it; rather, I will do so with the **Elders** <note>Also known as Presbyters; lay leaders in the Reformed church structure.</note>, who have obtained that honor not by paying a price, but by the testimony of their uprightness, just as **Tertullian** <note>An influential early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note> speaks concerning this <term>Censure</term> <note>The formal process of investigating and correcting the behavior of church members.</note>. 

Truly, those who refuse this healthy <term>discipline</term> <note>The system of rules and spiritual oversight intended to maintain the purity of the church community.</note> under the pretext of some kind of "tyranny," should take care that they are not among the number of those who, in the 19th chapter of Luke, sent an embassy to that powerful Lord saying: **"We do not want this man to reign over us."** For those who refuse to submit to this Censure, I ask you, Most Illustrious Prince, what else are they doing than being rebellious and disobedient to Christ, refusing to place their necks under his yoke? 

Therefore, there is no doubt that Christ also threatens them with the same punishment found in the words that immediately follow in the Gospel of Luke, when he says: **"Those enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slay them before me."** This is truly a horrible judgment which Christ himself announces to us, and it ought to rightly move our hearts—if they possess even a spark of the fear of the Lord—so that we do not refuse to be ruled by his scepter.

Furthermore, there is yet another danger, no less than the one I just mentioned, which Christ also announces to us in Matthew 21, where he says: **"The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits."** No one can deny that the kingdom of Christ has reached us; however, unless we wish to be utterly shameless, we cannot deny that we bear very little or almost no fruit. If we were to truly restore that Discipline which collapsed so long ago, it <unclear>would seem</unclear> to me to be like the digging around an unfruitful tree, and like the manure <note>original: *stercoris*; a reference to the Parable of the Barren Fig Tree in Luke 13, where the gardener pleads for one more year to "dig around it and dung it."</note> placed at its roots, just as Christ speaks—

# LETTER 221.
## II.

What I have done in person, and what my relative Caspar Lyser has done through his letters regarding **Church Discipline** <term>Ecclesiastical Censure</term> <note>original: *Censura Ecclesiastica*; the system by which church leaders supervised the morals of the congregation and excluded unrepentant sinners from the sacraments.</note> before Your Mercy, I have dared to address Your Mercy again by letter, lest you think it was done more out of levity than out of piety. For that which you had kindly and mercifully granted to us has been entirely retracted by the Counselors in Your Mercy's name, and has been most strictly forbidden to us. Just as we could not wonder at this enough, so we grieved most deeply, since nothing was attempted by us contrary to the Word of the Lord. And as far as can be gathered from past events, little hope is left to us among certain people for restoring the collapsed **Discipline**. 

But relying on your singular piety, we could not cast away all hope; for it is well known to you that "the throne is established by righteousness," <note>A reference to Proverbs 16:12. The author is arguing that a stable government requires a moral and disciplined populace.</note> because we also require an outward righteousness—besides that of faith—as its inseparable companion. We ourselves also hate confusion; we seek order and **good discipline** <term>eutaxian</term> <note>original Greek: *εὐταξίαν*, a term used by the Reformers to denote well-ordered behavior and church governance.</note>. No one is ignorant of the fact that there is a very great difference between the office of the **Magistrate** <note>The secular civil government.</note> and Church Discipline. Yet neither of these is contrary to the other, but one, as they say, "lends a hand" to the other. And these matters, under godly Emper[ors]...

*Regarding this, we would have no small hope if those public offenses were removed with a different severity than we have seen done until now. I myself know how much hatred I have garnered for myself even by the mere name of this <term>Ecclesiastical Censure</term> <note>original: "Censuræ Ecclesiasticæ"; the system of church discipline where the clergy monitored the morals of the community.</note>, especially among those <term>Evangelicals</term> <note>original: "Evangelicorum"; early Protestants who emphasized the Gospel.</note> who, pretending to be <term>Curii</term> <note>A reference to the Roman Manius Curius Dentatus, a symbol of ancient austerity and virtue; Brenz is criticizing people who feign moral strictness in public.</note>, live like <term>Bacchanals</term> <note>original: "bachanalia"; referring to the wild, drunken festivals of Bacchus, meaning they live riotously.</note>. *This zeal tends toward this goal above all: that, by cutting away the offenses—not those we have received from others, but those given by us, given, I say, by our own fault and unbridled license—we may walk worthily of the Gospel, lest perhaps at some point the Kingdom of God be taken away from us and handed over to a nation that produces fruit. But if I should achieve nothing (though far be it from me to distrust the help of Your Clemency in this matter), I nevertheless wished to testify by these letters to the gratitude of my soul toward Your Clemency. These letters may also serve as a testimony of my innocence before the tribunal of Christ, showing that the zeal to restore the collapsed Ecclesiastical Censure was not lacking in me, nor in either of us.*

*Ah, most Illustrious Prince, hear us, and having called a <term>Synod</term> <note>A formal assembly of church leaders and theologians.</note>, see to it that the matter is seriously deliberated upon again, to see if there is any way the churches might be better provided for! You, above all, Jesus Christ, Son of God, crucified for our sins, I invoke with burning prayers—You, whose glory is at stake, and who most strictly commended this Censure to us—so that through the Spirit [He may guide] this Synod...*

# LETTERS FROM THE YEAR 1653.
## *Sent later.*
### LETTER 222.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-
->my most beloved Friend,<-

I have received and read your response, but I shall send back not a single word this time that could be attributed to the vanity of praise. I am not unaware that every breeze, and even the smoke within the breeze itself, easily and suddenly vanishes, leaving behind nothing but a void trace of nothingness. *Piety alone is gain; Piety alone is the foundation which we both ought to acquire and are able to keep for ourselves.* <note>original: "Pietas sola est lucrum, Pietas sola est fundamentum..."</note> Nor do I disagree with you that dire things are portended everywhere for this century of ours, because wretched mortals seek rest in nothing so much as the destruction of their neighbor, whom the sacred laws command should be loved. To mortals in such great turmoil, the heavens, the air, the earth, and the water all seem to announce massive disturbances. The most secure and wisest of all seem to me to be those who, far from the "Prudence of the world," <note>Referring to the biblical concept of worldly wisdom vs. spiritual wisdom.</note> piously seek security only through harmless caution. You will, however, forgive this judgment of mine, which, out of my slightness of judgment, I could not help but add in place of a response to your severe and true complaints. Farewell happily. At Wolfenbüttel, <note>original: "VVelferbyti"; the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> the 6th of April, 1653.

->Your Reverence’s<-
->devoted<-
->Sibylla Ursula, Duchess of Brunswick & Lüneburg<- <note>original: "D. B. & L." (Ducissa Brunsvicensis et Luneburgensis). Sibylla Ursula (1629–1671) was a highly educated princess and writer, daughter of Duke August the Younger.</note>

<summary>A philosophical letter from Duchess Sibylla Ursula of Brunswick-Lüneburg to an unnamed clergyman, reflecting on the vanity of worldly praise and the social turmoil of the mid-17th century. She emphasizes that true security is found in piety rather than the "wisdom of the world."</summary>

### LETTER 223.

### *TO PRINCESS SIBYLLA URSULA,*

->Most Illustrious and Highborn Princess,<-
->Most Gracious Lady,<-

What you have discussed concerning piety—the Queen of virtues—piously and eruditely in your letter, I have read both gladly and with great approval. These thoughts proceed from a noble spirit and are expressed with sincerity, at a time when elsewhere Piety is an exile and grows cold. You rightly set this alone against all the evils of Germany, and the threats of evils looming and portending because of impiety. It is a safe shield for the innocent, and for the guilty, the sharpest of swords. Indeed, it is the highest Wisdom <term>Sapientia</term> <note>In this context, a spiritual insight into divine truths rather than mere worldly knowledge.</note> to believe and trust in God as Teacher, even when reason is unwilling; the highest Prudence <term>Prudentia</term> <note>Practical wisdom or the ability to govern oneself by use of reason.</note> to obey God as Director, even when the flesh resists; the highest Fortitude <term>Fortitudo</term> <note>Moral courage and strength of character.</note> to bear the burden placed by God patiently, even if upon unequal shoulders; the highest Opulence <term>Opulentia</term> <note>True wealth, found in spiritual contentment rather than material riches.</note> to rest without murmuring in whatever lot—perhaps a lower one—is assigned by the will of God the Provider. The highest tranquility is found in resigning everything completely to God, who works all in all; Piety alone encompasses, provides, and perfects all these things.

*Indeed, we live in a profane and most monstrous age, where luxury reigns under the guise of poverty; license under servitude; security amidst dangers; dancing amidst lashes; and even in the face of destruction itself, stubbornness and arrogance (the surest omens and portents of ultimate disaster) prevail. But let us arm ourselves all the more with piety against this, so that however much it is cheapened by others, and sits in chains with the Church, we may believe with certainty that it is established for us as a sure Refuge <note>original: "Asylum"</note>, even though Babylon, Sodom, Nineveh, and even Rome and Jerusalem itself have been overturned for the impious. These few thoughts I wished to offer for the present in response to your pious and ingenious meditations, Most Illustrious Princess; if you receive them with a serene countenance, according to your customary kindness and [praise]—*

<meta>catchword: [praise] (Latin: dat)</meta>

<summary>A letter of spiritual encouragement to Princess Sibylla Ursula, praising her theological reflections and defining piety as the ultimate defense against the moral decay and political instability of 17th-century Germany.</summary>

### LETTER 224.

->Hearty Greetings<- <note>original: "S. P.", abbreviation for "Salutem Plurimam," a standard Latin greeting meaning "much health" or "heartiest greetings."</note>

The greater the joy was in you, Reverend Sir, regarding my restored health, the more vehemently I am afflicted because your own has failed again. This is that inconsistent consistency of evils within us, which sometimes seem to yield, yet do not entirely flee; instead, by some hidden ebb and flow <term>reciprocatione</term> <note>Literally a "back-and-forth," describing the relapsing nature of chronic illness.</note>, they suddenly return and bring with them—and unroll upon us—I know not what new and atrocious things. Indeed, I have been tossed by these waves for several years now, and I cannot believe you are entirely immune to them, whatever you may write about the heavy and troublesome immobility of your body. Many anxiously search for the causes of the ebbing waves in the vast Ocean; yet almost no one searches for the cause of the instability within themselves. This, however, seems by no means hidden from Your Reverence, who knows all things well, and especially from where and for what purpose these things happen to us. Those persons whom I recently wrote were suffering heavily from fever among us are now, by God's blessing, well again; yet in their place, our younger sister **Maria Elisabetha** still lies bedridden. Regarding her hoped-for recovery (along with the others), we have no doubt, so that the joys which seem to be approaching around the wedding festivities might [remain] <note>The Latin catchword "neant" at the bottom of the page likely completes the word "maneant," meaning "might remain" or "might stay."</note> for us...

# LETTER 225.
## To Prince ANTON ULRICH.
**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**
->My Most Merciful Lord,<-

**T**hat you sympathize with my stubborn and repeatedly relapsing health, in this I both acknowledge and revere your kindness <note>original: "humanitatem"</note>. I, for my part, rejoice from my soul at your restored health; I pray to God that it may make your wedding celebrations <note>original: "Nuptialia... orgia." In the 17th century, "orgia" referred to sacred rites or festive ceremonies rather than modern debauchery.</note> joyful and cheerful in every respect. My youth was once sickly; afterwards, a stable and healthy manhood followed, but it had to be maintained with moderation. Now, by a common law of nature, Old Age <term>Senectus</term> itself has become my companion. In this very thin constitution of my body and with meager nourishment, I conceive the best hope that—once the boiling humors of nature <note>Early modern medicine believed health was governed by four "humors" or fluids; "boiling humors" refers to an imbalance or feverish state.</note> are expelled and the blood is purified—firm and lasting health will follow. May it continue through every age, following the example of your most lively Lord Father <note>Augustus the Younger (1579–1666), Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, one of the most learned rulers of his time.</note>. In him, should we not marvel and offer the highest praises to God? Having entered his 75th year of age, after seeing so many things and writings, his dimmed sight <note>The Latin "hebetatum" implies a dulling or weakening, likely referring to the Duke's eyesight, which was famously strained by his massive library and scholarly work.</note> has been happily restored. This "Eye of Germany" is the "Pupil of the Church"; he has been returned to all good men by the rays of divine light, and for a longer time promised...

# THE YEAR 1653.

### LETTER 227.

#### TO PRINCE ANTON ULRICH,

Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
->My most Merciful Lord.<-

I have seen your letters with joy and pleasure; they are signs of your firmer health, for which I keep diligent watch before God, and of your constant favor toward me, to which I confess I owe the greatest gratitude. I greatly congratulate you that your wedding festivities <note>original: "Nuptialia vestra Orgia"; while "orgia" can mean secret rites, here it refers to the elaborate public celebrations of a noble wedding.</note> were serene and without a single small cloud. For usually, sad occurrences lie in wait for great joys, and joyful beginnings are ended with a mournful conclusion; I can easily believe that you avoided this through the piety and modesty you brought to the celebration. Your messenger, Michael—an industrious and dutiful man and an eyewitness—will explain the state of my affairs in more detail. I am now preparing myself to visit the thermal baths, having received by the great kindness of your Most Serene Father a litter <term>lectica; a couch or chair carried by poles, used here because Andreae is too infirm for a carriage or horse</term>, without which I would be unable to endure any form of travel. We eagerly await the arrival of the illustrious pair of Spouses, yet I easily suspect that between their departure and arrival, there will be many obstacles as well as invitations standing in the way. May God lead them away, guide them, and bring them here safe and sound. If you yourself could be joined to them as a companion, oh, with what great happiness and joy you would overwhelm me! For I love and admire your character as much as possible, and I attend you with pious prayers and favorable omens, so that a future age may see in you a second August <note>A wordplay on the name of the Prince's father, Duke August the Younger, and the Roman Emperor Augustus.</note>. Farewell, renowned Prince, along with your Most Serene House, which may God continually increase, adorn, and crown.

->Your Illustrious Highness's<-

Bebenhausen, July 13, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Most humble client,
1653. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor.

Greetings to your tutor <note>original: "Informator"</note>, who is most worthy of all my love and service.

->Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord,<-

I congratulate myself greatly on your constant and remarkable favor toward me, and your perseverance in our literary exchange; I can find no thanks worthy of them. May GOD preserve this spirit in you, so that you may forever be known as a perfect rival to the virtues of your Most Serene Father and a full heir to his kindness toward me. Indeed, I wish that, by the will of your most prudent Father, you might be joined as a companion on the journey of your most beloved sister, so that our Württemberg might be moved by the doubled joy of a long-desired sight of the stars of Brunswick <note>original: "Brunoniorum syderum"; a poetic reference to the members of the House of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note>; yet I rightly subject these and all our affairs to his providence. 

As for me, while I have now spent a month here devoted to recovering my health, I have wasted both my effort and my oil <note>original: "operam oleumq;... perdidi"; a classical Latin idiom (from Plautus and Cicero) meaning to have labored in vain, referring to the oil burned in a lamp during late-night study.</note>, as my ruined stomach rejects medicine and nourishment alike. A single support remains: Abstinence <term>Abstinentia; here meaning a medically forced fast or extreme dietary restriction</term>, persuaded not so much by advice as commanded by necessity. By this, I divide my time between the tortures of digestion and the languor of hunger, while the soul sustains the body and the body drags the soul along in a troublesome exchange. Now I am contemplating a return home, where I may continue my mourning song <note>original: "lessum meum"; an ancient term for a funeral wail or lamentation</note> in solitude, to be refreshed by no more effective balms than your letters, which are more flavorful than any nectar or ambrosia.

# LETTER 230.

->Heartiest Greetings.<-

## Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir,

There is no need for you to seek my love and benevolence toward you with many entreaties, if any sufficient amount can be expected from me; for it is so established between us—indeed, I owe it to you by right because of your own deeds. For what less can I do in return for your frequent and most delightful letters than to testify to that same affection for you with my pen, while holding it constantly in my soul? It was not permitted for me to be a companion to our Sister <note>This likely refers to Princess Clara Augusta, whose journey was discussed in the previous letter</note> on this occasion; perhaps I shall be a follower at some point, for all hope has not yet abandoned us. In the meantime, may she fare well along with *your enclosed House* <note>original: "inclusa Domo Vestra"; likely referring to the courtly or religious circle she has joined</note>, which we do not cease to follow with favor and praise, especially since we have learned with how much greater honor our lady was received and honored by you. You now have many stars illuminating your world, so that there is no need for us, who are like stars of almost no magnitude. We have heard of a wretched accident in the *Illustrious*...

Regarding your affairs at Tübingen, which have arisen from an unhappy course, we mourn this as is fitting, and we pray for some long-awaited relief from these miseries for those whom it most concerns. It is not clear to us when the Count of Barby <note>original: "Comes Barbiensis"; the House of Barby was a noble family in Saxony-Anhalt</note> will depart from here; he has lived among us for a long time now, but he has never made any mention of this departure to you. He is the only one and the last of his lineage, and there will accordingly be many things that still delay him. You shall no longer expect our tutor <note>original: "Informatorem"; at this time, an "informator" was a high-level private teacher or mentor responsible for a prince's intellectual and moral upbringing</note>; he at least progressed as far as Nuremberg, and about fourteen days ago, because of the shortness of time and other intervening matters, he returned safely to us. It remains for me to pray to a propitious Divinity for every favorable and happy thing for you, and to humbly entreat for your perennial favor and kindness toward me. May God the Best and Greatest confirm and welcome this, and may He wish you to be safe and in good health for a very long time—which is my earnest prayer.*

## LETTER 233.

### To Prince ANTON ULRICH.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**Most Merciful Lord,**<-

Truly, I love Your Highness’s letters and value them greatly; they are signs of Your enduring favor toward me and sure pledges of Your succession to Your father’s fame. No one well-versed in history is unaware of how much it matters to the affairs of the Church and of literature—while others are carried away, each by his own whims—to have constant and perpetual patrons. The sad examples of history speak of ages that changed from well-ordered and learned times into barbarism and dissolution. Therefore, I pray that the genuine—nay, even a doubled—spirit of your Most Serene Lord Father <note>Duke August the Younger (1579–1666), famed for his piety and his massive library at Wolfenbüttel.</note> may be granted to You, so that You may both excellently protect and most widely promote the glory of the House of Brunswick, which is always most highly praised for its piety and learning, alongside its other more excellent virtues.

I heartily congratulate your "Ethiopian" <note>Referring to the young African man, named Augustus, whose baptism was described on the previous page.</note> on his entry into the Christian rites, and I pray to Christ that, since he cannot change his skin <note>original: "cutem mutare non potest"; a reference to Jeremiah 13:23. In the 17th century, this was a common rhetorical trope used to contrast physical appearance with spiritual "purity."</note>, he may nevertheless put on a white <note>In the sense of "pure" or "shining."</note> soul. I wish you had informed me whether he was from the Abyssinians <note>Referring to the historic Christian kingdom in modern-day Ethiopia.</note> themselves, or merely from the Mauritanians <note>A general term then used for people from North or West Africa.</note>, as they differ greatly in their religion. 

A few days ago, our "Wilderness" <note>original: "Eremus"; Andreae frequently used this term to refer to his residence or place of ministry as a spiritual retreat.</note> was honored by a most illustrious circle of guests; for a boar hunt, a very large number of the House of Baden of both sexes were brought here by the Hero Prince <note>likely referring to a local high-ranking noble leading the hunt.</note>. One person among them was missing whom we most desired: your brother-in-law Lord Frederick, along with his most praiseworthy wife, whose virtues her sister-in-law, the maiden Lady Anna Johanna <note>Anna Johanna (1622–1659), daughter of the Count of Salm-Kyrburg and wife of Frederick VI, Margrave of Baden-Durlach.</note>, could not sufficiently explain to me in words, nor express with enough inward joy. Yet we are still expecting them—I especially, with unbearable longing—no matter how much these letters, full of every sign of grace, have meanwhile smoothed the way.

I am very much in doubt whether I should write to your illustrious sister, Lady Sibylla Ursula <note>Sibylla Ursula (1629–1671) was a highly educated princess and writer, sister to Prince Anton Ulrich.</note>, that incomparable muse <note>original: "Nymphæ"; used here as a classical compliment for a learned woman.</note>, whose letters I nevertheless value more than gold and gems. ## LETTER 234.

Since you value my letters so highly, Reverend Sir, I wish I could satisfy you with more! But let these few words suffice in the meantime. You pray for the spirit and mind of my most merciful Lord Parent <note>Referring to Duke August the Younger.</note>, for excellent learning, and for a doubling of my own progress. At the start of this most auspicious year, I also wish a Spirit for you, with a simple prayer but one brought forth from my innermost heart—but most especially a vital spirit, which you may lead through many long years while keeping your body in good health. Other gifts, and indeed those of the soul, so perfect...

He is sending to me an excellent author <note>original: "Auctorem quendam Optimum"; this refers to a specific book or the works of a specific writer being gifted.</note>, recently brought in your name as a gift. From this, I was immediately and clearly able to see your greatest kindness toward me, which I almost thought had been offended because of my rather long silence; but I know you are of a stable and noble mind, one who willingly grants some allowance for poor health, for slightly longer travels, and also for other distractions. It will be evident from elsewhere that we returned from these shortly before the feast of the Nativity <note>Christmas.</note>. We experienced very heavy and constant rains there, which still persist even now, and they threaten not only the old illness—those constant and troublesome fevers—but also other very serious trials. I myself encountered something of that sort yesterday, and indeed with an unlucky omen, such that I feared an attack of tertian fever <note>original: "tertianae"; a form of malaria where the fever recurs every third day.</note> again; therefore, I kept myself in my study <note>original: "Musæo"; in the 17th century, a private library or room for scholarly contemplation.</note> and sought a remedy through sleep. Today, by God's blessing, I am doing well again, and I am taking some care of my body. This health—if it should be constant and perpetual, along with the greatest peace and tranquility—I also pray for you from my heart at the start of this coming year; for if that is granted by divine power, I know not what greater or happier thing could happen to us on earth. May you enjoy it to the furthest limits of life, and receive my greatest thanks for the aforementioned book. Farewell.

->To your Reverence,<-

Wolfenbüttel, 3rd of ->Your most devoted,<-

# LETTER CCXXXVI.
## TO PRINCESS SIBYLLA URSULA.

->Most Illustrious and High Princess, most Clement Lady,<-

Indeed, I was ashamed to write to You, lest I should seem a bothersome interrupter—I who have so often caused You trouble with my frivolous and unpolished letters—had your most beloved brother, the Illustrious Prince Anthony Ulrich <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714), later Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, was a novelist and poet.</note>, not restored my spirit. He gave me the certain hope that You would be thankful for my letters and would repay them with Your own most elegant and refined ones. Under his guidance and authority, therefore—to whom You will attribute all this confidence—I present myself to You. Before all else, I offer what I owe: a **PRAYER FOR HAPPINESS** of every kind in this coming year. I pray with my whole soul as a suppliant that **GOD THE BEST AND GREATEST** may deign to crown Your distinguished virtues and Your learning, which is rare for Your gender and rank. 

Next follows the debt of my gratitude, because You received my meager little paper gift <note>original: "levidensem meam strenulam chartaceam"; likely a small book or poem sent as a New Year's gift.</note> with a serene countenance and a gracious spirit, as Your Most Serene Lord Father <note>Duke Augustus the Younger, a famous book collector and scholar.</note> himself can witness. I am by no means unaware that Your dignity, age, and reputation demand far greater and rarer gifts than those for which I was once admitted by Your courtesy and kindness. But what else could I bring from this wilderness <note>original: "eremo"; Andreae often used this term to describe his relative isolation in the later years of his life.</note>, excluded as I am from almost all human society, not to mention the workshops or markets of craftsmen and refinements? Furthermore, cast down in bed for a great part of the day and confined to the house, I am hardly able to seek out those more subtle artistic works which might befit and delight Your sublime genius. 

Therefore, just as they say was the custom of the Persian Kings—that they would admit no one into their sight without a gift, yet they disdained no gift, whatever might be produced at home—so from Your gentleness and equity, I reverently—

### LETTER CCXXXVII.

## TO THE SERENE PRINCES ANTHONY ULRICH AND FERDINAND ALBERT.

### Much health and greeting,
### *and a most auspicious Year.*

-> **Most Illustrious and High Princes,** <-
-> **My by far most Clement Lords,** <-

As much great pleasure as I take from your letters, so much grief is brought to me by both the dullness of my mind and the feebleness of my body, through which it is by no means possible to respond to your letters as I wish and according to the requirements of my duty. Therefore, I must most humbly and earnestly seek pardon from your fairness, that I might respond to your two letters with this single one—yours being most flavorful and polished, while mine is tasteless and unrefined. I am fully promised that this pardon will be easier for me because of the fraternal concord that exists between you and your generous indulgence toward me.

But I do not have different or contrary things to write to you, but clearly the same: namely, **GOOD WORDS**, which in the many [days] of this year and the following...

# TRIBUTES
## TO THE PRINCIPAL
### Ancestors and Progenitors of the Most Serene AUGUSTUS, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, succinctly comprised.

If it were our intention to record in writing all the ancestors of the Brunswick <note>original: "Brunsuicensis"</note> lineage, and so many founders of that Royal stock who have commended their names to posterity with the immortal glory of praise, honoring them with worthy proclamations, so great a number of them would present themselves that there would never be an end to recounting them. Therefore, leaving the detailed praise of those families to their own historians, we shall select a few from among them—as if gathering a small gleaning from a bountiful harvest—whose fame and virtue have spread so far and wide that they are now known throughout the same regions of the sky that span the entire world. Among these, the first to draw our attention is:

## GUELPH IV <note>Welf IV (c. 1035–1101), the progenitor of the younger House of Welf and a pivotal figure in the family's history.</note>, surnamed the Brave

He was the son of Azzo IV <note>Alberto Azzo II, Margrave of Este (c. 997–1097); the "IV" reflects a specific genealogical tradition used by the author.</note>, Marquis of Este and Tuscany, Prince of Sardinia, Nordgau, and Carinthia, Marquis of Verona, and Duke of Swabia and Spoleto. He also obtained <term>Bavaria</term> <note>original: "Bojariam"</note> after his uncle's death <note>The catchword "exces-" indicates the word "excessum," referring to the death or departure of his maternal uncle, Welf III.</note>

<summary>This page introduces a series of biographical tributes (Elogia) to the ancestors of the House of Brunswick, beginning with Guelph IV, the first of the younger Welf line.</summary>
<keywords>House of Brunswick, Guelph IV, Welf, House of Este, Bavaria, genealogy, Azzo IV, Nordgau, Carinthia</keywords>

--- Page 293 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Welf IV (Guelph IV), whose entry began on the previous page. It details his political maneuvers during the Investiture Controversy, his participation in the Crusade of 1101, and his death in Cyprus.</meta>

<header>PRAISES OF THE EMINENT [ANCESTORS]</header>

[...continued from previous page] death <note>of his uncle</note>, he obtained the principality by the favor of Emperor **Henry IV**, after **Otto of Nordheim** <note>original: "Ottone Visurgiano," referring to Otto's origins near the Weser River</note> was removed in the year 1071. Six years later, having been drawn to the side of Pope **Gregory VII**, when he approved a cause condemned by the Emperor, he paid the penalty for his ill-advised boldness by being captured by the Emperor. However, having later successfully escaped from custody, he took **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustam Rhetia Vindelica"</note> by surprise and defended the dignity of Bishop **Wigold**, having expelled his rival **Siegfried** as an usurper of the bishopric and led him away in chains to **Ravensburg**. 

In the year 1097, after he had endured twenty years of exile and was reconciled with the Emperor, having recovered the principality of **Bavaria** <note>original: "Bojariæ"</note> by the Emperor's will, he sought **Italy** to enter into his inheritance, since his father **Azzo**, then over a hundred years old, had finally met his death in this year. 

In the following year, when his sons were brewing new plots in **Bavaria** <note>original: "Boica"</note> during their father's absence, he suppressed them in the very preparation of their rebellion; having smothered the fire at its first flame, he brought them back into favor with Emperor **Henry**. 

In the year 1100 <note>original: "Anno M. C."</note>, having raised a massive cross in the camp, he set out with a most well-equipped infantry army to serve in **Palestine**, accompanied by **William, Count of Poitiers** <note>original: "VVilelmo Pictavorum Comite"</note>. Both leaders had gathered forces numbering one hundred and sixty thousand men. But with great difficulty—the **Turks** indeed harassing them from all sides, and many of his companions being consumed by hunger and want—and further oppressed by plague and the conspiracy of the Emperor **Alexius** <note>the Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos</note>, while he prepared to return home, he died at **Paphos** in **Cyprus**. His heirs later exhumed his buried remains there so that he might be more worthily interred at **Altdorf** in the **Monastery of the Vineyards** <note>original: "Vinearum Monasterio," referring to Weingarten Abbey</note>.

## **Welf V**, nicknamed **the Fat**
### [Also known as Guelph V]

He was the Duke of the Bavarians, the **Ambrones** <note>original: "Ambronum," likely referring to the people near the Ammer river in Bavaria</note>, and the **Lechrainers** <note>original: "Lycantiorum," referring to the people living along the Lech river</note>, Margrave of **Verona**, and Count of **Altdorf**, who succeeded his father in the principality. He held the Duchies of **Spoleto**, **Tuscany**, and **Etruria** by right of his wife **Matilda** <note>Matilda of Tuscany, the "Great Countess" and a powerful ally of the Papacy</note>, who was the daughter of **Boniface**—a man who ruled widely across Italy and surpassed all other princes of that land in everything mortals value most. 

The Prince was of a mild and calm disposition, one who preferred to be loved rather than feared. He was easy to approach and courteous in speech, yet without any loss of his princely dignity; he was more powerful with a bare, almost gentle hand than others were with an armed one. He was considered the sole model of a praised Prince in his own age. His court was a school <note>original: "gymnasium"</note> of elegance and character: whenever a youth of great potential was seen, they were transferred by their ambitious parents into his training-hall for young men <note>original: "Ephebæum"</note> as if into a nursery of virtue. 

Nevertheless, he was also skilled in war; he gave clear proofs of his bravery, especially in Italy, where it is recorded that he waged many wars and repelled those who were hostile to his paternal and ancestral estates. Yet he excelled exceedingly in the arts of peace: he was accustomed to keep severity hidden and to keep mercy ready at hand, always blending the role of a Father with that of a Prince. He died <unclear>at a certain</unclear> age at **Kaufering** on the Lech <note>original: "ad Lycum"</note>. In the year 1120, he was laid in the tomb of his ancestors in the monastery of **Weingarten**.

## **HENRY THE PROUD**,
### *Duke of the Bavarians, Saxons, etc.*

Why do you recoil at the name "the Proud," gentle reader? It was not vanity or the swelling of a haughty spirit that imposed such a disparaging name upon this Prince, but rather his power, his magnificence, and the vastness of the lands over which he ruled—things for which he could rightly be proud above all other Princes. And why indeed should he not? When such a great number of titles and provinces flow into a single man, why should they not lift his spirit higher? 

To the principality of Bavaria—under which the **Navisci**, **Vindelici**, **Raetians**, **Noricans**, and **Ripuarii** <note>The author uses these classical tribal names to describe the various ethnic groups of the Alpine and Danube regions under Bavarian rule</note> are included—and his ancestral estates in **Swabia**, the Emperor added **Saxony** and the territories of **Brunswick** and **Lüneburg** as a dowry for his loyalty and the courage he displayed in the Italian wars. The Emperor also entrusted **Etruria** <note>Tuscany</note> and a great part of Italy to him as a legal trust, so that he held within his power everything lying between the Lower Sea <note>The Tyrrhenian Sea</note> and the Upper Sea <note>The Adriatic Sea</note>, and between the German Ocean <note>The North Sea</note> and the **Codanian Gulf** <note>The Baltic Sea or Kattegat</note>. # EULOGIES OF THE EMINENT

### HENRY THE LION

**Henry**, who—not without a foreshadowing of his future valor—borrowed his name from the bravest of animals <note>The lion</note>, was the Duke and Elector of **Saxony**, **Bavaria**, **Angria**, and **Westphalia**; Count of **Holstein**, **Stormarn**, and **Wagria**; Lord of **Lübeck**, **Brunswick**, and **Lüneburg**. He was the most powerful of all the Princes whom the sun has looked upon in **Germany** within a thousand years. Bound by an oath to King **Conrad**, he was a companion on the expedition undertaken to **Palestine** <note>The Second Crusade (1147–1149)</note>. Upon his return from that expedition in the year 1146, at the Diet <note>original: "Comitiis," a formal assembly of princes</note> held at **Regensburg**, Emperor **Frederick I** <note>Barbarossa</note> restored **Bavaria** to him.

In the many expeditions he led against the **Vandals** <note>In this context, "Vandals" refers to the Wends or West Slavic tribes of Northern Germany</note>, he departed more illustrious with every victory, and he brought those rude and uncultivated peoples toward a more civilized way of life. With great courage, he defended Emperor **Frederick Barbarossa** himself during a battle fought above the **Aelian Bridge** <note>original: "pontem Ælium," now the Ponte Sant'Angelo in Rome</note>; after the gates of the citadel were broken, he killed one thousand five hundred of the enemy. 

As a reward for this feat, having received the right of episcopal investiture from the Emperor, he founded three Bishoprics: **Lübeck**, **Ratzeburg**, and **Schwerin**. Afterward, having planned a new city, he named it **Leonstad** <note>Lion-city</note> after his own name, near **Hamburg**. He grandly restored **Lübeck**, which had been disfigured by fire, and was the first to lay the foundations of its great size, by which it stands out among other cities today. From the ruins and rubble of the city of **Bardowick** in **Saxony**—which **Burting** <note>A reference to the chronicler Heinrich Bunting</note> claims is two hundred years older than **Rome**—he built **Lüneburg**. 

He led away **Wartislaw**, the son of **Niklot**, Duke of the **Slavs**, as a captive. When the Slavs rose up against him, having suddenly gathered massive forces, he placed a curb on their boldness. As the glory of **Henry** grew, all the sacred and secular princes <note>The "princes of the church" (bishops/abbots) and the "profane" or lay nobility</note>...

He had two wives: first, **Clementia**, daughter of Duke **Conrad of Zähringen**; second, **Matilda**, daughter of **Henry**, King of England. He stands as a notable example of changeable fortune; like Marius <note>Gaius Marius, a Roman general known for his dramatic rise and fall</note>, he successfully achieved great power, but lost it very quickly. He left three sons: 1. **Otto IV**, elected Emperor of the Romans in the year 1199. 2. **Henry**, nicknamed "the Long," Duke of **Saxony** and Count Palatine Elector. 3. **William**, of whom we shall speak next.

## MAGNUS THE CHAIN-WEARER, Duke
## of Brunswick and Lüneburg

So named from the silver chain which he wore hanging from his neck <note>Magnus II (c. 1324–1373), called "Torquatus" in Latin, which refers to a twisted metal collar or chain</note>, he was Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, and Lord of Sangerhausen: the founder of the Wolfenbüttel line. William <note>William II of Lüneburg</note> designated him as the heir to the Duchy of Lüneburg in his will. He was a noble Prince of vast spirit, yet restless and degenerating into insolence—which is hardly surprising on the stage of mortal men, who find peace in the painted face of flattering Fortune <note>original: "fucata fortunæ blandientis fronte"</note> and take the omen of lifelong happiness from her first laugh.

From our Prince, however, Fortune always turned away with a harsh face. He brought war against the people of Mecklenburg <note>original: "Megapolensibus"</note>, but it was ill-fated; he was defeated and captured by them. Two years later, when he campaigned against Gerard, the Bishop of Hildesheim, he fought under an unfavorable star of war <note>original: "iniquo Marte," literally "with an unfavorable Mars"</note> and fell into the hands of his enemies, having lost many of his men. Because of this, he was forced to sell Landsberg and Sangerhausen so that he might ransom his freedom with that price. 

Finally, in single combat, having engaged with Count Otto of Schaumburg, while he was threatening death upon his fallen opponent, he was run through by the Count's servant and died in the year 1373. 

His wife was not Catherine, but Sophia, the daughter of Woldemar, Elector of Brandenburg; she later married Albert, Duke of Saxony, Angria, and Westphalia. Among his other children was Frederick, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, whom heroic virtues carried to the height of the Roman Empire <note>Frederick was elected King of the Romans in 1400, though he was murdered before his coronation</note>, but the more than monstrous envy of his rivals wickedly and through a nefarious murder <note>original: "parricidium," here used in the sense of a heinous assassination of a leader</note> cast him down from there. ## BERNHARD, Duke of Brunswick & Lüneburg

The beginnings of his reign were ill-omened. For in the year 1382, he was captured by John of Suicheld and Conrad of Steinberg and held in chains until the victory which his brother Henry—aided by auxiliary forces from Brunswick—won against the people of Lüneburg. After six years, he was finally released from captivity for a ransom <note>original: "Lytro," from the Greek 'lytron' meaning a price paid for freedom</note> of 7,000 gold pieces. He was a hero second to none in fortitude and military excellence, who, having joined his forces with those of his brother Henry, captured Uelzen <note>original: "Olsenium"</note>. He clashed in battle with Jobst <note>original: "Iodoco"</note> and Procopius, the Margraves of Moravia, with whom the Emperor had besieged Brandenburg. Seeking to avenge the murder of his brother Frederick, he campaigned against John of Nassau, the Archbishop of Mainz. With the help of his cousin, William the Victorious, he routed John, the Bishop of Hildesheim. He purchased the entire County of Homburg <note>original: "Comitatũ Hamburgensem," likely referring to the Lordship of Homburg which the Welfs acquired in 1409</note> with all its towns, citadels, villages, and hamlets from the last Henry, who died without issue. After an exchange of territories was made with William the Victorious, he received the Duchy of Lüneburg to govern, handing over the Duchy of Brunswick (which he had held since the murder of his brother Frederick) to William. He departed this life <note>original: "Humanitatem exuit," literally "he put off his humanity"</note> in the year 1434. His wife <note>original: "Thori consortem," partner of his bed</note> was Margaret, the daughter of Wenceslaus, Elector of Saxony, Angria, and Westphalia. Besides Otto of the Heath (commonly known as *den grossen Otto von der Heyden*), he had a son named:

Public fame offers this memorable testimony to this most gentle Prince: though he was himself illustrious in many virtues, he desired above all to see his sons become like him. He departed this life in the year 1478. His wife was Magdalene, the daughter of Frederick I, the Margrave and Elector of Brandenburg.

## HENRY, Duke of Brunswick
->and Lüneburg<-

Henry was the first <note>Henry "the Middle," 1468–1532</note> of that name when he began to grow into adulthood under his mother's guardianship. As he matured in age, he demonstrated a greatness of soul and the excellence of a sharp mind. He gave witness especially during the Hildesheim war <note>original: "Hildesiensi bello," referring to the Great Diocesan Feud of 1519–1523, a massive conflict over land and rights in Lower Saxony</note> to how much he excelled in counsel, nobility of spirit, and moderation. Allied with John of Lauenburg, the Prince-Bishop of Hildesheim, in the year 1519, he defeated the army of two kinsmen <note>original: "agnatorum," referring to male-line relatives</note>, Eric and Henry, in a great battle at Soltau. Having captured Eric on the field of battle and brought him to Celle, he treated him honorably; after a few days, when a peaceful settlement had been reached, he sent him back home. 

Five years before this war, he performed distinguished service for Henry the Elder, Duke of Brunswick, in that expedition against the Frisians <note>The Frisians lived along the coastal regions of the Netherlands and Germany</note>. This illustrious Prince departed from the living in exile at Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ Parisiorum"</note> in the year 1532 at the age of 64. He was exceedingly dear to many princes, but was especially welcomed by the Kings of France, in whose glowing grace and favor he remained. His remains <note>original: "corporis exuviæ," literally 'the spoils of the body'</note> were returned to Celle in Saxony through the pious care of his sons. His wife was Margaret, the younger daughter of Ernest, Elector of Saxony, whom her paternal uncle, Elector Albert, escorted to Celle in the year 1486. The wedding was celebrated in the castle, and was also attended by the Queen of Denmark, the bride's sister.
