## ERNEST, Duke of Brunswick
### & Lüneburg

In a fortunate birth (alongside Otto of Harburg and Francis, Lord of Gifhorn), this Ernest was brought into the light on June 26 <note>original: "sexto Kalend. Quintilis," the sixth day before the Kalends of July</note> in the year 1497. Raised in the court of Frederick III, the Elector <term>Elector: one of the high-ranking German princes of the Holy Roman Empire entitled to vote in the election of the Emperor</term> of Saxony, he was sent to Wittenberg to be successfully steeped in letters. He drew a laudable knowledge of these subjects from Georg Spalatin, a man of remarkable eloquence <note>Spalatin was a key figure in the Reformation and a close advisor to Martin Luther</note>. 

After he came of age <note>original: "ex ephebis," literally "leaving the rank of a youth"</note>, he lived for several years in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note> at the court of King Francis <note>King Francis I of France</note>, where he was held in great honor due to his extraordinary natural gifts and high virtues. During this time, he practiced his skills in the Latin language, thoroughly mastered the French tongue, and diligently studied and considered the procedures of the Royal court of justice. 

Upon returning to his fatherland, once he took the helm of government, he believed his primary duty was to ensure that the purer doctrine of the Gospel—according to the writings of Luther—was taught without discord, and that the study of literature and oratory should flourish in the towns.

For the sake of the Augsburg Confession <note>the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, presented to the Emperor in 1530</note>, he shirked no hatred and fled no danger; instead, he constantly demonstrated by the subscription of his name that he embraced that form of doctrine for which he was prepared to pour out both his life and his blood. He never failed the excellent Prince, Elector John <note>John the Steadfast of Saxony</note>, but loved and honored him as a son loves a father, and he entrusted the inspection of his own churches to him. 

Adorned with many ornaments of virtue, he was loved by all, and protected by this goodwill, he was formidable to those who were more fierce. He aided the common defense of peace with arms. He brought no wars upon his neighbors even when provoked; nevertheless, he took up arms for John Frederick, Elector of Saxony, against Henry the Younger of Brunswick—

### HENRY, Duke of Brunswick & Lüneburg, Father of the Most Serene Augustus.

Dannenberg witnessed the auspicious birth of your grandfather Henry, Rudolph Augustus <note>The author is addressing the current Duke, Rudolph Augustus, who ruled from 1666 to 1704</note>, at dawn on June 4 <note>original: "pridie Non. He paid his debt to nature <note>original: "Naturæ satisfecit," a polite Latin expression for dying</note> on January 17, 1598. He was a prince distinguished by his mild gentleness, the very embodiment of living humanity and mercy.

# AUGUSTUS
## Senior Duke of Brunswick & Lüneburg.

I am not unaware, Prince Augustus—the greatest of Princes (unless the fates deceive) and the best (whether they wish it or not)—that Alexander the Great issued an edict forbidding anyone from depicting him with a brush except Apelles, or carving him with a chisel except Pyrgoteles, or casting him in bronze except Lysippus <note>Apelles, Pyrgoteles, and Lysippus were the exclusive court artists of Alexander the Great, representing the pinnacle of Greek art</note>. With what boldness, then, and with what confidence should I bring my unwashed and profane hands to the most sacred matters of Your Serenity? 

For no such darkness has clouded my eyes that I would not recognize I am as much inferior to Apelles, lesser than Pyrgoteles, and a worse craftsman than Lysippus, as the undisputed calculation of public fame recognizes, declares, and admires You as a prince greater, more upright, and better than Alexander the Great. Your kindness and August benevolence will therefore excuse this crime or error of mine, if I shroud the splendors of Your virtues, of which the whole world speaks, behind the curtain of a religious silence. Deities are better worshiped within the inner shrines of the household altar <term>Lararium: a private shrine in Roman houses dedicated to the Lares, or guardian spirits</term> than in the open.

We do not ascribe praise to You merely as one placed among Your ancestors; we are deterred first by our own reverence, and then by Your modesty, which does not allow its own ornaments to be made public. This Sun <note>The author uses "Sun" as a metaphor for Duke Augustus</note> would entirely extinguish the light of Your ancestors, however great it may be—just like the rays of lesser stars—if he were shown in full to the lands; and even if it were permitted, this small handbook <note>original: "pugillaris hæc epitome," literally a "fist-sized summary"</note> would not contain it. 

But this so graceful abundance of virtues shall live and endure; and what the thinness of my eloquence does not dare, the grander pens of others will proceed at length to testify before all posterity. Fame herself will blow her trumpet and broadcast to the whole world the praises that were not silenced by choice. Which...

We present to you the lofty souls of your ancestors, Augustan heroes of such a kind that even Anchises could not have shown them to Aeneas in the Elysian grove <note>In Virgil’s *Aeneid*, the spirit of Anchises shows his son Aeneas a vision of their future Roman descendants in the underworld (the Elysian Fields)</note>. In this work, as if in a mirror, it will be possible to contemplate them and
->read the faces of those gone before and learn the countenances of those to come.<- <note>original: "Adversos legere & venientum discere vultus." A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid* regarding the parade of future heroes.</note>
My purpose was not merely that you should read of your birth's origin—though we have left behind ancestors stretching back many centuries—but that these family examples should be present for you in the world. I intended for you to carry their likenesses vividly expressed, not in a physical hall or a storage chest, but within your mind. For wherever you turn your eyes, you find the virtue and the lineage of your own house. And yet, what need is there to represent to you so many founders and protectors of your venerable lineage? These ancestors, like creditors of their own praise and virtue, might stir your burning spirit in your dreams, just as the trophies of Miltiades once haunted Themistocles <note>The Greek general Themistocles famously said he could not sleep because the "trophies of Miltiades" (the hero of the Battle of Marathon) spurred his own ambition for glory</note>. But you already possess all things uniquely in your father Augustus alone. You will not owe your life to one man and your virtue to another, nor will you seek your fortune from strangers. He, whose blood you share, is for you in all honors

it is enough: for even if he were to give nothing else, he would provide an Example, though he himself is without precedent <note>original: "sine exemplo" – meaning peerless or unique</note>.

> A beautiful youth and scion of the Lüneburg line,

And I made you a Leader of the people, to preside over many,

Ordering his words to prevail, he himself gave a sign of favor.

Already he sees that they have grown, and on the tender trunk
The tree promises its first riches; soon, beneath the shady foliage
Of its mother, and under the sun <note>original: "Phoebo" — Apollo, the sun god</note> and the warm breezes of the West Wind,

And now they breathe the spirit of the father himself, reflecting

Among the number of Brothers, you, Rudolf August, shine out
Excellently, illustrious in your beautiful mantle of virtue:
Just as at the prelude of dawn, Apollo <note>original: "Cynthius"</note> reddens
With gold and, scattering far the radiant spears of day,
Clothes the world in a rosy light.
While with a rare character and a powerful strength of mind
He rises quickly toward the high honors of praise,
You surpass the leaders of your own age in the splendor of your fame.
Nor does your August Father only show you the footsteps of praise
Through his own examples and warnings:
While he does not cease to fit your hands for scepters, to mold
Your capable mind, and to adorn your gentle character,
Teachers also join the task with skillful zeal,
Who exercise your youthful years <note>original: "pretextatos... annos" — a reference to the 'toga praetexta' worn by Roman youth before adulthood</note> in the honor of solid Virtue
And shape you with a learned thumb;
They who create the grace of your speech and provide
Pure rivers of eloquence, and—that which adorns every honor—
They instill in your soul learning, the foster-child of piety.

In clear signs—and the arts themselves, along with ancient customs,
Return to the gatherings of men and revisit the cities;
Bright once the stains are wiped away, and having cast off old age,
In a new spring, just as a cold snake sheds its skin.
O gods above, under whose name once grew...

# Another Congratulation to the Prince
## AUGUSTUS.
### In Iambic-Heroic Verse.

That Augustus, the glory of the Guelph household <note>original: "Guelphici Laris" — Lar refers to the Roman household gods, here used to signify the Welf/Guelph dynasty</note>,
The star of the more majestic ones, and in his own eyes
Always more majestic <note>original: "Augustior" — a pun on the Duke's name, "Augustus," and the Latin "auctior," meaning increased or made greater</note> than himself, like a river grown larger,
And always more untiring in his labors,
And alone, daily more learned than himself,
And daily more generous through well-deserving deeds,
Now renders his "Harmony" <note>original: "Harmoniam" — referring to the Duke's "Evangelische Kirchen-Harmonie," a scholarly work merging the four Gospels into a single narrative</note> more enlarged,
That marker of astounding erudition,
And the bright star of true simplicity,
A sacred treasure <note>original: "Cimelium" — a precious object or heirloom typically kept in a treasury or cabinet of curiosities</note> for late posterity.
Who would not give new thanks to this Hector <note>The Trojan hero, used here as a symbol of a noble and strong protector</note>,
And wish him increased in age, strength, genius, and wealth,
And adorned in every part! <note>original: "omnibus numeris" — a Latin idiom meaning "perfect in every respect"</note>
But you, House of the Guelphs, and the Church,
The Court, and the Academy, and the workshop, and every field,
For however many gifts God shall give to this best of men,
-> God, <-
So many honors flow from here to all of us.
Therefore may he live, act, study, and prosper well always,
Ever more blooming, and always more capable of deep
Strength and genius, and having become dutiful in all things,
May he make us bound to him, and mindful of the good
-> goods <-
Which, since it is not within the power of our land or wealth to repay,
May He repay who alone is able, and return it in heaven,
Every single one, the Savior and Author of the mortal race.

-> In the Year <-

Behold, the Guelph Duke, being refreshed, finishes his noble work on the books he has composed of the Harmony of the Gospels. <note>original: "En ConCorDIs EVangeLII DVX GVeLpherbItVs ConfCrIptIs LIbrIs nobILe fInIt opVs." This is a chronogram: the capitalized Latin letters (C, C, D, I, E, V, L, I, I, D, V, X, G, V, E, L, I, V, C, C, I, L, I, I, L, I, V) are Roman numerals that sum to the year 1646, the date of the work's publication.</note>

# APPLAUSE
## For the most August Library of Prince AUGUSTUS.

**A**t immense expense he founded this Library,
Collecting books with the highest diligence:
Here he also nourishes the learned, and the craftsmen alike,
A possessor of a far richer storehouse.
There is no need for any other here to bring books forth or put them back
Than he for whom the catalog of books was previously given, <note>Duke August was famously his own head librarian, creating a complex cataloging system—the "syllabus" mentioned here—that he managed personally.</note>
A moving and living library: The scribe of the books
And the very subject of the book adds the final flourish. <note>original: "Coronidem," the Greek term for a finishing stroke or the end of a scroll.</note>
Unless you are that man, Augustus, no one is;
Out of everyone, you alone are the pure Library of Libraries.
->Johann Valentin Andreae.<-

## Congratulation
### To Prince AUGUSTUS
#### On the restoration of WOLFENBÜTTEL.

**H**ow auspicious and happy, and how useful to your house,
Duke Augustus, and how good for your borders!
The Guelph citadel <note>original: "Arx Guelphica"—Wolfenbüttel, the ancestral seat of the Welf (Guelph) dynasty.</note> finally recognizes its genuine sun,
And that which was his before returns to its Lord,
After the Moon of the Castle <note>original: "Burgica Luna"—a poetic reference to the occupying forces (likely the Imperial/Catholic troops) who held Wolfenbüttel during the Thirty Years' War while the Duke was in exile.</note> had suffered its daily eclipse,
A total eclipse of its own,
For nearly three lustra <note>A lustrum is a five-year period; "nearly three" indicates almost 15 years.</note> and twice six months on every side,
While the sun often faltered through uncertain poles.
But finally it struggles out, and removes the shadows
By which it was obscured while the light remained silent.

O lofty Duke, for You; my poetic vein <note>original: "vena," a metaphor for natural poetic talent or inspiration.</note> now forbids me to say more
than what is already spoken; this is the prayer that the shores of Wolfenbüttel,
the Oker <note>original: "Ocra," the river flowing through Wolfenbüttel.</note> river, and your subjects everywhere confirm with bowed necks,
and what all good men pray for; finally, to these cheers, I add:
->Live, the glory of Dukes, for the benefit and<-
->glory of the fatherland!<-
->Live for the sake of piety! And as the second life of the good,<-
->live long: May the gods grant you the years of Nestor,<-
->and the days of Pylos! <note>Nestor was the legendary king of Pylos known for his extreme longevity and wisdom during the Trojan War.</note> May the martial ramparts of the Guelph<-
->be sustained forever by your Rule, and by the Rule of your<-
->grandsons!<-
->May wars flee your borders; and may every man be a friend!<-
->May the thrice-great GOD give weight to these prayers and<-
->Amen.<-
->*Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.*<-

# IN MEMORY
## OF THE GUELPH RESTORATION,
### On the anniversary of the Exaltation
### of the Cross, 1648. <note>The Exaltation of the Holy Cross is a feast day on September 14. In 1648, this date coincided with the final negotiations of the Peace of Westphalia, ending the Thirty Years' War.</note>

Wolfenbüttel, your peace was restored to you long ago,
*But for us, the times of a doubtful peace still pass,*
And at last, the clapper <note>original: "Pistillus," the internal striker of a bell.</note> has stayed within its bell,
*So that it might ring everywhere with a joyful sound.*
*But how long have we struck with a vain blow,*
Nor does anything yet crackle but the empty murmur of our prayers.
For you, Wolfenbüttel, the exalted cross <note>A play on words between the religious feast day and the "cross" of suffering borne during the war.</note> triumphs,
*Which still presses down upon our shoulders from every side.*
Applaud your "August" victor <note>A pun on the Duke’s name, August, and the title of the Roman Emperors, Augustus.</note>, O Guelph youth,
*For it is our lot to bear the cross, because the fates prepare it.*
And you, Prince August, live long among the God-fearing,
*So that you may be higher than any Cross.*

->Thus, applauding the Prince, he prayed.<-
->*Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.*<-

# On the 63rd Birthday of Prince AUGUSTUS.
## indeed, after the first Great Climacteric Year. <note>original: "Annum Magnum." In early modern medicine and astrology, the 63rd year (7 x 9) was known as the "Great Climacteric," a critical turning point in a person's life and health.</note>

O AUGUSTUS, Father of the fatherland: 
->Phoenix<-
of the Augustans, pillar of virtues, of noble lineage,
Whose celebrated fame in this wandering world has long
deserved eternal pride and the proclamations of praise,
I bring these words again, which, bearing them in your mind,
receive; with them I honor the Ducal Birthday,
For this is a day to be remembered, which brought You 
->into the ethereal<-
airs, SOUND IN HAPPY SOUL and BODY,
in which you have remarkably surpassed nine times seven years 
and twice six months: <note>The poet notes the completion of 63 years and 12 months, marking the transition into his 64th year.</note> this age is rare among men.
This is that day, formerly by the waves of the Jordan,
on which Joshua led the children of Israel through the 
foaming rivers; a Leader to be marked by us with a white pebble, <note>original: "niveo... lapillo." A Roman custom of marking lucky or auspicious days with a white stone.</note>
on which you likewise prepared to cross the waters of the Jordan
so that you might joyfully take entry into the Guelph 
->citadel,<- <note>Refers to the fortress and residence at Wolfenbüttel.</note>
which was closed to you, though to be entered freely, for so many years.
Thus Jehovah himself keeps watch for the righteous of the Lord,
nor does it help [others] to guard things acquired by the watches of strangers.
Therefore, this occasion offers happy triumphs to You,
and you are able to rejoice in YOUR OLD AGE, to rejoice:
May you therefore unlearn grief; the festive light of the day
demands the pleasant praises of lovely things.
Live long and happy, worthy of Augustan honor.

->Johann Valentin Andreae,<-
->Doctor of Theology.<-

# THE TEMPLE OF VIRTUE.

A great and August Temple, distinguished by a hundred
->columns,<-
When they wished for this to be made everywhere with pure hands,
Virtue herself, innocent of faults, built it for herself:
A temple fashioned from ivory, from Parian marble, <note>Marble from the Greek island of Paros, prized in antiquity for its whiteness and purity.</note>
Paneled with cedar and fragrant Cypress:
And beautifully, so that it might all shine, she decorated it with pure gold; <note>original: "obryzo." This refers to gold refined by fire to its highest purity.</note>
She completed this in every part, and for everyone equally.
The Goddess consecrated the work to be forever worshipped by mortals.
To all, the entrance is open here, nights and days,
Provided only that they glow with virtue: and within the inner shrines
No one is cast out: here there are no secrets to be feared.
Yet an altar was lacking in the Sanctuary, nor was it missed:
Because every mind is its own cultivator, not needing an external
libation, <note>original: "fusi." Referring to the pouring of liquids or offerings in ritual. The poet suggests that internal character is more important than outward ritual.</note> let it grow worthy honors for virtue.

As yet a Master of Mysteries <note>original: "Mystarcha." A high priest or leader of sacred rites.</note> was lacking for the place, who might rightly preside
over the sacred rites, and give a specimen of virtue in honor,
And an example of himself: nor was one more worthy found in the world,
Than he whom the Goddess herself fashioned with her own hands
And nourished with her own milk; no other was more worthy,
Who might better make an offering to the virtue of the goddess, his kinswoman.

Therefore she enters the Lunar Court <note>likely referring to the House of Lüneburg, the Duke's lineage.</note> and the Wolfenbüttel
->stronghold,<- <note>original: "Guelphbytica castra." Refers to the residence of the Guelph family at Wolfenbüttel.</note>
And calls upon Augustus: to whom by chance, as a Son entering into the breezes
of life, she had stood by and heard Clotho <note>One of the three Fates in Greek mythology, who spins the thread of life.</note> praying kind words;
Hence with fresh milk she, his nurse, mixed her own for him,
So that from this might arise a Hero of steadfast Virtue.
The great Pupil recognized the voice of his nurse,
The face and shoulders of the Goddess, and he goes to meet her as she comes.
Then by chance a Library Case was holding Augustus
As he weighed symbols with the learned ones of a noble leisure, <note>original: "ignobilis otî." A classical paradox; while "leisure" (otium) could mean idleness, for a scholar like Duke August, it referred to the productive, quiet time spent in study.</note>
From which he longs to place the final touch <note>original: "colophonem." A finishing stroke or crowning touch.</note> upon his Harmony: <note>Refers to the Duke's theological work, the *Harmonia Evangelica*.</note>
If the sixty-eighth year should bring this
To the dawning of his Birthday, by a favorable Divinity.
Illustrious, a work of piety, and a stupendous specimen,

<meta>This page continues the allegorical praise of Duke August the Younger. Having established the Temple of Virtue on the previous page, the narrative now describes the meeting between the Goddess Virtue and the Duke, followed by a description of his physical and intellectual traits, and finally introduces his wife, Sophie Elisabeth, and their daughters.</meta>

The noble hero and best Duke rose when he saw the Goddess. "Put everything aside," he said, "and cease your current labors." Then, with a bended knee and with learned grace, he greeted her. He then ordered the royal halls to be prepared for the guest, rejoicing to kindly offer his authority to his nurturing Teacher.

Meanwhile, the Goddess lingered, observing many things. She stood transfixed, and rejoicing in such a Prince, she could not satisfy her mind; she burned with pride as she watched him. She marveled that her own training <note>original: "palæstram." Traditionally a wrestling school or place of exercise, here it refers to the discipline of education and moral training the Goddess provided him.</note> could achieve so much. She surveyed everything, her eyes scanning over every detail: now admiring his pleasant face and serene brow, now his joyful eyes, adorned with majesty; now the gray hair of his flourishing and vigorous old age, now his well-composed steps in a tall body—yet tempered by his own gravity—and his strong arms. She noted his hands, agile in all things, and weighed every quality within herself.

But as for the gifts of his intellect, who would think to deceive the Goddess? Above all, she noted the riches which divine <term>Mathematics</term> <note>original: "Mathesis." In the 17th century, this term referred broadly to the "mathematical sciences," including astronomy, geometry, and music.</note> had bestowed upon the Augustus—wonderful to say! Indeed, through the more diverse <term>Mechanical</term> <note>original: "Mechanicas." This refers to engineering, the use of instruments, and practical craftsmanship, which Duke August famously mastered.</note> arts, he is able to be a guide and judge of craftsmen. Truly, it would be a shameful thing for the eyes of a learned man to be unpracticed. He stands out among others as much as he excels among the greatest.

From there, they visited the inner chambers of the women’s quarters. There stood the Princess, born of the Kings of Sweden <note>Sophia Elisabeth was the daughter of Johann Albrecht II of Mecklenburg and Margaret Elizabeth of Mecklenburg; the "Swedish" connection refers to her maternal lineage and the broader house of Mecklenburg's ties.</note>, the wife of Augustus: **SOPHIA ELIZABETH of Mecklenburg** <note>original: "Megapyrgis." A Greek-styled translation of "Mecklenburg" (Mega = Great, Pyrgos = Tower/Burg).</note>. She is a Juno in her command, a Venus in beauty, and a Pallas Athena in her character. Like a tenth sister to the nine Muses, she stands by them in learning and art. Three daughters stood in order by their mother's side: first, **SIBYLLA URSULA**, eldest in years and spirit; then **CLARA AUGUSTA**; and the distinguished **MARIA ELIZABETH**. They flourish amidst a rare growth of character and virtue, like the nymphs whom the ingenious ancients...

To him, the snowy Arion <note>Arion was a divine horse of Greek myth; here it represents the "Lower Saxon Steed" (the white horse) on the Guelph coat of arms.</note> of the Guelphs submits, to be restrained for the sake of Justice and True Worship with a jagged bit <note>original: "lupato."     Here, where Naples <note>original: "Parthenope." Nor would the boy wish for license to wander under such a governor. Just as wool holds fast the color of the dye it drinks in, so will he mold these minds toward whatever you lead them to. This is their nature.
    At last, Ferdinand Albrecht follows into the world, a bloom of untarnished flower and tender youth, the delight of his Father, the hope of his Mother, the glory of his brothers, the star of the nobles, the flower of the princes, the jewel of the fatherland. Now he is being taught his first letters under Master Crohne <note>Johann Crohne, another scholar serving as a tutor at the Wolfenbüttel court.</note>, who exercises these tender characters—born for all the greatest things—with frequent practice, lest they perhaps melt away through idleness and luxury and the perverse habit of vices; he is raised according to the example of his Father and the grown hope of his great Mother.

Human filth <note>original: "Colluvie humana." Referring to the moral corruption or "rabble" of the outside world.</note> which they thought had long since departed,

Happy to promise life to Augustus with his prayers,

With good right I would compare this to a cloister of ascetics,
Which lacks neither Religion nor a Rule of conduct.
I would rightly call this the sanctuary of highest Jove <note>original: "Iovæ." A Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, used here to mean the Christian God.</note>,

An Emporium of doctrine, a storehouse of art, and a vessel of charms.
Which no other Augustus should occupy unless he holds the Empire.
Why then should the care of my temple not be handed over to You?
You shall be my Prelate; hold the tiller of virtue."
Thus she speaks, and brings forth the tiller <note>A rudder or steering oar, symbolizing the guidance of the state or soul.</note> hidden beneath her garment;
Thus she departs, and having honored her Augustus with a greeting,
She left mortal eyes in the middle of her speech.

*I came into the acquaintance and service of such a great Prince.*

# DEVOTED VOWS,
# On the BIRTHDAY of Prince AUGUSTUS.

Hail to a good deed! The Birthday of **Augustus** has returned to the world—
*He who fosters the camps of the Moon and of Bruno;* <note>The "Moon" (Luna) refers to Lüneburg and "Bruno" to Brunswick (Braunschweig), the territories of the Duke.</note>
*By the omen of the Divine Power, the Birthday has returned to the world,*
*Which the renowned Hero enters as his sixty-ninth year.*
A Hero, *whom you might call entirely "Harmonic."*
*For here the Hero has bestowed a Harmonic work upon us,* <note>A reference to the "Harmony of the Four Evangelists," a massive theological project started by Chemnitz and completed by Lyser and Gerhard, which Duke Augustus helped patronize and promote.</note>
->Hero,<-
*Which even* Chemnitz, Lyser, *and* Gerhard <note>Three of the most influential Lutheran theologians of the era who worked on the Gospel Harmony.</note>
*Would approve, and to which the* Great Luther *himself would have applauded.*
*Indeed, he procures* Harmony *for the entire world,*
*In which he now labors to reconcile the Princes to peace:*
*And he will appease the* Imperial <note>original: "Cæſareum." Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> *Power with a new treaty.* <note>A likely reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War.</note>
*He has long prepared* Harmony *for the learned Muses,* <note>original: "Camœnis." The Muses of poetry and the arts.</note>
*To soften good character by setting aside fierceness,*
*Lest any confusion disturb the Letters and the Arts.*
*And he sanctions* Harmony *for his people with a faithful omen,*
*To obey his fatherly* commands *with just compliance:*
*He sent* Harmony *especially into the Family House,* <note>original: "Gentilem Ædem." Referring to the harmony within the ruling House of Welf.</note>
*Firm with the concordant bond of his three sons,*
*Which breathes with the friendly unison of his relatives:*
*And he offers that song in* Christian *harmonies,*
*Whereby the* Good *may accord with the* True, *and* Words *with* Deeds.
*Therefore, for him who resonates entirely with* Harmonic *ears,*
*Let the harmony of Heaven and Earth deservedly applaud.*

<meta>This page concludes a celebratory poem for Duke Augustus’s 70th birthday and begins a new tribute for his 71st birthday. Both poems were composed by Johann Valentin Andreae, a famous 17th-century theologian and scholar who shared a close intellectual bond with the Duke.</meta>

Indeed, may the Goddess of Harmony <note>original: *Harmoniae Diva*</note> always survive; let the entire choir of the learned sing along with her. To her, I—among the least of men—whisper from the very threshold: Long live he whose life is Harmonious! May he live through the ages! Until, following after and drawing closer to the radiant stars, he may increase the angelic concerts with his late years: where the spheres of heaven shall immediately respond in the harmonious melody <note>original: *melismate*</note> of perpetual Harmony.
->Johann Valentin Andreae,<-
->Doctor of Theology.<-

## Another APPLAUSE,
## For the Birthday of Prince AUGUSTUS.
### 71st [Year].

And so the seventieth harvest <note>Andreae uses "harvests" (*messis*) as a poetic metaphor for years lived.</note> has now passed for you, Prince dear to God, and for that reason, even dearer to me! As much as you surpass others in your distinguished deeds, by just as much do you outlast other leaders on this earth in lifespan. Among the common people, this happens to barely one in a thousand—much less to one who carries such a heavy burden of Rule <note>original: *Imperii*; the Duke was a sovereign ruler, and Andreae notes the physical and mental toll of leadership.</note>. Nor would this happen to anyone unless it were by the Supreme Power, who weighs out his own strength to each person. For it is by His goodness that we live for a long life, until sooner or later we are buried in the earth. He who clothes the temples of the head with feathers rivaling the swan <note>A poetic description of the white hair of old age.</note>,
<margin>*Proverbs 16:31 <note>This Bible verse reads: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness."</note></margin>
just as a golden crown * adorns the head of a King—which does not happen to just anyone by chance, nor is it beautiful unless it comes from piety. For this, Duke Augustus, I congratulate you with all my heart, and I pray for this distinction for you on your birthday. Thus, live long for yourself, you who are most worthy of a long life; and that you may be able to live long, fare well often.
->Joh. Val. Andreae, Doctor of Theology.<-

# THE ALTAR OF THE EXALTED CROSS,
<meta>catchword: Sta</meta>

->Erected as a crowning finale <note>original: *coronide*; literally a "curved line," a Greek-derived term for the flourish at the end of a book or the finishing touch of a building.</note> to the most exquisite work of GOSKY,<-
->September 17, 1650.<-

A vast, August Temple stands in the Hall at Wolfenbüttel <note>original: *Guelphbytî*; the seat of the Duke’s power and site of his famous library.</note>,
->Open to the public in the Court,<-
*So I saw recently while awake in the hours of a dreamless night,*
*A Hall open to the light, hallowed with solid piety,*
*Where marbles shine with painted veins:*
*But an octagonal altar is placed in the middle of the temple,*
*Displaying from above the sublime sign of our salvation,*
*On which the Ransomed One <note>original: *Lytrata*; a reference to Christ as the one who paid the ransom for humanity.</note> once hung in that deadly slaughter.*
*Eight Nymphs stand around it, girded in feminine robes,*
*With virginal faces and shining in their attire,*
*And each of them, with a long-extended and reverent covering,*
*Veils that venerable sign with laurel.*

*Here shines that piety which marks the honor of Religion*
*In the August Power <note>original: *Numine*; Andreae uses "Numen" (divine will/power) as a high-style poetic reference to the Duke himself.</note> of Lüneburg, just as much*
*As the Bibles testify, refined by the wise printing press,*
*Which he cherished as milk when a boy, and as life-fluid <term>chyle <note>chyle is the milky fluid of digested food; the poet suggests the Duke absorbed the Bible as fundamental nutrition throughout his life.</note></term> as an adult;*
*And also that harmonious sound, with which he sweetly expressed*
*The Gospels of the God-Man <term>Theandrus <note>from the Greek *theos* (God) and *aner* (man), referring to the dual nature of Christ.</note></term>.*
*His worship and the many structures of his sacred rites speak of*
*His knowledge and zeal for holy things,*
*And have long since earned for Augustus the perennial laurel.*
*Hence his vigilance stands for the flock of Christ,*
*Of which he acknowledges himself a sheep, not the shepherd—a noble member,*
*Not the head—nor does he seek to be a Bishop:*
*But a guardian, as one who has taken up not the shepherd's crook, but the sword,*
*The rods of office <note>original: *Fasces*; the Roman symbol of magistrate power.</note>, not the keys <note>The "power of the keys" refers to the spiritual authority of the clergy; the Duke explicitly denies having this, claiming only secular authority.</note>, so that with the sacred book of the law*
*He may bring truth to the empire and repel what is false,*
*Preserving the rights of the key-bearing ministers unimpaired.*

*The inventress of works <note>Refers to Pallas Athena/Wisdom, who was introduced on the previous page.</note>, she herself aided by a keen mind,*

*who drains the life-blood <note>original: *succum*; literally "juice" or "sap," implying the state's wealth.</note> of the fatherland into his wine-bowls.*

### An Augustan New Year's Gift
## TO THE AUGUST HOUSE of Brunswick
### & Lüneburg.
->In the Year 1648.<-

Let others worship the stars, or fear them, whether bright or
dark,
As if each man's fate flowed from the heavenly fields;
To me, there are five wandering stars <note>Likely referring to the five living children of Duke Augustus at this time, contrasting family "stars" with astrological ones.</note> that are never
an ill omen,
But are faithful, kind, and always rising with favorable motion.
You, O Thrice-Great Triune source of light,

<meta>This page continues the poetic "New Year's Gift" for 1648 by Johann Valentin Andreae. While the previous page introduced the five "wandering stars" (the Duke's children), this page elaborates on the celestial hierarchy of the House of Brunswick, moving from the Sun (Christ) to the Moon (Duke Augustus) and the three stars of Orion's belt (his three sons).</meta>

And the Sun of Justice, sent down from the high axis of heaven,
Dispelling the shadows of Erebus <note>The dark underworld of Greek mythology, representing spiritual darkness.</note>, illuminates the world:
Now even toward the inscrutable citadels above,
The seat of unapproachable light, the life-giving Divinity
Looking down upon the lands from above, and brightening our
Hearts as He is revealed in the Word, just as you allow the
Sun to go out in open light with no distinction, whose
Grace of justice outweighs the equal balance of the scale.
Another shines back at us from this one, O *August Moon* <note>original: *Selene*; a clever wordplay on the name "Augustus" and the Greek moon goddess Selene.</note>,
You are a bright light taking your light from the heavenly light,
And like the moon’s image on a Moon-stone <note>original: *Seleniten*; a mineral thought by ancients to wax and wane with the moon.</note>,
You reflect back upon me below with a gentle ray:
From which vigor, nourishment, sense, and movement within me
Tinge the breaths of my soul with a vital spark,
Always leaping from an inexhaustible fountain of favors.
Finally, the three-fold stars <note>Referring to the Duke’s three sons: Rudolph Augustus, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albert.</note> surpass in this world,
Which one might not vainly call the constellation of *Orion*,
Three rays of August light, an enclosed trio
Of brothers, upon whom all my future affairs, hopes, and
Strengths lean—a triple divinity in earthly power,
Oh, the prognosticators of great safety for the lands!
For where a star stands more rarely in the heavens,
Which nowhere harms the world, by this radiating star [the world]
        will stand firm,
And it will restore all the stars of the sky everywhere
        for the better:
It will shatter the bright sword of furious Hercules <note>Hercules often symbolized war or raw power; his "sword" represents the violence of the Thirty Years' War.</note>,
And a spring-like temperament will rule the whole world:
And such great Peace will arise for settled affairs, and
Janus <note>The Roman god of beginnings; his temple doors were closed only during times of absolute peace.</note> will thus close the gates of war with iron and tight joints,
So that there becomes one Harmony in all parts of the world.
Applaud, O people! And may I not prophesy with empty words;
Thus Apollo once sang to the boy at his cradle.
By these stars I shall stand (may Jesus grant it),
That star of Jacob <note>A reference to the biblical prophecy in Numbers 24:17, identifying the Duke’s line with divine favor.</note> never to set in the sky,
The Morning Star <note>original: *Phosphorus*</note> of eternal light, the one Torch of salvation,
The light of Justice for us, the Sun itself providing:

May the very Salvation of mankind <note>Refers to Christ, the *Salus Mundi*.</note> wish these guardians of my safety to remain safe, and grant me the prize <note>original: *brabejum*; a prize or reward, typically in a contest.</note> of every kind of prosperity from January to December <note>original: *à Iano ad Sylvestrum*; from the month of Janus to the feast of St. Silvester on December 31st.</note>. # OF GOSKY’S WORK
## Elaboration,

->*Sent in place of a New Year’s Gift for the year 1650.*<-

### I. The Indian Fig.
Just as the Indian fig <note>The Banyan tree (*Ficus benghalensis*), famous for its aerial roots that grow into new trunks.</note> spreads itself with broad shoots, its branches curving toward the earth, sinking under their own weight. And as a new generation rises up into the air above, a single tree creates a shady grove all around. Thus the first cradles of life mark us; what might the native *Soil* <note>original: *Humus*; a likely pun on the Duke's humble piety or the earthly realm.</note> hope for from Augustus?

### II. The Juniper.
The power of the *Juniper* is believed to heal poison, so that every viperous tribe flees its shadow. Thus *Baptism* puts to flight the lethal poison of Satan, and calls upon AUGUSTUS, and makes him a FOLLOWER OF CHRIST <note>original: *CHRISTIADEN*; a reference to the "Societas Christiana," a Christian union Andreae promoted.</note>. Thus let him boast that he was born a man alongside ALPHONSO <note>Refers to King Alfonso V of Aragon, a Renaissance model of the "Scholar-King" whom Duke Augustus admired.</note>, in a rank between Augustus and the followers of Christ.

### III. The Oak.
Once sacred to *Jove* <note>The Roman god Jupiter.</note>, and likewise the ancient *Oak*, such as they say existed in the valley of *Mamre* <note>The biblical site where Abraham pitched his tent and was visited by God (Genesis 18:1).</note>. Beneath this, the Lions of BRUNSWICK place their banners—trophies won by the hand of the *Guelphs* <note>The Welf dynasty, the noble house to which the Dukes of Brunswick belonged.</note>. May the *Divine Power* protect these, lest any anger of *Jove* threaten them; rather, while the ancient *Oak* stands, may they remain equally renowned.

<meta>This page continues the series of plant-based emblems dedicated to Duke Augustus of Braunschweig-Lüneburg by Johann Valentin Andreae. The previous page introduced the Indian Fig and the Juniper as symbols of the Duke's lineage and faith. ### IV. The Sycamore.

He heals the wild fig who pierces it with a spear: <note>A reference to the ancient practice of "scarifying" sycamore figs to make them ripen, a metaphor for how the "sting" of education refines the soul.</note>
In this way, all study of a matter supplies what is lacking.
The honor of art, the nurse of a noble life from tender years,
Does this, and does not allow manners to remain wild.
While you, AUGUSTUS, crown your line with this nobility,
The Academies <note>original: *Lycéa*; referring to schools or places of higher learning.</note> everywhere rightly approve this in You.

### V. The Fir Tree.

The Fir tree goes farther than others, reaching for the heights,
And undergoes the dangers of the sea once made into a ship.
This symbol advises one to visit foreign skies,
So that you may know the languages, customs, and many peoples.
It is the mark of a small mind to remain at home: thus Travel
Lifts you from the ground and blesses you with varied knowledge.

### VI. The Mulberry.

The Mulberry receives praise, lest folly should commit any fault;
It commands all things to be weighed in an Augustan balance. <note>The mulberry was known as the "wisest of trees" because it waits for the frost to pass before budding. The "Augustan balance" refers both to the Duke's name and the Roman ideal of careful judgment.</note>

### VII. The Palm.

The pairing of the two sexes of Palms is a sweet union,
Nor does the female bear fruit unless joined to the Male.
From this, they weave mutual treaties with entwined branches,
And the female becomes as if pregnant by her union with the Male.
Thus the Lion of Brunswick <note>Duke Augustus.</note>, overcome by social love,
Brought forth many pledges of his joyful treaties. <note>A poetic reference to the Duke’s many children and his diplomatic successes.</note>

### VIII. The Almond.

From here, like the many-flowered nut-tree, it clothes itself 
In the woods and calls the others to its fruits:
Now, in a beautiful succession, imitating festive births,
It brings forth a lineage and a triple marriage. <note>A reference to the Duke’s three successive marriages which secured his dynasty.</note>

### IX. The Cedar and the Passionflower. <note>The *Granadilla* or Passionflower was a popular 17th-century symbol for the suffering of Christ.</note>

And now he even writes things most worthy of the Cedar and of Apollo, <note>original: *Phœbo*. Cedar oil was used to preserve precious manuscripts; Apollo is the god of poetry and learning.</note>
And gives forth published monuments in eternal type.
From these, even Momus <note>The god of mockery and criticism; if even Momus approves, the work is considered perfect.</note> himself approves
The games of Chess, <note>Referring to the Duke’s book *Das Schach- oder Königs-Spiel* (1616).</note> and the Secret Writing, <note>original: *Cryptomachiam*; referring to the Duke’s massive 1624 work on cryptography, *Cryptomenytices et Cryptographiae*.</note>
And the Sacred Harmony.

### X. The Vine.

> *Just as a fertile vine-shoot spreads itself around*
> *The garden trellis, and thickens everywhere with grape-bearing foliage:*
> *So, August Duke, does your Royal Library bless you*
> *With an abundant harvest of books.* <note>Duke Augustus was the founder of the Herzog August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel, one of the most significant libraries of the 17th century. The "harvest" refers to his massive collection of over 130,000 items.</note>

### XI. The Pomegranate.

> *Pomegranates are known to give off pleasant scents;*
> *Augustus <note>The Latin text plays on the Duke's name *Augustus* and the adjective for "majestic" or "venerable."</note> commands, and a pleasant fragrance reaches his people.*
> *He is skilled at sparing the submissive and punishing the proud,* <note>original: *Parcere subjectis... punire superbos*; a direct reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*, defining the Roman ideal of just governance.</note>
> *Just as the Lion, the King and head of the four-footed beasts, does.*

### XII. The Olive & The Myrtle.

> *The Olive is sacred to Pallas, <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> while the Myrtle is most dear to Venus;*
> *Both are graceful signs of a Good Peace.*
> *These suit Augustus, who conquers without slaughter or blood,*
> *Indeed, by yielding, he establishes public trophies.* <note>This praises the Duke's diplomacy and preference for intellectual or peaceful victories over military ones.</note>

### XIII. The Cypress.

> *But yet, as sad things are always mixed with the joyful,*
> *The Cypress also has its place among the fruit trees:*
> *He undergoes many sorrows, and the fatal deaths of his kin,*
> *All of which, however, he has borne with a brave heart.* <note>The cypress was a traditional symbol of mourning and the underworld. This likely refers to the Duke's personal losses, including the deaths of his wives or children.</note>

### XIV. The White Poplar.

> *The white poplar signifies the Duke’s gifts and the prayers of the pious:*
> *From this Titus, <note>Emperor Titus was famously called "the delight of the human race" because of his generosity. To Andreae, Duke Augustus is a modern Titus.</note> no one departs empty-handed.*
> *Hence, as his generous hand is always open to the worthy,*
> *So the altar of vows for the Duke is always warm.*

### XV. The Plane Tree.

> *And now under the Plane Tree he celebrates birthday feasts,*
> *This tree holds this honor with royal luxury.*
> *Extending its branches with a happy lineage,*
> *It triumphantly crowns the table with pleasant flowers.* <note>The Plane tree was associated in antiquity with luxury and leisurely scholarly discussion. Here, it represents family celebrations and the growth of the Duke’s dynasty.</note>

### XVI. The Withered Apple Tree.

> *The withered Apple Tree finally provides a figure to whom you might say,*
> *“It is not pleasing,” as every evil flows together in old age.*
> *The fallen leaves drop, the branches finally dry up,*
> *And the path remains to be plowed toward the funereal Sea:* <note>The "funereal Sea" is a metaphor for death and the vast unknown that follows life's "harvest."</note>

<meta>This page continues the poetic and symbolic tributes to Duke Augustus of Brunswick-Lüneburg. While the previous page focused on botanical emblems (the Vine, Pomegranate, Olive, and Cypress), this page transitions into a direct birthday panegyric written by the prominent theologian Johann Valentin Andreae. The imagery shifts from general emblems to the specific liturgical timing of the Duke's birthday near Palm Sunday, blending the "Palm" of victory with the "Palm" of Christ’s passion.</meta>

May it be well! But may [death] yield to you only late, O Greatest of rulers, 
Duke of Dukes. Receive these prayers of my heart!

->**Johann Valentin Andreae,**<-
->**Doctor of Theology.**<-

The annual birthday of **AUGUSTUS** flows back into the 
world, 
Which now begins for him his seventy-second year, <note>original: *novies illi octonum* (nine times eight). Duke Augustus was born in 1579; this poem likely dates to 1651.</note>
At the time when it is customary to meditate upon the *Passion of Christ*, 
A Passion, bitter indeed, but than which nothing is sweeter to the world, 
Nor has anything more useful come to weary mortals: 
He who, dying for us—unworthy of Heaven and lacking in piety—
Saved us for the highest Olympus. <note>The author uses "Olympus" as a classical metonym for the Christian Heaven, a common practice in Renaissance Latin poetry.</note>
All our vigor is from **HIM**, as is the Palm of Salvation, 
Without whom we would have withered through eternal ages. 
The present noble feast of Palms reminds us of this, 
And the Day of Branches, <note>Palm Sunday.</note> hallowed by the light of spring. 
Indeed, in Christ—without whom we are but dry wood—
We know that all things, bedewed by His blood-like nectar, 
Shall grow green, just like a flowering Palm tree. 
So now, **Augustus**, when we see your birthday 
Growing green among the Palms and the verdant branches, 
We take an omen from the example: that all things, 
Under Christ’s protection, shall flourish for you; and we rejoice in such an omen. 
We offer good words today: may the Year flourish for you, 
A Year that has become a Jubilee for us now that peace is restored. <note>A reference to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the devastating Thirty Years' War in Germany.</note>
May the nourishing crop flourish, and the vintage be happy with clusters. 
May the nourishing <term>Themis</term> <note>The Greek goddess of divine law and order; here representing the justice of the state.</note> of the fatherland flourish while the people prosper; 
May Religion, the glory and protection of the fatherland, grow green. 
May the nourishing Trio of Sons and the Trio of Sisters flourish, <note>The Duke had three sons (Rudolf August, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albrecht) and three surviving daughters (Sibylla Ursula, Clara Augusta, and Maria Elisabeth).</note>
With <term>Sophia</term> <note>Greek for "Wisdom."</note> blooming for you! May life-giving vigor 
Flourish in your limbs, and in the joyful honor of your brow!

<summary>A celebratory poem by Johann Valentin Andreae marking Duke Augustus's 72nd birthday, which coincided with the season of Palm Sunday and the restoration of peace in Germany.</summary>

## TO THE COURT
# Of Prince AUGUSTUS, Duke
### of Brunswick & Lüneburg,

*See how brightly the Royal Palace of the Moon <note>original: *Regia Lunae*. A poetic play on the name Lüneburg, which was historically associated with the Moon (Luna).</note> shines with its own stars:*
*What wonder is it, then, that the heavens stand still while the earth moves?*
*All things now run in a reversed order of Fate,*
*And the sky, the Moon, and the Sun suffer changes;*
*Yet the Court of the Moon shall stand, with Christ as leader and protector,*
*Along with the Sun, the Moon, and its own stars.*
*It is a wonder that the Gods should change their palaces in heaven,*
*When they see stars more spendid here on the ground.*

### To the same Prince.
*The Moon on earth, and the Sun shining in the high heavens,*
*Is enough for me: by these two, I am carried safely through the world.*

### On the motto of SIBYLLA URSULA <note>Sibylla Ursula (1629–1671) was the daughter of Duke Augustus. She was highly educated and a writer herself.</note>,
->Strive.<-

*They equal the Hebrew mothers and the Greek Heroines,*
*It is a marvel to see the Italian shields and those of the Thracian Amazons,*
*But one Leader of the Sibyls from the Weser <note>original: *Tulisurgis*. The Latin name for the region around the Weser river, where the Duke's territories were located.</note> loves*
*To contend for the prize with men in every kind of talent.*

### On the Prince’s motto: The die is cast <note>original: *Jacta est alea*. This famous phrase, attributed to Julius Caesar, was used by Duke Augustus as a personal motto, signifying a point of no return in a grand undertaking.</note>.

*One must explore the art of navigation from the land,*
*If one is able and has the diligence;*
*But once one has reached the deep sea,*
*It is necessary to run with whatever wind is present.*

Whoever has entered this Selenian <note>The term "Selenian" refers to "Selenus," the scholarly pseudonym used by Duke Augustus. It is derived from the Greek *Selene* (Moon), a play on the name of his city, Lüneburg.</note> place,

As I receive this, O snowy-white right hand! Deservedly, the more learned world
*Offers kisses in devoted service.*
Why, O Prince, did you smile upon a little man <note>original: *homullo*. A diminutive of "man," used here by Andreae as a gesture of humility before the Duke.</note> in obscurity?

*That you consider a virtue what the common crowd considers a fault.*

I myself shall recall your gifts with an unforgetting mind,

**Renowned and noble lineage of the House of Guelph** <note>The House of Guelph (Welf) is the ancient European dynasty to which the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg belonged.</note> **endure in praise.**

    When you recall the sweet Fates of your first marriage bed.

    When your love was half-buried in the earth.

    Whence the womb burst and gave you the day.
    <gloss>[*Augustus, born April 10, in the year 1579.*]</gloss>
    <gloss>[*Rudolph-August, born April 10, 1627.*]</gloss>

### BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

*Whether the name **AUGUSTUS** was born for you from "increase,"* <note>original: *augmine*. A play on the Latin word *augere* (to increase), from which the name Augustus is traditionally derived.</note>
*Or whether it was given to you by chance from "Augury,"*
*The omen is good on both counts: for just as the head of the world was in the City,*
*So your Rome was founded with an August Augury,* <note>original: *Augusto Augurio... Roma Tua*. A reference to the legend of Romulus founding Rome after seeing a favorable augury of birds; here, the poet compares the Duke's territories to a new Rome.</note>
*Wherefore your people deservedly venerate you, a Living Man, with honor,*
*And cherish you with a certain silent reverence.*
*Whence everyone now wishes for you a lively old age and vigorous spirit* <note>original: *vegetabilis Humor*. Literally "animating moisture," a concept in early modern medicine referring to the vital fluids that keep a person healthy in old age.</note>
*From each of their own days,*
*Since now even your seventy-third year*
*Shines upon your birthday, Great **SELENUS**!* <note>original: **SELENE**. A play on the Greek goddess of the moon, Selene. Duke Augustus used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus" for his famous works on chess and cryptography; "Selenus" refers to Lüneburg (*Luna* = moon).</note>
*Now the whole land of Wolfenbüttel prepares festivals for you,*
*The poets acclaim you and prepare their hands.*
*You who are the public concern of the Fatherland and its supreme salvation,*
*So that everyone desires to speak of you.*
*Thus age carries you nearly to the old age of the original Augustus,*
*From which barely a short three-year period is missing.* <note>The Roman Emperor Augustus died at age 76. As the Duke is 73, he is three years away from matching the Emperor's lifespan.</note>
*This is rare among the common people, and even rarer in a Prince;*
*There will scarcely be one or two like Evander here.* <note>Evander was a legendary king of Roman mythology known for his great wisdom and extreme longevity.</note>
*Whether it is because the weight of Empire does not allow them to live long,*
*Or luxury and softness forbid it.*
*But we have not truly extended the old age of Augustus to that point*
*As if it were to be the final goal of your life.*
*"Let him be a God, so long as he is not living"—this is the well-known voice of a Tyrant;* <note>original: *Sit Divus, modo non vivus*. A quote attributed to Emperor Caracalla regarding his murdered brother Geta. The poet rejects this, wishing the Duke to remain alive rather than just a "divine" memory.</note>
*Let this be far away! May the omen be absent from your white hairs!*

Indeed today the Calendars <note>original: *Fasti*. A reference to the Roman ritual calendar, famously chronicled in poetry by Ovid.</note> offer us better things,
*So that you may be spoken of by us as Divine and Living forever.* <note>original: *Ut Divus nobis, Vivus & usque cluas*. The poet plays on the Roman tradition of deifying emperors (*Divus*) after death, wishing instead that the Duke be honored as "divine" while still "living."</note>
Augustus and Methuselah <note>A biblical patriarch said to have lived 969 years; a common symbol for extreme longevity.</note> are noted here in these titles,

I prophesy, O Citizens! **AUGUSTUS** will touch the centuries,
And among the *August ones, he will be a Methuselah.*
*The land of Brunswick will find an Augustus as its Lord,* <note>original: *Brunsuigides oræ*. Referring to the territories of the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note>
*Both the Great-great-grandson, and the Grandson born from him.*
*Nor is there fear that the Son might inquire into his father’s years,* <note>original: *patrios inquirat in annos*. A classical literary trope (found in Ovid) describing an impatient heir who calculates how much longer his father might live.</note>
*To grasp for the coveted symbols of power before his day.* <note>original: *fasces*. The Roman bundle of rods signifying judicial and executive authority.</note>

*Content with his portion of the Realm, he will live as his* **FATHER** *did before.*
*And by the same augury, he will also guide his Father's world,*
*And he will direct the public gifts of the Realm abroad.*
*For whom we pray for the years of his Father, and the spirit from his Father,*
*So that no part of his prayers may fail.*
Thus with Father and Grandfather, he celebrated the Feast for the year,
->into the year<-
*Alternately from the knees of Grandmother and Mother,*
*Little Augustus; so many times and again and again,*
*Until the Great-grandson smiles upon the Father, and a Grandson upon him.*

# SACRED MOTTOS,
## ON THE ROYAL GENEALOGY 
## OF THE SAVIOR,
### Translated and condensed from the *Illustrious Savoyard Garden* 
### of EMANUELE TESAURO.
<note>Emanuele Tesauro (1592–1675) was a famous Italian rhetorician and poet. The author of this text has adapted and shortened Tesauro's "Sacred Mottos" which trace the lineage of Jesus.</note>

### 1.
### The World’s Infancy. THE SHEPHERDS.

### 1. Adam.

Adam, the first Man, created without human seed,
Cast both himself and his descendants into eternal death.
He had made all people damned before they were even born:
In whose loins we committed every evil. <note>A reference to the doctrine of Original Sin, suggesting all humanity was "present" in Adam when he fell.</note>
But this would have been a lesser thing, had he not sinned in such a way that,
By the wood through which he perished, Salvation stands restored. <note>original: *Ligno, quo periit, stat reparata Salus*. A classic theological parallel (typology) comparing the wood of the Tree of Knowledge in Eden to the wood of the Cross.</note>

### Cain.

To him, the forest is the Forum, to which a guilty mind
Brings its sin; even a shadow presents the defendant for judgment.
The blood of the slain man himself testifies to the crime; by the judgment 
Of the Thunderer, <note>original: *Tonantis*. A classical epithet for Jupiter, here applied to the Christian God as the judge of the world.</note> he is thereafter punished for his own fault.

### Abel.

A king here among the sheep, and famed among kings 
For his sheep-like simplicity, he perishes through his own trustfulness. 
From this, he endured a death to be wept over bitterly by all— 
But not a life; for his life was surely shameful to no one.

<summary>This page introduces a series of poetic reflections on the biblical genealogy of Christ, beginning with the "infancy of the world" through the figures of Adam, Cain, and Abel. It uses classical and theological imagery to contrast the Fall of Adam with the redemption of the Cross, and the guilt of Cain with the innocence of Abel.</summary>
<keywords>Adam, Cain, Abel, Emanuele Tesauro, Original Sin, Typography, Redemption, Biblical Genealogy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Mottos" on the genealogy of the Savior, transitioning from the cursed line of Cain to the righteous line of Seth. The previous page ended with the description of Cain as a fugitive.</meta>

<page-num>337</page-num>

### *Cain's Offspring.*
<note>original: "Caini proles"</note>

For their deeds, they deserved the silence of a hiding place and a tomb,
For what they did lies buried, hidden in the night.

### *Lamech the Bigamist.*
<note>Lamech was the first man in the Bible to take two wives (Adah and Zillah), marking a departure from the monogamy of Eden.</note>

<margin>V</margin>
Twice mad, twice a lover; he is the first to make his loves public:
Scorched by the flame of passion, he perishes amidst the waters. <note>original: "Flaminis ambustus." Likely a reference to the Great Flood which eventually wiped out Cain's line.</note>

### *Jabal and Jubal.*
<note>In Genesis, Jabal is the father of those who live in tents/herd livestock; Jubal is the father of those who play the harp and flute.</note>

Should he who refuses to look at Heaven be watched by it?
I would think that he who laughed when he should have wept has perished.

### *Tubal.*
<note>Tubal-cain, the first blacksmith and forger of bronze and iron tools.</note>

Guilt gave a shorter life, the art of the forge none at all;
He who discovered iron was himself a man of iron. <note>original: "Ferreus ille fuit." A play on words suggesting Tubal was as hard-hearted or "steely" as the metal he discovered, which brought weapons and war into the world.</note>

### 2. *Seth.*
<note>The third son of Adam, whose line replaces the murdered Abel's.</note>

Seth’s posterity remained interrupted for a long time,
And after this, one line alone swims forth from the submerged ground. <note>A reference to Noah—Seth's descendant—surviving the Flood when the rest of the earth was "submerged."</note>

### 3. *Enos.*

When God ceased to speak to mortals long ago,
This man taught men to speak with the Ruler of the Stars. <note>original: "Astripotente." This refers to Genesis 4:26: "At that time people began to call on the name of the Lord."</note>

### 4. 5. *Cainan and Mahalaleel.*

These twin initiates made sacrifice with mourning and song:
Truly, the tear was the mother of pleasure.

### 6. *Jared.*

No one ever fathered offspring for himself later than he, <note>Jared was 162 years old when his son Enoch was born.</note>
Nor did anyone endure this life later after him.
No one was to have offspring for a longer duration than he;
Hence the son survived the father, and the father survived his own offspring.

### 7. *Enoch.*

Having departed while still alive, he survived the dead,
While like a Phoenix he carries a youthful old age for himself. <note>Enoch "walked with God; then he was no more, because God took him" (Genesis 5:24). The Phoenix is a traditional symbol of resurrection and renewal.</note>

### 8. 9. *Methuselah and Lamech.*
<note>Lamech here is the son of Methuselah, distinct from the bigamist Lamech of Cain's line mentioned above.</note>

These men, born for Heaven, show the stars to mortals;
Let them be raised to Heaven, which they taught to their own.

<summary>This page presents poetic epigrams (mottos) on the biblical patriarchs, contrasting the "iron-hearted" and doomed descendants of Cain with the righteous line of Seth, who taught humanity to pray and "walk with God."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the chronological overview of biblical figures following the line of Seth. While the previous page discussed the earliest patriarchs like Enos, this page moves toward the Great Flood and the new beginning of humanity through Noah and his descendants.</meta>

# The Adolescence of the World. SOLDIERS.
<note>original: "Mundi Adolescentia. MILITES." In this context, "Soldiers" likely refers to the "Soldiers of God" or the prominent figures who fought the spiritual battles of their eras.</note>

## 10. Noah.
<note>original: "Noës"</note>

Truly he is a Janus; he saw the world behind him and before him:
<note>Janus was the Roman god of transitions, usually depicted with two faces—one looking toward the past and one toward the future. Noah is compared to him because he lived through both the world before the Flood and the world after.</note>
For he was indeed the doorkeeper in the middle of both.
A new sailor built a ship—or rather an ark—as a fortress;
With this timber, he sustained the riches of the whole world.

->Ham.<-
<note>original: "Cham"</note>

He brought a new stain to the purged world;
And upon the sea, the father’s single lapse becomes his own lustful ruin.
<note>Reference to the biblical story where Ham uncovers and mocks his father Noah’s nakedness while Noah was drunk, leading to a curse upon Ham's lineage.</note>

->Nimrod.<-

By his strength, this man planned a Giant-like Tower,
A work that was not a solid achievement for the weak, but a foolish one.
<note>original: "Non solidum... quod stolidum." A play on words between "solidum" (solid/lasting) and "stolidum" (stupid/senseless). Nimrod is traditionally credited with the construction of the Tower of Babel.</note>

## 11. Shem and Japheth.
<note>original: "Sem & Iaphet"</note>

This noble pair of brothers rejoices in equal piety,
And as many sons as he bore, so many kingdoms he also produced.
One is the father of the Roman race, the other of the Hebrew;
The one whom Christ honored here, the other brought forth for himself.
<note>In early modern interpretations of the Bible, Japheth was often seen as the ancestor of Europeans (Romans), while Shem was the ancestor of the Semitic peoples (Hebrews).</note>

## 12. The Progeny of Shem.
<note>original: "Semi Progenies"</note>

With their exiles divided by Heaven so that he might animate the world,
That line had to be preserved for the new world.
So that it might bring forth the Savior of the entire world,
This new seed had to be preserved.

## 20. Abraham.
<note>original: "Abrahamus"</note>

How great he was, measure by your own bosom:
For indeed, he receives all the righteous into his fold.
<note>Reference to the "Bosom of Abraham," a place of comfort in the afterlife for the righteous (Luke 16:22).</note>

->Lot.<-
<note>original: "Loth"</note>

Unhappy father, for what fire will you be saved?
In a jar he carried with him the very thing he fled.
<note>A reference to Lot's escape from the fire of Sodom, only to fall into the "fire" of sin (drunkenness and incest) involving wine jars in a cave.</note>

->Lot’s Wife.<-
<note>original: "Lothi Vxor"</note>

While she looked back at her homeland, she lost herself,
And she stands entombed as a tasteless statue of salt.
<note>original: "insulsa... salis." A Latin pun: "insulsa" means both "unsalted" and "foolish/absurd." Because she lacked the "salt" of wisdom and looked back at Sodom, she was turned into a pillar of salt.</note>

<summary>This page uses brief Latin verses to profile key figures from the post-Flood world, including Noah as a transitional "Janus" figure, the building of the Tower of Babel, and the establishment of the lineages of Shem, Japheth, and Abraham.</summary>

<keywords>Noah, Ham, Nimrod, Shem, Japheth, Abraham, Lot, Tower of Babel, Ark, Pillar of Salt, Biblical Genealogy</keywords>

->21. *Isaac.*<-

Is he a more mournful priest, or a victim? He had drawn the sword
Against the throat of his son, and suddenly he becomes a father <note>original: "sit subitoq; pater." This refers to the Binding of Isaac, where Abraham is stopped from sacrificing his son; Isaac is "reborn" to him through God's mercy.</note>.

->22. *Jacob.*<-
<note>original: "Iacob"</note>

Emerging by deceits from a blind father, and by his mother's sharp wit through gifts,
He mourned long joys for a long time. <note>Refers to Jacob tricking his blind father Isaac to receive the blessing intended for Esau, guided by his mother Rebekah. His "long mourning" refers to the many trials of his life, including the loss of his son Joseph.</note>

->*The Twelve Tribunes.*<-
<note>original: "Tribuni XII." These are the twelve sons of Jacob who founded the Tribes of Israel.</note>

You see as many stars of Heaven changing their shape;
For him, as many beautiful signs of the earth shine forth. <note>The author draws a parallel between the twelve signs of the zodiac and the twelve tribes of Israel.</note>

### I I I.

# *The Youth of the World.* LEADERS.
<note>original: "Mundi Iuventus. DUCES." This marks a new chronological age in the author's scheme, moving from "Adolescence" to "Youth."</note>

->23. *Judah.*<-
<note>original: "Iudas"</note>

For him, a long and perpetual line of Kings running down,
Bore a throne higher than the sun thereafter.
And you could call him a new Atlas of the world,
Upon whose shoulders God himself had sat. <note>Judah is compared to Atlas (who held up the heavens) because the lineage of King David and eventually Jesus ("God himself") descends from his "shoulders."</note>

->*Joseph.*<-
<note>original: "Ioseph"</note>

Thrice wretched, he received back all his things besides his homeland <insert>(received;</insert>;
By the oracle of his homeland, he had gathered his own bones.
He underwent fate once, was mourned three times, buried twice,
Thereafter four times, by the law of fate, he was Blessed. <note>Joseph was "buried twice" because he died in Egypt but his bones were later moved to the Promised Land. The "thrice mourned" likely refers to the different times his father or brothers believed him lost or dead.</note>

->24. *Perez.*<-
<note>original: "Phares"</note>

The royal posterity of Christ is proud of that stain,
And the Virgin boasts of ancestors born of an illicit union. <note>original: "Incestosque fatus." Perez was the son of Judah and his daughter-in-law Tamar. The author notes the humility of Christ's lineage including such "stains."</note>

->*Job.*<-
<note>original: "Iob"</note>

Increased twofold in power, children, and wealth than he had been
Before, he himself sings of his own sorrows.

->25. 26. 27. *Hezron, Ram, Amminadab*<-
<note>original: "Erom, Ram, Aminadab"</note>

Fortune first applauds deceitfully, then stamps its feet in disapproval,
And finally drives them off; from this, you understand the fates of the Court. <note>A theatrical metaphor. The author suggests these minor figures in the genealogy represent the fickle nature of political or courtly life—rising and falling quickly.</note>

->*Moses.*<-

No one saw him dying, no one found him
Buried, and no one gave him a tomb accordingly. <note>According to Deuteronomy, God buried Moses in a secret location that remains unknown.</note>

<note>original: "Salma." Salmon was the son of Nahshon and a key figure in the genealogy of David.</note>

**This man bore his fatherland in exile, and exile in his father’s seat;**
**And this merit he received from a harlot.** <note>original: "meretrice." This refers to Rahab, the woman of Jericho who assisted the Israelite spies; she is identified in the New Testament as the wife of Salmon and an ancestor of Jesus.</note>

->*Joshua.*<-
<note>original: "Iofue"</note>

**Joshua kept the laws which Moses had given:**
**And God Himself obeyed his prayers.** <note>Refers to the miracle at Gibeon where Joshua prayed for the sun and moon to stand still so the Israelites could finish their battle (Joshua 10:12-14).</note>

->*Samson.*<-
<note>original: "Samfon"</note>

**He was stronger than Hercules here, as often as he conquered; but in love**
**He was softer, acting as a servant: let him bear arms more safely.** <note>original: "Alcide." Alcides is a common classical epithet for Hercules. The poet contrasts Samson's physical strength with his weakness for Delilah.</note>

->30. 31. *Boaz. Obed.*<-
<note>original: "Booz. Obed."</note>

**Born chaste from a harlot; a poor woman marries a rich man:**
**And to him come the nations, whom the Synagogue bore.** <note>This refers to the story of Ruth (the "poor woman"), a Moabitess who married the wealthy Boaz. Their son was Obed. The "harlot" reference again points back to Rahab, Boaz's mother in this genealogical tradition.</note>

->*Gideon*<-
<note>original: "Gedeon"</note>

**Happy, if he had been less fruitful by just one son,**
**He could have been more joyful in his own fate.** <note>Gideon had seventy sons. After his death, his son Abimelech murdered sixty-nine of his brothers to seize power, a tragedy the poet suggests Gideon was spared from seeing only by death.</note>

->*Jephthah.*<-
<note>original: "Iephtes"</note>

**He was more skilled at fighting than at weighing his vows:**
**For the sake of victory, he sold his own daughter.** <note>Jephthah made a rash vow to sacrifice the first thing that came out of his house if he won the battle; it was his daughter. The poet criticizes his lack of judgment despite his military skill.</note>

->32. *Jesse.*<-
<note>original: "Iefse"</note>

**The palm of Leaders, the root of Kings, the Bethlehemite**
->**Hero,**<-
**His native countryside provided a seat worthy of God.** <note>Jesse was the father of King David; his "root" refers to the "Root of Jesse" prophecy in Isaiah 11:1.</note>

### IV.

## *The Manhood of the World.* KINGS.
<note>original: "Mundi Virilitas. REGES." This marks the fourth stage of the author's historical scheme, moving from the "Youth" of the Judges to the "Manhood" of the Monarchy.</note>

->33. *David.*<-

**Free** from foreign foes, but subject to his own fatherland’s rages;
He made others happy, he who was the most wretched of all. <note>Likely referring to David's many trials, including being hunted by King Saul and the rebellion of his son Absalom, despite his successes as a king.</note>

### 33. Samuel.

Priest of the Most High GOD, the one most just Judge;
Drenched in zeal and tears, the very pinnacle of honor. <note>Samuel was the last of the biblical Judges and the first of the major prophets who anointed the first kings of Israel.</note>

### 34. Solomon.

The insane Wise Man, a Hero with a woman’s heart;
He was both the shame and the glory of the Hebrews. <note>original: "Insanus Sapiens." This refers to Solomon's legendary wisdom contrasted with his later life, when his many foreign wives led him into idolatry.</note>

### 35. Rehoboam.

He who was wise but once, or perhaps never—is he not the more insane?
Kingdoms grow old and frail when young men comprise the Senate. <note>Rehoboam, Solomon's son, caused the rebellion of the ten northern tribes by rejecting the advice of elder statesmen in favor of his young, arrogant peers (1 Kings 12).</note>

### 36. Abijah.

An "all-man" married an "all-woman," and through his father’s vices
He loses both his life and his crown, lacking all honor. <note>original: "Abias." The Latin uses "Omnivir" and "omnivirae," likely a poetic play on his reputation or the scale of his household.</note>

### 37. Asa.

He brings back the rewards of virtue—the palm of victory and peace;
Yet he nourishes a noble poison as punishment for sin:
The knotted Gout. Yet virtue is fragrant everywhere;
Even when it burns, it alone escapes the well-known funeral pyre. <note>original: "Podagram." Asa was a reformer king, but the Bible records that in his old age he was "diseased in his feet" and sought help from physicians rather than God (2 Chronicles 16).</note>

### 38. Jehoshaphat.

Truly he was ignorant of nothing, nor did he ever pardon anything too harshly,
Such was his great vigor.
He committed no injustice, lest he leave behind much to be answered for:
He conquered the fierce not by striking them, but by praying. <note>Jehoshaphat is remembered for his judicial reforms and for a miraculous victory over a coalition of enemies achieved through prayer and song rather than combat (2 Chronicles 20).</note>

### 39. Jehoram.

Though safe, he feared; and in bitter circumstances, he grew fierce.
Thus, at last, the kingdoms pay for the crimes of the royalty. <note>original: "Ioram." Jehoram's reign was marked by the loss of territories and a gruesome death by disease, interpreted as divine punishment.</note>

### 40. 41. 42. Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah.

Are these to be numbered among the living, or among the silent dead?
They were unworthy, even of their own praise.
Though at first they may have done worthy things, consider those whom
The oblivion of history weighs down to have never lived or existed at all. <note>The author groups these three kings together because their reigns ended in assassination or spiritual failure, suggesting they are "forgotten" by God or history.</note>

### 43. Uzziah.

Swollen with pride from his victories, he burned holy incense at the Altar;
Because of this, he became a living corpse. <note>original: "Ozia." Uzziah (or Azariah) attempted to usurp the role of the priests by offering incense. He was immediately struck with leprosy ("a living corpse") and lived in isolation for the rest of his life (2 Chronicles 26).</note>

44. Jeho-
