<meta>This page continues the chronological catalog of biblical figures, specifically the Kings of Judah following the reign of Jehoshaphat. It maintains the poetic style of couplets summarizing the moral character and fate of each ruler.</meta>

### 44. *Jotham.*

He established the mutual duties by which those nurtured might be protected, and he might nurture those who protect: the gifts of the plowshare and the sword. <note>Jotham is remembered for both his building projects and his military successes; the "plow and sword" represent the balance of civil industry and national defense.</note>

### 45. *Ahaz.*

This man taught the Sun to speak and marked the shadows; despoiling himself, he acted so that, once conquered, he might not be plundered further. <note>original: "spolians." Ahaz stripped the Temple of its gold to pay tribute to the King of Assyria.</note> Having shut God away, he, lost himself, loses all: happy in one thing alone—that though a reprobate himself, he gave birth to a righteous son. <note>Ahaz closed the doors of the Temple (2 Chronicles 28:24). The "righteous son" is his successor, Hezekiah.</note>

### 46. *Hezekiah.*

What is solid on Earth? If a sundial marks one’s life, as many small lines as the shadow touches, it kills. <note>This refers to the sign given to Hezekiah when he was ill: the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz moved backward ten steps as a promise that his life would be extended (Isaiah 38).</note>

### 47. *Manasseh.*

The Evening Star of the East <note>original: "Hesper Eoi." A poetic way of describing Manasseh’s late-life repentance after a long period of darkness.</note> corrects by his example those whom he once seized; that he might grieve longer, he rules the world longer. <note>Manasseh had the longest reign of any King of Judah (55 years), much of which was spent in idolatry before his eventual repentance in captivity.</note>

### 48. *Amon.*

He divides his age between vices and virtues: at last he lies among flowers, but without fruit. <note>Amon followed his father’s early path of idolatry but was assassinated before he could find the "fruit" of repentance.</note>

### 49. *Josiah.*

He alone neither committed crimes nor endured them: whether he conquered by falling is a matter of doubt. <note>Josiah was a great reformer king who died in battle at Megiddo; the poet questions if his death in battle was a form of spiritual victory.</note>

### 50. *Eliakim & Jehoahaz.*

One subverted the kingdom, surpassing the former; this one lives in a tomb, while that one, once dead, is cast out. <note>original: "Eliacim & Ioachaz." Eliakim (Jehoiakim) was known for his wickedness and was denied a proper burial, while Jehoahaz died in exile in Egypt.</note>

### *Zedekiah.*

He lived among deaths; deprived of his eyes and his children, he did not see the City while within his own city. <note>original: "Sedecia." After the fall of Jerusalem, the Babylonians killed Zedekiah's sons before his eyes and then blinded him, fulfilling the prophecy that he would be brought to Babylon but not see it.</note>

### *Susanna.*

For her, while she wavered between the dangers of life and reputation, the truth shone forth, and she broke through the clouds, triumphant. <note>Susanna is a figure from the Book of Daniel (Apocrypha) who was falsely accused of adultery but saved from execution by Daniel’s wisdom.</note>

### 51. *Jeconiah.*

The vast palace falls, now nothing but smoke and shadow: what homeland could he leave behind, who had already cast out God? <note>original: "Iechonia." Also known as Jehoiachin, he was taken captive to Babylon, marking the end of the independent Davidic monarchy.</note>

# V.

## The World’s Old Age. THE SOLITARIES. <note>The "World's Old Age" refers to the fifth or sixth "Age of the World" in traditional Christian historiography, representing the period from the Babylonian Exile until the birth of Christ. "Solitaries" likely refers to these figures being private citizens or "solitary" leaders rather than reigning kings.</note>

### 52. Salatiel. <note>Shealtiel, the father or uncle of Zerubbabel.</note>

This man rules himself while he serves under harsh reins:
->And for his own people, he conquered three leaders by weeping.<-

### 53. Zorobabel. <note>Zerubbabel, the leader who led the first wave of Jewish exiles back from Babylon and laid the foundations of the Second Temple.</note>

Prayers bend hard things, and ripen all things for Heaven:
->Whoever receives God has done enough in every place.<-

### 54. Abiud. <note>Abiud, a descendant of Zerubbabel mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:13).</note>

This child is the first to be born outside the city of Babylon,
->He is famous for both his trowel and his sword.<- <note>This refers to the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls; the builders famously held a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other to defend against enemies (Nehemiah 4:17-18).</note>
With the former, he performs the sacred work beneath the world's walls,
->With his sword drawn, he repelled hostile threats.<-

### Ezra. <note>original: "Esdræ." Ezra the Priest and Scribe, credited with restoring the Torah to the people of Israel after the exile.</note>

He gave eyes the power to hear, and made the fingers 
Speak; the written tablet notes the feelings of the soul.
Indeed, through this the world lived again, once the night was driven away,
->While it reads of itself and its origins therein.<- <note>Ezra is traditionally credited with standardizing the Hebrew script and the biblical canon, allowing the "fingers to speak" through writing and the "eyes to hear" through reading.</note>

### 55. 56. Eliazim, Azor. <note>Ancestors of Jesus listed in Matthew 1:13-14.</note>

Born from unknown parents so that Jesus might be born,
->He wished to be ruled by these men, rather than to be read about.<- <note>A poetic observation that very little is recorded in scripture about these specific individuals other than their place in the genealogy of the Messiah.</note>

### 57. Sadach. <note>Sadoc, another figure from the lineage of Christ.</note>

He soothed God by weeping with tears instead of incense:
->The weeping of the desert was an eloquent tongue.<-

### 58. Achim.

He laughed and wept by turns, perhaps because of a stepmother;
->He held back neither his joys nor his tears.<-

### The 70 Interpreters and Ben Sira. <note>original: "LXX. Interpp. Syracides." The "LXX" refers to the Septuagint, the seventy (or seventy-two) scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek. "Syracides" refers to Ben Sira, author of the Book of Sirach.</note>

A single head presided over these hands, and a single 
Refinement <note>original: "Lima," literally a "file" used for polishing.</note> over the books; because there was one mind among many.

### 59. 60. Eliud. Eleazar. <note>The final names in the lineage before Matthan and Jacob.</note>

Martyrium pressed upon them; hence, beneath the walls 
Of the city of Bethlehem, they undergo an exile greater than they deserved.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of figures from the Second Temple period. # VI. Next Age... <note>The heading "VI. Ne" is likely a fragment of "VI. Next Age" or "New Testament context," signaling the final era before the birth of Christ.</note>

->Eleazar the Martyr.<- <note>Eleazar was an elderly scribe who chose to die rather than eat pork or pretend to eat it, as recorded in 2 Maccabees 6.</note>

He preferred to be given as food to death than to feed on forbidden foods:
An old man, he did not wish to be a cause of stumbling for the young.
Whole, he was unable to support his falling fatherland,
But broken, he could; yet he does not entirely die. <note>original: "nec tamen omnis obit." A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s phrase "non omnis moriar," suggesting his fame and spirit live on through his sacrifice.</note>

->The Mother of the Maccabees.<- <note>The unnamed woman who encouraged her seven sons to accept martyrdom rather than renounce their faith, before dying herself (2 Maccabees 7).</note>

This distaff <note>original: "Colus." The distaff was a tool for spinning wool, here used as a symbol for womanhood or the female domestic sphere.</note> is to be numbered among great trophies;
Let the mother be well known for her own martyrdom.
Watching heroes, a Hero herself watched by tyrants;
For as often as a son died, she herself gave birth. <note>The poet suggests that each son's death was like a new spiritual birth into heaven.</note>

->Razis.<- <note>Razis was an elder of Jerusalem who committed suicide in a gruesome manner to avoid capture and humiliation by the Syrian army (2 Maccabees 14).</note>

This man is a new Tityos, <note>original: "Titius." In Greek mythology, Tityos was a giant whose liver was perpetually eaten by vultures. The comparison likely refers to Razis’s act of pulling out his own entrails.</note> rushing headlong for Liberty:
That was done with virtue as his leader; but it is shameful and wicked to follow the example. <note>The author praises Razis's bravery but, following traditional Christian theology, condemns the act of suicide itself.</note>

<margin>priest;</margin>
->Mattathias.<- <note>The priest who sparked the Maccabean Revolt by killing a royal official and an apostate Jew at an altar.</note>

He was a leader without a people, perhaps a Priest without a temple;
Both the judge and the executioner of the one he found guilty.
He sounds the trumpets with his voice, bartering his life
For religion; he makes a banner from his dagger.

->Judas Maccabeus I.<- <note>The most famous of Mattathias's sons, a brilliant military commander.</note>

Twice a leader, in sacred and military affairs, he performed
Greater deeds abroad than seemed possible, but he perished by treachery at home.

->Jonathan II.<- <note>The successor to Judas, who secured the high priesthood and leadership through diplomacy.</note>

He had divine strength, and a wisdom greater than fate;
The Lord fought for him, and he fought for God.
But by "Hellenizing" <note>original: "græciſſando." Adopting Greek customs or participating in Greek politics.</note> with the Greeks, he paid the contribution with blood:
Such a lot often awaits victors. <note>Jonathan was eventually captured and killed through the treachery of the Syrian general Tryphon.</note>

->Eleazar III.<- <note>Eleazar Avaran, another brother, who died at the Battle of Beth-zechariah.</note>

He preferred to be crushed beneath a beast rather than endure a tyrant;
And the defeated elephant supplied the ivory. <note>Eleazar died by stabbing a war elephant from below, causing it to fall and crush him. The "ivory" here is a metaphor for the glory he won in death.</note>

->Simon IV.<- <note>The last surviving brother, who established the Hasmonean dynasty.</note>

He fell by treachery, deceived at a friendly table;
Thus he gave himself, his sons, and his own people to the fatherland. <note>Simon was assassinated at a banquet by his son-in-law, Ptolemy.</note>

->John Hyrcanus.<- <note>The son of Simon, who expanded the kingdom and served as High Priest.</note>

He cut down the brigands, a vigorous warrior in arms,
And rebuilt the walls; that was the height of his praises.
After him no one, after everyone he himself is proven:
His entire eulogy is expressed in a trilogy. <note>According to the historian Josephus, Hyrcanus was the only leader to hold the three highest honors: the government of the nation, the high priesthood, and the gift of prophecy.</note>

-> VI. <-
-> The New Age. THE SAINTS. <-

-> 61. St. Panther & St. Mathan. <- <note>Panther and Mathan appear in traditional Christian genealogies, such as those by John of Damascus, as ancestors of the Virgin Mary.</note>
They fled the pride of the Tyrant toward the sea of Bethlehem:
In this case, the best kind of war is surely a noble flight.

-> 62. St. Barpanther & St. Jacob. <- <note>Barpanther (literally "Son of Panther") and Jacob are further links in the ancestral line leading to Joseph and Mary.</note>
They show the Virgin ship to the heavenly Pilot,
Ready to set sail through a more favorable channel.

-> 63. St. Joachim & St. Anne. <- <note>Traditional names for the parents of the Virgin Mary.</note>
These two fathered the High Priest of kings and a royal grandson,
Both being famous for their royal and sacred lineage:
So that they might shape a sacred king from this endowed peak,
Marveling that they are numbered among the Grandparents of the Deity.

-> St. Joseph. <-
The child rules the world, the mother rules him, and the Spouse <note>Joseph</note> rules her:
Does he not possess the August One <note>original: "Augustum," referring to the majestic Christ</note> in his own house?

-> St. Mary, the Virgin Mother of God. <-
Daughter of GOD, Spouse and Lady of the Son, servant of the Thunderer, <note>original: "tonantis." A classical epithet for Jupiter used here for the Christian God.</note>
She joined heavenly things to earthly, with GOD acting.
Jehovah preserved the virgin flower for the mother;
She herself preserved the flower of the virgin for God.

-> St. John the Baptist. <-
As a herald, no one was both greater and lesser than him, <note>A reference to Matthew 11:11, where Jesus says no one born of woman is greater than John, yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.</note>
No one was more silent, yet no one was so eloquent.
He is the evening of the Morning Star, and also the Morning Star of the Sun:
He teaches that he survives even his severed head.

-> JESUS CHRIST, the God-Man, <-
-> Savior of the World. <-
Whither shall he proceed, who approaches You, the final goal of all things,
The Omega and Alpha <note>original: "Omega & Alpha." The last and first letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing Christ as the beginning and the end.</note> of the sacred book?
Whoever wanders from this path is lost to the whole of Heaven;
He goes rightly, whoever prepares his mind to strive toward this one.
In You, therefore, I halt my course; in You let my undertaking end,
And for You I fix this retired pen of my work. <note>original: "Emeritumque operis hunc Tibi figo stilum." The author is signaling the completion of his manuscript by "retiring" his pen.</note>

<meta>This page continues the poetic descriptions of the Holy Family, expanding on the themes introduced on the previous page regarding Mary and Joseph. # More fully, these things are from EMANUELE TESAURO. <note>Emanuele Tesauro was a famous 17th-century Jesuit rhetorician and poet.</note>

## Icon of MARY, the Virgin Mother of God.

Luke, the sculptor, had fashioned her in the house of Loreto; <note>Refers to the tradition that St. Luke the Evangelist was an artist who created the first icons of Mary; Loreto is the site of the Holy House of Mary.</note>
it will be a greater thing if a scribe now records her life.
The supreme power of events transforms the duty of history,
whence the nobility of her Lineage comes to be noted.
She who bore this unwed woman, illustrious in both stock and branch,
whence she is luxuriant with twenty Thrones.
Yet from a sterile mother; for what should result but a virgin,
from a worn-out Venus <note>original: "Venere effætâ." A classical way of referring to St. Anne’s old age and miraculous conception of Mary.</note>, thereafter dedicated to GOD?
She herself kept her virginal honor for God, and God kept it for her,
and the gift she offered to God, she herself received.
She entered a happy marriage with the Craftsman; <note>original: "Fabro," referring to Joseph the carpenter.</note> thence
the Virgin becomes a mother, daughter and parent at the same time.
Behold the offspring with the mother, the parent with the divine child,
how each plays in a double and yet single bosom!
So that you might doubt which is born of the other: O great
wonder! She who was born of God herself gave birth to God.
Daughter to God, Spouse and Handmaid of the Son of the Thunderer, <note>original: "Tonantis." A classical epithet for Jupiter used here for the Christian God.</note>
joining heavenly things to earthly, and vice versa.
But she flees to the Egyptians, <note>original: "pharios."</note> now blessed by a double Sun; <note>Referring to the Flight into Egypt; the "double sun" represents the natural sun and the Christ child.</note>
here the frightened Doe <note>Mary</note> hid from the fierce fox <note>Herod</note>.
Here she redoubles her embraces for the boy, hanging in fear,
while she fears to the end the very snares she flees.
Fortunate parent, and yet the most wretched of mothers,
she stood before the cross, suffering a cross likewise.
For after the pious Woman felt the death of her son,
she felt Simeon’s sword enter her very heart. <note>original: "fibras." Referring to the prophecy in Luke 2:35 that a sword would pierce Mary's soul.</note>

## Titles of JOSEPH, Spouse of the Virgin.

Measure the great Craftsman <note>original: "Fabellum," a playful diminutive of "Faber" (craftsman/carpenter).</note> by a triple Title;
he was the Husband of Mary, chosen in all the world.
Happy Marriage! which the favorable Wing <note>original: "Ales," referring to the Angel who appeared to Joseph in dreams.</note> prospers:
a Virgin joined to a Man, and he himself ignorant of the marriage bed.
To whom the Deity was the bridesmaid, the Spirit set aflame by Divinity,
through the Word; this unique torch lacks all smoke.

<keywords>Emanuele Tesauro, Virgin Mary, St. Joseph, Loreto, St. Luke, Flight into Egypt, Simeon's Prophecy, Holy Family, Baroque poetry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the poetic sequence from the previous page, which featured the works of Emanuele Tesauro. While the previous page focused on the Virgin Mary, this page shifts the focus to Saint Joseph, her husband, exploring his unique role as the "Craftsman" (Faber) and foster father of Jesus.</meta>

*These bonds of marriage bound nothing but their minds;*
*equal vows kept them chaste within the bedchamber.*
*You might call it a celibate marriage, and virginity*
*doubled for the spouses; in this way, even the palm tree is said to wed.* <note>A common Baroque metaphor; it was believed that palm trees "married" through the air without physical contact.</note>
*From here a greater Title rises: He is called the Father of JESUS;*
*by nature an uncle, and a stepfather by the marriage bed,*
*and a Father by his duty; he nourished the Divine Stepson,*
*preserving that life which the Deity had given to himself.*
*Thus with his own eyes he "begot" the Lord <note>original: "Iehovam." Tesauro uses the Hebrew name for God here to refer to the Christ child.</note> so many times, a father himself;*
*He who, even by obeying, had made this man a father.*
*Oh, what a pleasing exchange! This one preserves, but that one serves:*
*and the little Ward nourishes his own Nourisher.*
*Son of the House of Jesse; <note>original: "Isaidæ." Referring to Joseph’s royal descent from Jesse, the father of King David.</note> thus add the supreme title:*
*Thus the Craftsman <note>original: "Faber." Usually translated as carpenter, but implies a skilled creator or smith.</note> is the ultimate goal of that Kingdom.*
*Thus the Lineage ascends from the Craftsman to ancestral kings;*
*and every lineage from GOD ends in the Craftsman.*
*The first Adam was the splendor of the Race, Joseph the last;*
*Joseph cuts away the material of the crime which Adam sowed.* <note>A play on words: Adam "planted" the wood/material of sin (the Tree of Knowledge), while Joseph the carpenter "works" the wood to remedy it.</note>
*Nor does God shrink from such labor; for indeed the works*
*of a craftsman are his: to turn the world on a lathe, to hew the fields by hand.*
*To sharpen the mountains into peaks, to carve out little men:*
*so that you might say both the Father and the Son are Craftsmen.*
*Nor does the death of Christ differ from his birth;*
*He lived and died amidst the same craft.*
*For whom the tools of life and death were the same:*
*The tongs and the nails, the hammer and the drill.* <note>Tesauro draws a direct parallel between the carpenter's tools in the workshop and the instruments of the Crucifixion.</note>
*For the Mother, the cradle and the crosses are made from the same wood:*
*thus, by being born, he seemed already to play with his own death.*
*No less a son of Jesse, Joseph already takes hold*
*of his ancestral kingdom in his little hut and workshop.*
*No less does he display his signs of Empire: the axes*
*and the bundles of rods; <note>original: "secures Et fasces." These were the Roman symbols of magisterial power and authority.</note> this boy binds them together with wood.*
*By his own majesty he rules over mortals equally;*
*nor is the omen of his Name far from the Empire.*
*Joseph sounds like "Augustus"; <note>original: "Ioseph Augustum sonat." A piece of wordplay: Joseph (from the Hebrew 'to add/increase') and Augustus (from the Latin 'to increase').</note> just as at one time*
*Rome boasts of its Augustus, so Nazareth boasts of its own.*

<summary>A Baroque poetic meditation on Saint Joseph, emphasizing his royal Davidic lineage and the symbolic connection between his trade as a carpenter and the Passion of Christ. It concludes by comparing Joseph's name to the title of the Roman Emperor Augustus.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Joseph, Holy Family, Carpenter, Craftsman, Jesse, Davidic Lineage, Passion of Christ, Augustus, Nazareth, Emanuele Tesauro</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the poetic sequence dedicated to Saint Joseph and transitions into a series of epigrams concerning Saint John the Baptist and Jesus Christ. It maintains the Baroque obsession with paradox—the silent father, the unborn herald, and the "Goal" who is both first and last.</meta>

*O happy Joseph! Who possesses the Lord of the world*
*under his own roof, and with Him every Good that exists anywhere.*
*For those nursing cares are brought as a grace to Joseph,*
*through whom it is established that gifts come to others from the heavens.* <note>original: "polo." Literally "the pole," used poetically to mean the sky or heaven.</note>

### The Proclamation of JOHN THE BAPTIST. <note>original: "IOHANNIS B. Prœconium." John the Baptist is the "Precursor" or "Herald" of Christ.</note>

*The Divinity is present, the herald of the Divine Power stands near,*
*than whom no one was greater, and no one was less.* <note>A reference to Matthew 11:11, where Jesus says no one born of woman is greater than John, yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.</note>
*The last of the prophets, but the first Martyr by blood:*
*The evening of the Morning Star; <note>original: "Luciferi." Meaning the planet Venus or "Light-Bringer" as it appears before dawn.</note> the morning star of the day itself.*
*How great he would be, Christ marked with His own image;*
*while still lacking light, he saw that God was present.* <note>Refers to the Visitation, where the unborn John "leaped" in Elizabeth's womb upon meeting the pregnant Mary.</note>
*He sanctified the Purifier of the world with the water of purification:*
*Could the Jordan wash the Eridanus <note>The Eridanus is a celestial river/constellation. The poet asks paradoxically if an earthly river (Jordan) could possibly wash a heavenly one (Christ/Eridanus).</note> any better?*
*How small he was compared to the Great One: he reduced himself to nothing;*
*he allowed himself to be increased by heaven by diminishing himself.* <note>Refers to John 3:30: "He must increase, but I must decrease."</note>
*No one was more silent, though no one was more resonant:*
*Scarcely conceived, he thereafter made his father mute.* <note>John's father, Zechariah, was struck dumb by an angel until John's birth.</note>
*Still enclosed in the Womb, he adores the Divinity of the Parent:*
*From the mute one he thereafter learned what he himself must speak.*
*Scarcely able to speak, the deserts made him eloquent:* <note>original: "disertum."</note>
*Nothing but a voice, he terrified his own Kings with his speech.*
*Nay, even having become loud with a severed head,*
*he teaches that he, though dead, now survives death.*
*Thus the herald of life descends to the lowest spirits:* <note>original: "manes." Refers to the souls in the underworld; John is seen as the herald even in Limbo.</note>
*Be silent with your mouths; the Herald is silent, the Redeemer is present.*

### JESUS CHRIST, Son of God and Mary.
### The Goal. <note>original: "Meta." This refers to the turning post in a Roman racecourse, signifying the final destination or the point where everything turns back to its source.</note>

*At last we are set before You, O most merciful Savior,*
*the Beginning and the End; nor is it permitted to go further.*
*For where might he proceed, who approaches You, the ultimate line of things,*
*the supreme Goal of Your own Race?*
*You who, about to count the maternal age among the fathers,*
*reshape the lineage <note>original: "Stemma." A family tree or genealogical scroll.</note> of sixty-three ancestors,*
*You, newer than all, yet the same one who is uniquely most ancient,*
*both greater than the fathers, and later than the newcomers.*
*From You comes Your Nobility, and in You it ends:*
*thus you are known as the goal of divine works.*

<summary>This page contains Baroque Latin poems celebrating Saint Joseph's domestic holiness, John the Baptist's role as the paradoxical herald of Christ, and Jesus Christ as the final "Meta" or goal of human genealogy and divine creation.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Joseph, John the Baptist, Jesus Christ, Genealogy, Paradox, Jordan River, Eridanus, Martyrdom, Zechariah, Salvation History</keywords>

--- Page 380 ---
<meta>This page continues the poetic reflections on the Incarnation, shifting focus from John the Baptist to Jesus Christ himself as the "Meta" (the goal, boundary, or turning point) of all human history and divine law. It picks up from the previous page's discussion of the transition from the old world to the new.</meta>

*And with a celestial status, you join mortal things to Heaven;*
*The one thing that was missing from all things: Man and GOD.*
*Born at the Solstice <note>The Winter Solstice, traditionally associated with Christmas, marking the point where days begin to lengthen.</note> in the depth of night, as the year was waning;*
*Thus you likewise establish the goal of Time itself.*
*When you drive away our darkness and, with the Sun led back,*
*You renew the fallen seasons of the new year:*
*Truly a double Janus, <note>Janus was the two-faced Roman god of beginnings, gates, and transitions, looking both to the past and the future.</note> you are seen in both worlds,*
*And you cause us now to keep a holiday of peace.*
*In you, Honor places its goal; the Court supplicates you;*
*And entering the stable, the royal purple <note>A reference to the Three Kings or Magi, whose "purple" robes represent royalty.</note> worships upon the ground.*
*For what pride could display itself beyond that stable?*
*Where hay serves as a bridle, <note>original: "frænum ubi dat fœnum." A Latin pun on the words for bridle (fraenum) and hay (foenum).</note> lest any swollen hearts should burst.*
*Behold the Mathematicians! <note>original: "Mathematicos." In the 17th century, this term often referred to astronomers or astrologers, here meaning the Magi.</note> They find a Star in the manger,*
*Which others note is supported by the stars beneath the axis of the sky.*
*Wisely, therefore, they threw their crowns before your feet,*
*Knowing to end their journey here, where Honor just begins.*
*The boundary of the Mosaic law, the harshest decrees*
*You circumcised, O Hebrew <note>original: "Heber." Referring to Eber, the traditional ancestor of the Hebrew people.</note> cut in the flesh.*
*From here you even marked the boundaries of the Synagogue’s unpleasant enclosures;*
*The boundary-stone placed in the field was a sharp knife.*
*You are the goal of Wisdom, <note>original: "Sophiæ."</note> for with you as the Infant Teacher,*
*The learned fathers dedicated themselves as your pupils.*
*You are the boundary of the Stygian realm, you conquer the Evil Demon;*
*You force Lucifer <note>In this context, the fallen "Light-Bringer" or Satan.</note> to retreat to the western regions.*
*You are the goal of Crimes, you who wash away all filth,*
*And willingly cleanse the unclean with your blood.*
*In you the forefathers hoped, the goal of their prayers,*
*You who are always and everywhere the desire of the pious.*
*You are also the goal of death, who prepared life through death:*
*Death, swallowed up, lies conquered by your own funeral.*
*You are also the goal of the heavens, carrying us with you to the stars,*
*And you open an easy way to Heaven from the earth.*
*In you, therefore, I halt my course; for you I fix my tablet; <note>A "tabella" or votive tablet was a plaque left at a shrine to fulfill a vow or offer thanks.</note>*
*So that all things may return to Him, from whom all things are accustomed to come.*

## The Proclamation of JOHN THE BAPTIST

The Divinity is present; the herald of the Divine Godhead stands near,
*Than whom no one was greater, and no one was less.* <note>A reference to Matthew 11:11, where Jesus says no one born of woman is greater than John, yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.</note>
The last of the prophets, but the first Martyr in blood:
*The evening of the Morning Star; the morning star of the day itself.* <note>John is the "evening" that ends the Old Testament era and the "morning star" that announces the "Day" of Christ.</note>
How great he shall be, Christ marked with his own image:
*Still lacking light <note>original: "Lucis adhuc expers," referring to John being in the womb during the Visitation.</note>, he saw that God was present.*
He consecrates the Purifier of the world with the purifying wave:
*Could the Jordan better wash the Eridanus?* <note>The Eridanus was a mythical great river or constellation; here it represents the vastness of Christ being baptized in the humble Jordan.</note>
How small a man from how great a God: he reduced himself to nothing;
*He gave himself, increased from heaven, by diminishing himself.*
No one was more silent, when no one was more resounding:
*Scarcely conceived, he had then made his father mute.* <note>Refers to the story of Zechariah, John's father, who was struck mute until the child's birth.</note>
Still enclosed in the Womb, he adores the Godhead of his Parent:
*From the mute one he learned, thereafter, what he himself must speak.*

*Nothing but a voice, he terrified his Kings with his words.*
Nay even, having become a clamorous witness by his severed head,
*He teaches that he, though dead, now survives death.*
Thus the herald of life descends to the lowest spirits:
*Favor him with your silence; the Herald is silent, for the Redeemer is present.*

## JESUS CHRIST, Son of God and Mary
### The Goal

We are presented at last to You, O most merciful Savior,
*The Beginning and the End; it is not permitted to go further.*
For where might he proceed, who approaches You, the ultimate line of things,
*The supreme <term>Goal</term> <note>original: "Meta." In Latin, a meta is the turning post or finish line in a racecourse; here it signifies Christ as the climax of history.</note> of Your Lineage.*
